pages.title: App or Workflow
pages.description: Whether a request is a View, an App, an App action, a `code` action or a Workflow, as one decision table with a worked row, the route for outside data and the order to build in.
body: The line between an App and a Workflow:

> An App shows data and lets the person using it do one thing at a time. Anything that is a process (several steps, a schedule, history, notifications, rules business users change) is a Workflow the App starts with a button. A live read through a Connection respects the viewer's rights. Stored data read through an App is shared with its audience.
## The decision table

| What                                                     | Use when                                                                                                                                             | Not when                                                                                              | Runs as                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Who sees the result                                                                                                              | The sign to switch                                                                                                                                              |

| View (`show_view`)                                       | A table, chart or overview that belongs to one answer                                                                                                | The person wants to come back to it or work with it                                                   | Nothing runs: it shows what the agent read as the person in this conversation                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Whoever sees the conversation                                                                                                    | "Keep this" or "show me this again": an App                                                                                                                     |

| App (`workspace.open`, then `app.save`)                  | A person comes back to see data and do one thing at a time: a list, a form, a dashboard                                                              | The work is a process: several steps, a schedule, history, notifications, rules business users change | Its screens run in the viewer's browser and reach data only through its named actions                                                                                                                                                                                               | The builder at once, builders of the workspace in the draft, the workspace once a person publishes it                            | A second step that needs the first, a schedule or a run history: a Workflow the App starts                                                                      |

| App action (`sql`, `connection`, `decision`, `workflow`) | One call per click: read or insert in a Data Store, call one operation of a Connection, start a published Workflow, decide a waiting `approval` step | One call needs the answer of another                                                                  | Live Connection reads use the viewer's rights. A published `sql` action on a Data Store uses the store's app role, with the store right checked against the publisher; viewers need no right on the store. A `workflow` action starts a run that acts as the Workflow's own account | The viewer who called it; what it writes, everyone who reads that Data Store                                                     | Two dependent calls: a `code` action for a read, a Workflow for work that acts                                                                                  |

| `code` action                                            | A read for the viewer that combines or checks the answers of the App's own actions on the server                                                     | It needs a call that depends on another, a network request, or a schedule                             | Its reads and its one write as the viewer; the script itself calls nothing                                                                                                                                                                                                          | The viewer                                                                                                                       | A `code` action that needs a dependent call becomes a Workflow                                                                                                  |

| Workflow                                                 | A process, or work that acts on its own: start a case, send a letter, check every month                                                              | A read that must respect the viewer's rights                                                          | Its own account (the service principal it runs as), never the viewer. A published Workflow runs through                                                                                                                                                                             | Who may read the Workflow sees its runs; what it writes into a Data Store, the readers of that store, for example through an App | A read for one viewer: back into the App as an `sql`, `connection` or `code` action                                                                             |

| Worked row: the Buchhaltungscheck                        | Five checks of each Mandant's bookkeeping every month, and an extra run when someone asks                                                            | Checks in the App's browser code                                                                      | A scheduled Workflow with a manual start: it reads the accounting source through an `http_api` Connection, runs the five checks as steps and writes findings per Mandant and month into a Data Store; missing data is "nicht prüfbar"                                               | The App lists the findings through `sql` actions and starts an extra run with a `workflow` action                                | A viewer who may see only some Mandanten: say who the App is for, under the [build rules for data scope](/configure/release-config/#build-rules-for-data-scope) |

Not in this release: the `decision` action and the `code` action. The build refuses `kind: code`; until it comes, logic that combines reads for the viewer stays in the App's browser code, and anything that is a process is still a Workflow.
## Outside data

An API that needs a key, has no CORS or is also used by a Workflow is an `http_api` Connection, called through a `connection` action ([connect a system](/configure/build/#connecting-an-outside-system)). A public API only the App calls is a host in the App's `externalHosts`. In this release such a host takes effect when the App is published: its draft and the preview cannot reach it yet.
## The order to build in

One conversation builds the Data Store, the Workflow and the App, the App last, and the agent says what it creates before it does. The App comes last because its actions name the Data Store and the published Workflow. [Build an App](/apps/build/) says how to write each action; [Workflows](/automate/workflows/) says how a person tests and publishes one.

pages.title: Build an App
pages.description: How an agent writes an App's folder, opens it in the preview, saves it as an App and gives it named actions on a Connection, a Data Store or a Workflow, and how the App's code calls them.
body: This page is the technical guide an agent follows. [Apps for people](/automate/apps/) says what a person clicks.

An agent writes an App's files in its execution workspace and shows the folder beside the conversation with `workspace.open`. Opening shows and does nothing more: it keeps nothing and creates no App. When the person asks to keep it, `app.save` makes it an App with a draft, and asks the person nothing: the App is in their Apps list at once and opens at its draft. A person publishes the draft; an agent never publishes.

A quick preview may show data the agent wrote into it. Live data comes through named actions: one file per action in the folder `actions/`, which the build compiles into the manifest. The browser calls an action by its name and nothing else: it never calls a Connection, a Data Store or a Workflow directly, and it never holds a key.
## Sandbox, forms and personal state
Apps run with `allow-scripts allow-forms allow-downloads`, without `allow-same-origin`.
A form's validation and `submit` event work. Handle `submit` with `event.preventDefault()`
and call a named action; `form-action 'none'` blocks navigation to every form target.
Inline `onclick` and `onsubmit` attributes are refused: use `addEventListener` or React handlers.
An App or unsaved preview gets a `window.localStorage`-compatible shim before its first script runs.
It reads only the current person's state in that App; it never exposes the platform's browser
storage. The state is stored on the instance, survives reloads and App revisions, and is erased
with the App or the person's account. Native `getItem`, `setItem`, `removeItem`, `clear`,
`key`, `length` and property access work. Writes are synchronous in memory and persisted
in batches about every 250 ms, with the last write to each key winning. A
`catalyst-storage-error` event reports a persistence failure. A builder's draft preview
shares the same per-person state with the published App, so trying a draft can change
that person's preferences in the published App.
There is no `sessionStorage` shim: accessing it throws `SecurityError` in the sandbox.
The `localStorage` shim is not a native `Storage` object: `localStorage instanceof Storage`
is false. On `pagehide` and when the document becomes hidden, it tries to flush the batch,
but this is best effort. A write is lost if the page closes before its batch is saved.
An immediate reload within the batching window can also lose the write; await kit
`storage.set` before navigating or reloading when the save must persist.
Prefer the JSON API in kit **1.6.0**, whose save waits for persistence and rejects on failure:
```ts
import { storage } from "@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit";
const filters = await storage.get("filters"); // null until set
await storage.set("filters", { status: "open" });
Personal state holds at most 64 KiB of UTF-8 JSON per App and person. Catch storage errors
and show a retry beside the action. An unsaved preview keeps temporary in-memory state only.
When running outside the App runtime, catch `SecurityError` from native storage and keep rendering.
Use a **Data Store** and named actions for shared business records such as leave requests;
personal storage is for preferences and a person's unfinished input, not shared records.
Network requests are restricted by `connect-src`: an unsaved preview or a draft has no
outside network, and a published App reaches only reviewed hosts declared in its manifest.
Where the release turns on [outside hosts in a draft](/configure/release-config/#outside-hosts-in-a-draft),
the builder can allow a declared host for their own preview with one click.
Use named actions for Connections and Data Stores, never fetch the instance API directly.
Bundle fonts and libraries or use the kit; public CDNs do not load. When diagnosing a failure,
check form handlers, storage availability and the declared network policy before blaming the data.
## Preparing data scope
Follow the [build rules for data scope](/configure/release-config/#build-rules-for-data-scope).
- Read per-Mandant tables and group aggregates by the Mandant column.
- Keep Mandant data out of a free-SQL Knowledge Base.
- Say who an App is for when it serves only part of the firm. Everyone in that audience must be allowed to see every Mandant the shared source credential can read.
## The folder
```text
<folder>/
app.yaml                    the manifest
index.html                  a plain HTML App: its entry
src/routes/__root.tsx       a React App: TanStack Router file routes
src/routes/index.tsx
src/components/*.tsx        optional
actions/<name>.action.yaml  a call of a Connection's operation, or the start of a Workflow
actions/<name>.sql          a statement on the App's Data Store
assets/                     images and other static files

Write the files with the workspace file tools, then open the folder that holds `app.yaml` with `workspace.open`. An open builds the folder and shows it. It answers the revision, or the build errors with file and line: fix the files and open it again. A single HTML file opens as it is, and a folder without `app.yaml` opens its `index.html`. `app.save` with the same path and a name keeps what the preview shows as an App; each later `app.save` of the same path in the conversation writes the App's next draft revision, so keep working in the same folder and open it before each save.

A React App imports only its own files, `react`, `react-dom`, `@tanstack/react-router` and `@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit`. Nothing is installed. A plain HTML App names `entry: index.html`; inline scripts work, inline event handler attributes such as `onclick` do not.
Put fonts and libraries in the App's folder or use the kit's; an outside address (Google Fonts, Adobe Fonts or a CDN) will not load.

Kit 1.6.0 supplies Inter (400, 600, 700), Lora (400, 700 and 400 italic), IBM Plex Mono (400, 600) and Bungee (400), with Latin coverage including German: link `/app-runtime/kit/1.6.0/fonts/fonts.css` and use the family name in CSS. The font sources and licences are in `/app-runtime/kit/1.6.0/fonts/README.md`.
A React App imports its CSS from a route (for example, `import "../fonts.css"`); in that CSS, write `@import url("/app-runtime/kit/1.6.0/fonts/fonts.css");` and `body { font-family: Lora; }`.
## The manifest
`app.yaml` names everything the App reaches. A Connection or a Data Store that the manifest does not list cannot be called.
| Key                   | What it holds                                                                                                                            |
| `id`                  | Lowercase letters, digits and `-`, at most 63 characters.                                                                                |
| `name`                | The name people read.                                                                                                                    |
| `description`, `icon` | Optional.                                                                                                                                |
| `kit`                 | The exact kit version. Use `1.6.0` for a new App; actions on a Connection need `1.1.0` or later and `workflow` actions `1.3.0` or later. |
| `entry`               | `index.html` for a plain HTML App. A React App leaves it out.                                                                            |
| `connections`         | The Connections the App's actions call, by name.                                                                                         |
| `dataStores`          | The Data Store the App's `sql` actions use: `{ name, minSchema }`. One at most while the App has `sql` actions.                          |
| `actions`             | One line per `sql` action: `{ name, file, effect }`. Optional for the other kinds.                                                       |
| `externalHosts`       | Internet hosts the browser code may fetch from, such as `api.example.com`.                                                               |
Any other key is refused. `pages` is derived from `src/routes/` and is not written by hand.
## Named actions
An action's name is the name of its file without the ending: `actions/load-bookings.action.yaml` is the action `load-bookings`. A name has lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`.
| Kind         | File                                                                  | Reaches                                          | Effect                       |
| `connection` | `actions/<name>.action.yaml` with `connection`, `operation`, `effect` | One operation of a Connection the manifest lists | Written in the file          |
| `sql`        | `actions/<name>.sql` plus a line under `actions` in `app.yaml`        | The Data Store the manifest lists                | Written in the manifest line |
| `workflow`   | `actions/<name>.action.yaml` with `workflow`                          | A run of the published Workflow                  | Always `changing`            |

Every call runs as the person who looks at the App, through the platform's policy and audit. In the published App the viewer needs the right to use the App; in its draft, the right to write it. Beside that, for a `connection` action the viewer needs the right to use the Connection, for a `workflow` action the right to use the Workflow. An `sql` action of a published App needs no right on the Data Store: the person who published the App answered for it.
### A `connection` action
```yaml
connection: accounting_source
operation: list_bookings
effect: reading
description: The bookings of one client in one month.
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
client: { type: string, maxLength: 40 }
month: { type: string, description: "The month as YYYY-MM" }
required: [client]
mapping:
clientId: "{{client}}"
period: "{{month}}"
- `connection` is the Connection's name, which `connections` in `app.yaml` lists.

- `operation` is the name of one operation of that Connection, exactly as the Connection lists it. For an MCP Connection that is the name of the server's tool. Only an operation an editor accepted on the Connection's page, enabled and offered to Apps (exposure `bridge`), can be called. `platform.assets.operations` with `for: app` lists the operations an App may call, as far as the person may use them, each named `connection.<connection>.<operation>` with its effect: write the two parts as `connection` and `operation`. `platform.assets.get` on the Connection shows all its accepted operations with name, effect and exposure, where the person may read the Connection. Without these tools, ask the person for the operation's name.
- `effect` is `reading` or `changing`, as the operation was accepted. A `reading` action that stands for a changing operation is refused.

- `input.schema` declares the parameters the browser passes: JSON Schema with `type: object` and `properties` of type `string`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean` or `array` of one of them. A parameter not declared is refused at the call.

- `input.mapping` is the operation's input. A value `"{{name}}"` stands for the parameter `name`; every other value is passed as written. A mapping computes nothing: a text that holds `{{` other than as the whole value is refused by the build. A parameter the caller leaves out leaves out its key.

The answer's `result` is the MCP tool's result: `{ content, structuredContent }`, where `content` is a list of blocks such as `{ type: "text", text }` and `structuredContent` is there when the tool gives one. A tool that answers an error rejects the call.
### An `sql` action
The statement is one file. Its first lines declare the parameters, and the statement names each as `$name`:
```sql
-- @param client text optional
select id, client_id, title, created_at
from findings
where $client is null or client_id = $client
order by created_at desc
limit 100
The manifest says what the statement does, with one line for it:
```yaml
actions:
- { name: list-findings, file: actions/list-findings.sql, effect: reading }

- A parameter line is `-- @param <name> <type>`, with `optional` after it where a call may leave it out. A type is `text`, `integer`, `number`, `boolean`, `date` or `timestamp`, or one of them followed by `[]` for a list.
- A `reading` statement is one `SELECT` or `WITH`.
- A `changing` statement is one `INSERT` of one row whose values are all parameters, with `on conflict do nothing` after it where an existing row is skipped.
- A value is bound to its place in the statement and never written into it.

A reading statement answers `{ columns, rows, truncated }`: `rows` is a list of objects by column name, at most 1,000 rows and 2 MiB, and `truncated` says the result was cut; page with `limit` and `offset` parameters. A `numeric` value comes as text. An insert answers `{ table, inserted, skipped }`.
### The Data Store

The App lists its Data Store under `dataStores` in `app.yaml`, by name, with `minSchema` where it needs at least that migration of the store. The `dataStores` module has to be on. Where the App needs a Data Store that does not exist yet, the agent creates its draft in the same conversation with `platform.assets.put` (kind `data_store`, its files `store.yaml` and `migrations/0001_<name>.sql`), after it says what it creates. The draft stays beside the App: the conversation stays about the App, and the person stays on the page they are on. The agent keeps saving the draft from that conversation, and a person publishes it, which applies its migrations. A person can also write a store with `catalyst data-store put`. The statements read and write the tables those migrations made.

An `sql` action runs only in an App: in a preview that is not yet saved a reading `sql` action is refused with `data_store_needs_app`, and a changing one with `draft_safe_mode`. In the App's draft it runs with the viewer's own right on the store: to read it, and for an insert, which the draft simulates, to insert.
### A `workflow` action
```yaml
workflow: monthly-check
description: Checks the bookings of one client.
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
client: { type: string }
required: [client]
mapping:
client: "{{client}}"

`workflow` is the Workflow's name. The mapping makes the input the Workflow declares. The call starts a run of the Workflow's published revision as the viewer, who needs the right to use that Workflow. The answer's `result` is the Workflow Run; follow it with `useWorkflowRun(result.id)` from the kit, or `workflowRuns.get(result.id)` in a plain HTML App. A `workflow` action has no `effect` key and no `connection`; it needs kit `1.3.0` or later.
## Effects, drafts and publishing
A `reading` action runs live everywhere, with the viewer's rights. A `changing` action is carried out only in the published App; before that it runs in safe mode:

- In the draft of an App, a `changing` action of each kind is simulated. It changes nothing and answers `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }`: `message` says what the call would have done, and whether live it would wait for another person's approval; `result` is the input it would have done it with. The call goes through the viewer's rights and the policy as a live call would, so a call that would be refused live is refused here too, and it leaves an Operation Run with the target `dry_run`. Show `message` as it is.

- "Run live once" on the App's Actions list, under "Technical details" on the draft page, carries out the next call of one changing action of the draft for real. A person who may write the App switches it on for themselves; it covers only their own next call of that action, and every save or discard of the draft clears a switch nobody used, so an `app.save` clears it too. A call it sends live that the policy holds for another person's approval is refused with `approval_unavailable`, since a draft cannot wait. An agent cannot switch it on: when the person wants to try a change for real, tell them where the switch is.

- In a preview that is not yet an App, a changing `connection` or `sql` action is refused with the code `draft_safe_mode`, and nothing is called. A `workflow` action answers `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }` as in a draft, but leaves no run.

A changing call passes `{ idempotencyKey }` in the draft as in the published App. The published App carries out every action. An action may ask for a stricter `policy` than the instance sets (`confirm`, `approval` or `deny`), written in the action file or, for an `sql` action, in its manifest line. A call that waits for another person's approval answers `status: "pending_approval"` without a result.

An agent never publishes. Tell the person to publish the draft: with the Publish button on the App's page, or with `catalyst app publish <name> --revision <n> --workspace <id>`. Publishing needs the right `app.publish`, which administrators hold. It checks again what a save checked, and that each Data Store is published, at `minSchema` or later, readable (for an insert, `data_store.insert`) by the person who publishes, and of the App's workspace; a retired store, or one of another workspace, is refused. Guardrails may answer the publish too.

Saving checks what it can: when a save writes the App's draft, it refuses a Connection that does not exist, a Data Store that does not exist, an operation the Connection does not accept and a `reading` action on a changing operation. `app.save` then answers `saved: false` with what was found: fix it, open the folder and save again. Whether the operation is enabled and offered to Apps (exposure `bridge`) is checked only at the call, which is refused as forbidden: check the operation's exposure on the Connection's page first.
## Calling an action from the App

Import `actions` from `@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit`. `actions.call(name, params, options)` calls a named action and answers `{ runId, status, result }`. `result` is what the action answered, as described for each kind above: check its shape before using it. A call that is refused or fails rejects with an `AppCallError`. Show its `message` as it is, since it is the platform's sentence in the viewer's language, and offer no button to try again when `retryable` is false.

A changing call passes `{ idempotencyKey }`: make the key when the person acts, and send the same key again when the answer was lost. In a draft the answer to a changing call is `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }` unless "Run live once" sent it live: show `message`, which says what the published App would have done.
`getContext()` answers the viewer, the locale and, under `can`, what the instance says for each action: `allow`, `confirm`, `approval` or `deny`. The server asks again at every call.
## A complete example

A dashboard for one client of an accounting data source: it reads bookings from the Connection `accounting_source`, lists findings kept in the Data Store `findings`, adds a finding and starts the Workflow `monthly-check`. Replace the names of the Connection, its operation, the Data Store and the Workflow with those of the instance, and the mapping with the input the operation declares.
```yaml title="app.yaml"
id: accounting-dashboard
name: Accounting dashboard
connections:
- accounting_source
dataStores:
- name: findings
actions:
- { name: list-findings, file: actions/list-findings.sql, effect: reading }
- { name: add-finding, file: actions/add-finding.sql, effect: changing }
```yaml title="actions/load-bookings.action.yaml"
connection: accounting_source
operation: list_bookings
effect: reading
description: The bookings of one client in one month.
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
client: { type: string, maxLength: 40 }
month: { type: string, description: "The month as YYYY-MM" }
required: [client]
mapping:
clientId: "{{client}}"
period: "{{month}}"
```sql title="actions/list-findings.sql"
-- @param client text optional
select id, client_id, title, created_at
from findings
where $client is null or client_id = $client
order by created_at desc
limit 100
```sql title="actions/add-finding.sql"
-- @param client text
-- @param title text
insert into findings (client_id, title) values ($client, $title)
```yaml title="actions/run-check.action.yaml"
workflow: monthly-check
description: Checks the bookings of one client.
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
client: { type: string }
required: [client]
mapping:
client: "{{client}}"
```tsx title="src/routes/__root.tsx"
import { createRootRoute, Outlet } from "@tanstack/react-router";
export const Route = createRootRoute({ component: () => <Outlet /> });
```tsx title="src/routes/index.tsx"

export const Route = createFileRoute("/")({ component: Dashboard });

function messageOf(error: unknown): string {
return error instanceof AppCallError ? error.message : "The call failed.";
function Dashboard() {

const [error, setError] = useState<string>();
const [note, setNote] = useState<string>();
const [runId, setRunId] = useState<string>();
const { run } = useWorkflowRun(runId);
const load = () => {
actions
.call("load-bookings", { client: CLIENT, month: "2026-09" })
.then((answer) => setBookings("result" in answer ? answer.result : undefined))
.catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure)));
actions

.then((answer) => setFindings("result" in answer ? answer.result : undefined))
.catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure)));
useEffect(load, []);
const addFinding = () => {
actions

"add-finding",
{ client: CLIENT, title: "Booking without receipt" },
{ idempotencyKey: `add-finding-${Date.now()}` }
.then((answer) => {
// In the App's draft a change is simulated: say what it would have done.
if (answer.status === "dry_run") setNote(answer.message);
else load();
.catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure)));
const startCheck = () => {
actions
.call("run-check", { client: CLIENT }, { idempotencyKey: `run-check-${Date.now()}` })
.then((answer) => {
if (answer.status === "dry_run") {
setNote(answer.message);
return;
const started = answer.result;
if (typeof started === "object" && started !== null && "id" in started) {
setRunId(String(started.id));
.catch((failure: unknown) => setError(messageOf(failure)));
return (
<main>
Client {CLIENT}

<Button onClick={addFinding}>Add finding</Button>
<Button onClick={startCheck}>Run the monthly check</Button>

{JSON.stringify({ bookings, findings }, null, 2)}

## A plain HTML App
The same call from a plain HTML App, with one action on the Connection.
```yaml title="app.yaml"
id: accounting-bookings
name: Accounting bookings
entry: index.html
connections:
- accounting_source
```yaml title="actions/load-bookings.action.yaml"
connection: accounting_source
operation: list_bookings
effect: reading
input:
schema:
type: object
properties:
client: { type: string }
required: [client]
mapping:
clientId: "{{client}}"

<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>

</head>

Bookings
Loading…

import { actions, AppCallError } from "@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit";
const state = document.getElementById("state");
try {
const answer = await actions.call("load-bookings", { client: "10023" });
state.textContent = "";
document.getElementById("rows").textContent = JSON.stringify(answer.result, null, 2);
} catch (error) {

</script>

## When a save fails
The build answers each fault with its file and a sentence that names the fix. The common ones:
- `connection_not_declared`: the action calls a Connection that `connections` in `app.yaml` does not list.
- `data_store_not_declared`: an `sql` action and no `dataStores` in `app.yaml`.
- `key_reserved`: a reserved key, such as `rights`, `requires` or an action of `kind: code`; remove it.
- An `sql` file without its line under `actions`: add `{ name, file, effect }`.
- A YAML file in `actions/` without the ending `.action.yaml`: rename it.
- A missing `connection`, `operation` or `effect` in an action file: add it.
- `sql_statement_not_allowed`: a reading statement that is not one `SELECT` or `WITH`, or a changing one that is not one `INSERT` of parameters.
At a call, `action_unknown` means the manifest of the shown revision has no action of that name: open the folder and save it again after adding the file.

pages.title: Apps for people
pages.description: Ask an agent for an App, keep it as a draft, try its actions safely, run one live once, and publish it for your workspace.
body: An App is a small tool with its own screens, such as a form for new clients or a list of open offers. You get one by asking an agent in a chat. It can show data and, through its actions, read from or write to a connected system, a Data Store or a Workflow.
The German interface shows the labels in quotes. [Build an App](/apps/build/) is the technical guide the agent follows.
## Ask for it in a chat
Describe what you need: who uses it, what it shows, what it should let people do. For example: "Build an app where I can enter a new client and see the last ten."

The agent builds it and shows it beside the chat. **Preview** ("Vorschau") shows it working; **Files** ("Dateien") shows what it is made of. Keep asking for changes in the chat; each one the agent opens is the preview's newest revision.
The preview belongs to its conversation. It cannot change anything in other systems. To keep it, save it as an App.
When you have no App yet, the **Apps** page offers **Build one with the agent** ("Eine mit dem Agenten bauen") and two examples. Each opens the agent with your request already started.
## Keep it as an App
Tell the agent "keep this as an app". It saves the App under the name it was given and asks you nothing.
The App is yours at once: it is in your **Apps** list and opens at its **draft**, with live data. Builders of the workspace see the draft too; nobody else sees it until you share it by publishing.
You can also save it yourself:
1. In the preview's header, click **Save as app** ("Als App speichern").

2. Check the **Name**. It is filled in with the name the App's folder gives itself, its `app.yaml` name or its HTML title, or else the folder's name. The App's address is made from the name, as when the agent saves it, and does not change later.
3. Click **Save** ("Speichern").

After that, each change you ask for in the same chat goes into the App's draft once the agent saves it again. When that did not happen, for example because someone changed the draft elsewhere, the preview offers **Update app** ("App aktualisieren"): **Replace draft** ("Entwurf ersetzen") puts what the preview shows now into the draft.
## Try it safely

Open **Apps** in the main rail and the App, then **Edit** ("Bearbeiten"). The draft opens on its **Preview**. **Technical details** ("Technische Details") beside it shows two more tabs, **Files** and **Actions** ("Aktionen"); your browser keeps them open until you fold them again.
In a draft, nothing changes for real:
- An action that only reads gets real data.

- An action that would change something is **simulated**. It answers with what it would have done and changes nothing. In the **Test** dialog the result says **Not carried out in the draft** ("Im Entwurf nicht ausgeführt").
On the **Actions** tab, **Test** ("Testen") calls one action with input you give.
## Run one action live once
To check that a changing action really works before you publish:

1. On the **Actions** tab, find the action and click **Run live once** ("Einmal live ausführen"). The button shows on actions that change something and are allowed to run without someone else's approval.
2. It now says **Your next call runs live.** ("Dein nächster Aufruf läuft live.")
3. Use the action once, in the preview or with **Test**. That one call is carried out for real, under the instance's usual rules. The next one is simulated again.

The switch is yours alone: it does not affect anyone else trying the draft. Saving or discarding the draft clears it. A call that would need someone else's approval is refused here, because a draft cannot wait for one.
## Publish it
1. On the draft, click **Publish** ("Veröffentlichen").
2. The dialog names the workspace that gets it, such as "Everyone in Sales gets revision 3 when they open the app.", and lists the Connections it uses and the outside hosts it calls.
3. Click **Publish** ("Veröffentlichen") in the dialog.

Now everyone in the workspace finds it on the **Apps** page, and up to five published Apps appear under **Apps** in the main rail. In a published App, every action runs for real, with the rights of the person using it. An action that starts a Workflow is the exception: the Workflow runs with its own account.
An agent never publishes. A person decides.

Later changes go to the draft again. The App shows **Unpublished changes** ("Unveröffentlichte Änderungen") until you publish them. **Discard** ("Verwerfen") throws the draft away, and **Revisions** ("Revisionen") under **More actions** ("Weitere Aktionen") shows every saved state.
## Who may do what
- Everyone in the workspace can open a published App.

- Saving an App, editing the draft, **Run live once** and publishing are rights of the administrator role. They cannot be given to one person. If you do not see **Save as app** or **Publish**, ask an administrator.
- An action reaches only what the person using the App may reach. The App's screens never hold a key: they call actions by name, and the instance makes the call.

pages.title: Workflows
pages.description: Let the platform do work by itself, step by step, on a schedule or when you start it; try it with a test run and publish it.
body: A Workflow is work the platform does by itself, step by step: every morning, or when someone starts it. It runs without a chat. Each step reads or changes something, for example in a connected system or a Data Store.
The German interface shows the labels in quotes.
## Find your Workflows
Click **Workflows** in the main rail. The row shows when the instance has Workflows switched on and you may see at least one, or may write Workflows. The list shows each Workflow with its last run.
Open one to see its page:
- The **Workflow** tab shows the steps as a canvas, from **Starts** ("Startet") at the top down to the last step. A step is marked **Reads data** ("Liest Daten") or **Changes data** ("Ändert Daten").
- The **Runs** tab ("Läufe") lists every run, with what each step did.
- The trigger says when it runs: **Started by hand only** ("Startet nur von Hand") or the schedule, such as "Every day, 07:00 AM" ("Jeden Tag, …").
## Make or change a Workflow

A new Workflow is created with the CLI (`catalyst workflow put <name> --from … --if-revision new`); see [the CLI](/configure/cli/). After that, change it with **Edit with the agent** ("Mit dem Agenten bearbeiten") on its page. A chat opens that is about this Workflow: describe what should change, and every change the agent saves becomes the next draft.

A change is always a **draft** first. The banner says **Draft, not published yet** ("Entwurf, noch nicht veröffentlicht") or **Draft differs from published** ("Entwurf weicht von der veröffentlichten Version ab"). Runs keep using the published version until the draft is published.

The line **Runs as** ("Läuft als") under the heading names the active account by its display label. An unpublished draft shows the account configured in that draft too. No line is shown when that account is disabled or missing.
## Try it with a test run
1. On the draft banner, click **Test run** ("Testlauf").
2. Read the dialog and click **Start test run** ("Testlauf starten").

A test run reads real data, but only what both you and the Workflow may see. Steps that would change something are only simulated: each says what it would have done, and nothing is changed. Each step shows where its call went: **Live**, **Test** or **Simulated** ("Simuliert"). A test run writes no new draft and changes nothing about the published version.
To try one changing step for real:
1. On the page of the test run, select the step.
2. In its panel, click **Run live once** ("Einmal live ausführen").
3. Click **Test again** ("Erneut testen"). That step runs for real once, under the instance's usual rules. The others stay simulated.

A step marked "A published run asks for approval here" needs someone's approval under the instance's rules. A published run stops at this step, because a run cannot wait for an approval. Change the step before you publish.
## Publish it

Click **Publish** ("Veröffentlichen") on the draft banner. The revision becomes the version that runs, by hand and on its schedule. **Discard** ("Verwerfen") takes the draft back to the published version.
A Workflow runs with its own account, not with yours, so it can read and change what you cannot. That is why publishing is held tight: it takes a superadmin.
## Start it by hand

Click **Start now** ("Jetzt starten") on a published Workflow, fill in what it asks for, and click **Start** ("Starten"). The run appears under **Runs**. On a run's page, **Run again** ("Erneut starten") starts the published version once more.
## Who may do what
An administrator gives these rights under **Settings > Instance > Access** ("Einstellungen › Instanz › Zugriff"), for one Workflow:
| Right             | What the Access page says                                                                                            |
| View workflows    | See the Workflow, its steps and its runs.                                                                            |
| Use workflows     | Start the Workflow. It then runs with the Workflow's own rights, not with this person's.                             |
| Edit workflows    | Change the draft of the Workflow. A draft does not run until it is published.                                        |
| Publish workflows | Make a draft the version that runs. Publishing also needs every right of the service principal the Workflow runs as. |
Administrators hold every right. A test run needs the right to edit the Workflow.
## Process rows in batches
An operation marked `batch: true` takes a list or dataset and returns `{ done, failed, failures }`.
`failures` is a dataset of `{ item, code, message }` for retrying individual items. The operation
step completes when the call succeeds, even when some items failed. Messages name the field and
error code, without repeating item values or provider responses.
Use `batch: 500` on a dataset loop to hand each iteration a dataset view: 1,200 rows become
500, 500 and 200 rows. Reference the loop with an empty path to pass that view to an operation,
code step or child Workflow. The loop item limit counts batches; `onItemFailure` still decides
what to do when an iteration itself fails. A batch loop requires a dataset, rather than an
inline list. It shares the parent's objects, permissions and expiry; it does not copy rows.
A view adds `offset` to the dataset reference and reports its own `rowCount`. Its `bytes` is
the parent's upper bound; consumers enforce byte limits against the rows actually read.
## Continue a long run
A long loop can continue in a fresh run when it reaches its step or duration budget.
Set `continueAsNew: { position: offset }` on the loop and declare `offset` as an optional
integer in the Workflow's inputs. The next run receives the next row offset. You can
request a smaller history with `after`, for example `{ position: offset, after: 1000 }`.
For a paged source, add `cursor: id` to pass the last completed row’s `id` as the
position input instead. A nonempty page continues and an empty page finishes the
loop. Map that position input into the source operation’s paging parameter.
The runs list groups these histories into one expandable run. Each part has its own
status and a numbered key. Work and usage count once across the parts. Labels and the
failure policy stay with the original run. A change published between parts applies
to the next part, and the list marks the version change. If the new version refuses
the carried input, that part fails and names the field that needs attention.
Until resume positions and finished-step outputs are carried between histories, publishing
and draft test runs refuse these shapes, naming the step and rule in English and German:
- A write, send, notify, child Workflow start, or loop containing one before a
`continueAsNew` loop at the same or any enclosing level. Reads, triggers and code
steps may precede it; those steps run again in every history.
- A loop after a `continueAsNew` loop at the same or any enclosing level.
- A loop with `concurrency` above 1 enclosing a `continueAsNew` loop, at any depth.
The refusal names both loops: a checkpoint cannot record unfinished sibling items.
Concurrency on the continuing loop itself remains allowed.
- A `limits.stepRuns` budget smaller than the steps before the loop, the loop containers,
one item and the tail together. The refusal states the minimum count and the limit.
A `continueAsNew` loop can be the last loop, with non-loop steps after it. These are
publish-time restrictions pending EW-CAN-RESUME, which will resume at step boundaries
without repeating finished work.
Loop outputs `total`, `done` and `failed` cover the whole continuation chain (one Lauf),
including items finished in earlier histories. Later steps reading `each_x.done` or
`each_x.failed`, and a parent reading its child's output, receive these cumulative totals.
The checkpoint carries only fixed-size counts per loop level; it does not keep item results.

pages.title: Agents and skills in Studio
pages.description: Create, edit, restore and delete agents and skills in Studio, connect outside systems, and read the other lists Studio holds.
body: **Studio** is the area of the interface where agents and skills are made. It stands in the main rail as a row of its own and opens at `/build`. The old address `/admin/config` leads there. Beside **Agents** (German: **Agenten**) and **Skills**, Studio lists **Connections** (**Verbindungen**), **Data stores** (**Datenspeicher**), **Knowledge bases** (**Wissensbasen**) and **Guardrails** (**Leitplanken**), each for a person who may read one. Apps and Workflows are not in Studio: each has a row of its own in the main rail.

Studio works on the [asset API](/reference/api/assets/): it reads a list page by page, reads one asset when its page opens and writes one asset at a time. It never loads the whole set of agents and skills.
## Who sees Studio
The Studio row shows for a person who holds a right on at least one agent or skill:
- `config_assets.read` or `config_assets.write` on the instance, or
- a [grant](/operate/rights-for-one-person/) in a Shared Workspace or on one asset.
A person with no such right has no Studio row, and the address says that Studio is not available.

A grant on one single asset, or on what one workspace owns, is checked by the instance on every read and write. The interface learns only that the person may read some asset of the kind: a read grant gives the Studio row and the list of the kind, which holds the assets the person may read. Such an asset opens read-only. A grant that allows another action and no reading gives no Studio row.

On an instance with the module [`connections`](/configure/modules/#connections) on, Studio also lists Connections for a person who may read every Connection of the instance, which the administrator role allows, and for a person with a read grant on one Connection, who sees that Connection. A read grant written earlier on a workspace shows the Connections it covers until it is revoked. A grant to use a Connection gives no entry in Studio. A row shows the connector type, whether the instance or a workspace owns the Connection, and whether it is enabled. A row opens the [page of the Connection](#the-page-of-a-connection). The list is **Studio > Connections**; the German interface names it **Studio › Verbindungen**.
## Connecting an outside system
[Connect a system](/connect/connect-a-system/) walks through these steps for the person who sets it up.

A Connection reaches a remote MCP server (connector type `mcp`) or a REST interface that it reads by GET (connector type `http_api`). An MCP server lists its tools itself. A REST interface lists nothing: each operation is declared in the Connection's definition with its path and parameters, as [release config](/configure/release-config/#a-rest-interface-http_api) shows. A person pastes such declarations as YAML into the approval list, or asks the agent beside the page to draft them from a vendor's public OpenAPI description. An agent that holds `platform.connections.draft_tools` checks its draft as a save would (GET only, the effect `reading`, no header or parameter that can carry a credential, no `.` or `..` path segment) and refuses a schema that carries a value of its own (`default`, `const`, `examples`, `example` or an `enum` with only one value, at any depth). It answers the draft as a card in the conversation; the card names the tools and holds the Connection's id, address and header names, never a key, and an existing Connection by its own title. Its button opens the Connection's approval list with the draft, which shows each tool's request, the description an agent reads and each parameter's allowed enum values, folded where long, for drafted and pasted declarations, or, for an id no Connection has, the New connection dialog filled with it. The person's approval there is the save: an agent never saves a Connection. A REST interface that must be written to needs a [custom tool](/extend/custom-tools/) in the client assembly.

1. **New connection** in Studio > Connections takes a name, the server's https address with the path of its MCP endpoint, and the authentication: none, a bearer token, or a key in a header the server names.

2. The key is entered in that form or later on the Connection's page under **Credential** (German: **Zugangsdaten**), with **Enter the key** or **Enter a new key**. It is stored encrypted and never shown again, to anyone. A key is never typed into a chat: an agent cannot take it, and an agent that asks for one is wrong. Give the key on the Connection's page only.
3. The instance reads the tools the server offers. On the Connection's page, accept the operations agents may call. **Test connection** checks the address and the key.
4. Give an agent the tools, as the next section says.

A build can ship further connector types with a form of their own, such as a document source a Knowledge Base syncs from. **New connection** offers each as a card beside **MCP server** and **REST API**. Its form asks for a name and the fields the type declares, with the secret hidden as it is typed; **Connect** saves the Connection, stores the secret and runs the type's test. A refused secret empties its field and says so; the Connection is saved already and waits for the right one. Such a Connection reads no tools, and its page shows its settings without changing them. The list of these types is the operation `connections.connector_types`, answered to a person who may change Connections (`connection.write`).
The rights this needs:
| Step                                                                          | Right                                                                                                |
| See Studio > Connections and a Connection's page                              | `connection.read`                                                                                    |
| Create a Connection, enter or replace its key, test it, accept its operations | `connection.write`, which the administrator role holds; the Access page does not grant it            |
| Delete a Connection                                                           | `connection.delete`, which the administrator role holds                                              |
| Give an agent a tool of the Connection                                        | `agent.write` on the agent, and `connection.read` to see the Connection in the agent's Tools section |
| Give an agent the approved tools with **Give to an agent**                     | `agent.write` and `agent.publish` on the agent, and `connection.read`                                |
| Have an agent call the tool                                                   | `connection.use` for the person the agent works for: an agent acts with that person's rights         |

The administrator role holds every right on Connections. Beside the rights, the operator must have turned the module [`connections`](/configure/modules/#connections) on, listed the server's host in [`egress.allow`](/configure/release-config/#egress) and set a [Secret Store key](/configure/release-config/#secret-store-keys); without the host on the list the save is refused with `egress_denied`. A Connection that comes from the release config is read-only on the instance, and its credential comes from the instance's environment.
## Giving an agent the tools of a Connection

The **Tools** section of an agent's page lists the instance's own tools under **Instance tools** and then, under **Connections**, one group for each Connection you may read (`connection.read`). A group holds a check box for each operation that agents may call and that is enabled and ready, with its description and whether it reads or changes. Ticking a box gives the agent the tool `connection.<name>.<operation>`. A group with more than 12 operations starts folded and shows how many of its operations the agent holds, and so does every group the agent holds nothing of when there are more than 6 groups.

**Give to an agent** (German: **Einem Agenten geben**) gives all of a Connection's approved tools to one agent in one step. It is offered after you approve operations that agents may call, in the **New connection** dialog and on the Connection's page, and on a card in a conversation when an agent that holds `platform.connections.offer_to_agent` offers it. It lists only the instance's agents you may change and publish. Before anything changes, it names the agent and the tools, and your confirmation publishes the agent as one new revision with them added: rights, approval policy and audit are those of a publish on the agent's page. Every conversation with the agent, the one you are in included, can use the tools from its next message.

If another person has an unpublished draft of the agent, the give is refused and names them. Nothing is written, and **Open** leads to the agent's page. If you have a draft of your own, the tools are added to it, and it is published only if you tick **Publish the whole draft now**, which publishes your other changes with them. A draft of yours that is based on an older published version is refused until you bring it up to date or discard it on the agent's page. A publish an approval policy holds waits in the Inbox.

A tool the agent already holds whose Connection or operation is gone, switched off, not offered to agents or not visible to you stays on the page in a group **No longer available** at the end of the section. Saving keeps it until you remove it. At run time the agent goes on without such a tool.

The instance checks on save that a name starting with `connection.` has the form `connection.<name>.<operation>`. It does not check that the Connection or the operation exists, because Connections change without a release.
The list is read once when the page opens, in one answer without pages. A Connection accepts at most 100 operations (`CONNECTION_MAX_ACCEPTED_OPERATIONS` in `packages/core/src/connections.ts`).
## The page of a Connection

A Connection made in Studio is changed on its page by a person who may change Connections (`connection.write`): its address and authentication under **Settings**, its key under **Credential**, and the operations agents may call. A Connection that comes from the release config opens read-only and says so; it is changed in the release config. The page never shows a credential or a reference to one.
- **Settings**: the connector type, the authentication scheme and the settings of the connector type.

- **Status**: whether the instance reaches the outside system, when it was last tested, and whether the credential is set, not set or unreadable. A Connection has one credential for everyone who may use it, and the page says so. A Connection with the authentication scheme `none` needs no credential, and the page says that instead.

- **Operations**: each accepted operation with its tool name `connection.<name>.<operation>`, whether it reads or changes, who may call it (agents, Apps, Workflows, outside clients or nobody) and its status. On a Connection made on the instance, a person with `connection.write` opens an operation to outside clients with the check box **Outside clients (CLI, MCP)** (German: **Externe Clients (CLI, MCP)**), and closes it again by clearing it. It is off on every operation until somebody ticks it, because what such a call returns is copied to the computer that holds the key. Only an operation with the status **Ready** can be called. **Awaiting discovery** means the instance has not read it from the outside system yet, **Needs review** that the outside system describes it differently than was accepted, **Unknown** that the outside system does not offer it, and **Disabled** that the operator switched it off. On a Connection made in Studio, **Accept new description** clears **Needs review**, and **Remove** takes an operation away.

- **Discovered tools** (German: **Gefundene Tools**), for a person who may change the Connection: the tools the server offers. For each, check **What it does** (**Was es tut**: Reading or Changing), untick **Agents can use it** (**Agenten dürfen es nutzen**) if agents should not call it, then **Accept** (**Akzeptieren**) to add it as an operation. **Read tools again** asks the server once more.
- **Used by**: the agents that carry a tool of the Connection, of those the reader may read.
- **Additional use rights**: the people and service principals given a right on this Connection itself. Workspace members use it through **Available in** and are not listed here.

**Test connection** asks the connector type to check the Connection and records the answer. It is offered to a person who may change Connections (`connection.write`); a person who may only read sees the recorded state. A test that a policy holds for an approval has not run: it waits in the Inbox.
What to do depends on where the Connection comes from. A Connection made in Studio is repaired on its page; one from the release config needs the operator.

| Status                | What it means                                                                                                                    | Made in Studio                                                                                                                                  | From the release config                                                                                                     |

| Ready                 | The outside system answered the test.                                                                                            | Nothing.                                                                                                                                        | Nothing.                                                                                                                    |

| Not tested            | Nobody has tested the Connection yet.                                                                                            | Test it.                                                                                                                                        | Test it.                                                                                                                    |

| Testing               | A test runs.                                                                                                                     | Wait for it.                                                                                                                                    | Wait for it.                                                                                                                |

| Unauthorized          | The outside system refused the credential.                                                                                       | Enter a new key under **Credential**, then test again.                                                                                          | The operator sets a new credential in the instance's environment and restarts the instance.                                 |

| Network denied        | The host is not in [`egress.allow`](/configure/release-config/#egress), or it resolves to an address the instance may not reach. | The operator adds the host to `egress.allow`, or for a public HTTPS host on port 443 sets `egress.allowPublicHttps`, and restarts the instance. | The same.                                                                                                                   |

| Unavailable           | The outside system did not answer.                                                                                               | Check the address under **Settings** and change it if it is wrong.                                                                              | Check the address under **Settings**. The operator changes it in the release config.                                        |

| Not configured        | The credential is missing.                                                                                                       | Enter the key under **Credential**, then test again.                                                                                            | The operator supplies it in the instance's environment and restarts the instance.                                           |

| Credential unreadable | A credential is stored and the instance cannot read it.                                                                          | Enter the key again under **Credential**, then test again.                                                                                      | The operator restores the Secret Store key it was stored with, or supplies the credential again, and restarts the instance. |

| Failed                | The test failed for a reason the instance does not name.                                                                         | Test again, then ask the operator.                                                                                                              | Test again, then ask the operator.                                                                                          |
## The list
Each kind has a list. For **Agents** and **Skills** a row shows the name, the id and when it was last changed. A row is a link, so it opens in a new tab like any other link.
- **Search** asks the instance for names and ids that contain the text.
- **Show more** reads the next 50 rows.
The names in the list are in the instance's default language.
## Create

Where no agent that builds is offered, **New agent** or **New skill** opens a dialog that asks for the name, and for an agent what it should do. Its address, the id, is made from the name under **Advanced** and follows the name until you change it. It is checked while you type: a taken address, or one the kind does not allow, is named at the field, the fold opens, and **Continue** waits until it is fixed. The address cannot be changed after the asset is saved.
An asset made while you work in a Shared Workspace belongs to that workspace, and a right in the workspace covers it. See [What a workspace owns](/operate/how-rights-work/#what-a-workspace-owns).
**Continue** opens the page of the new asset. Nothing is stored until you press **Create agent** or **Create skill** there.
## Building from chat
The Build Agent reports only actions confirmed by successful tool results. A table in chat,
an HTML preview, generated SQL or a saved migration does not prove a record was inserted,
changed or found. A draft is not published, a simulated test is not a live write, and a call
waiting for Allow has saved nothing.
A request to keep a table creates a **Data Store draft**: `store.yaml` and a migration
that creates a table with a primary key and no rows. Until a person publishes it, no row is
stored. Example rows requested in chat are ordinary data; `seed/` fills only a test copy.
After publication, continue the conversation about that store. An agent with platform tools
is offered that ready store's `describe`, `query`, `preview_rows`, `insert`, `update` and
`delete_rows` tools. An agent reads or changes rows only with a `data_store.<store>.<verb>` tool in its list; it may also carry row tools explicitly in its definition. Tools
grant no rights. Each write asks for confirmation by default and the preview shows the
frozen keys and values. `insert` is reversible; changes and deletion are irreversible and cannot use a remembered allow decision.
A declined or pending confirmation changes no row. The agent reports a write only from the
tool's confirmed count, and reports when a query was `truncated`, paging before concluding
that a row is absent.
Without the tool, the agent says that no row was stored. Publish the Data Store and continue
a conversation about it, or publish and use an App or Workflow that writes rows. The Data
Store page under **Studio > Data stores** (German: **Studio > Datenspeicher**) shows the store
and its rows. It has no row editor: continue the conversation about the store to write rows. A table managed by `records` accepts corrections through records review.
A structured Knowledge Base may read described tables with `knowledge.query` where available.
Creating an agent or skill from chat is live at once and requires confirmation of the exact
call. Existing agents save a shared draft that a person publishes; existing skills are changed
on their page or through a skill change request. The save's `workspaceId` is the actual owner,
not a name prefix such as `team-`. Without a workspace id the owner is the instance. To build in
another workspace, switch to it before starting its Build conversation.
A newly created agent is available nowhere. Open **Studio > Agents > the agent > Available in >
Selected workspaces**, choose the requested shared workspace, then **Save changes**. In German:
**Studio > Agenten > the agent > Verfügbar in > Ausgewählte Arbeitsbereiche**, choose the workspace,
then **Änderungen speichern**. **Personal workspaces** includes every person's personal workspace;
it is not a selector for one person's workspace. Availability belongs to the instance: a person who may change
agents across the instance performs this step if you lack the right. Changes to an existing agent's draft also need **Publish** (**Veröffentlichen**).

Knowledge Bases and Connections the agent uses need the same workspaces under their own **Available in**. Publish and **Available in** list any that are missing; a person who may change them can tick **Make them available there too** (**Dort auch verfügbar machen**), anyone else is told which admins to ask.
For orientation, point to the places enabled for the person: **Workflows**, **Apps**, **Inbox**
(**Eingang**), and Studio's **Agents**, **Skills**, **Connections** (**Verbindungen**),
**Data stores** (**Datenspeicher**) and **Knowledge Bases** (**Wissensbasen**). On an agent page,
**Knowledge** (**Wissen**) selects its Knowledge Bases. A Knowledge Base is a **Wissensbasis**, plural **Wissensbasen**.
## Edit
An asset page has sections, and an index of them beside the content or above it on a narrow window. The save bar appears with the first change. It counts the changed fields and offers **Discard**.

Texts that exist in English and German are written in one language at a time. **Texts in** switches the language for the whole page. The switch marks a language in which texts are still empty. A field left empty in one language shows the text of the other one to people, and the field says so.
If you may read an asset but not change it, the page says so and has no save bar.
### The files of a skill

A skill's page shows the skill as a folder under **Files**: `SKILL.md`, which holds the instructions, and the files below `references/`, `scripts/` and `assets/`. The **+** of a folder uploads a file into it or starts a new, empty one; the type of a file is read from its name. A text file, such as a reference or a script, is edited in place. Any file can be renamed, replaced with a new version, downloaded and deleted, and the page shows its size and, once saved, its SHA-256 hash. A file that is not text is not shown, only replaced.

The changes are saved with the save bar like any other field. Where a file beside the instructions changed, the save writes the whole folder; otherwise it writes the text alone and the other files stay. The instance holds the limits and says which one a save broke, with the path of the file: a file of more than 2 MiB, more than 500 files or 8 MiB in a skill, a compiled program, or a file under `scripts/` that is not UTF-8 text. See [A skill as a folder of files](/configure/config-assets/#a-skill-as-a-folder-of-files).
### When a save is refused

- **A tool, model or skill that is not allowed.** For example a tool the instance does not enable, or a model setting you may not change. The refusal stands under the field it concerns, and the form keeps what you typed.

- **Somebody else saved first.** The page saves against the revision it loaded. If the asset changed in between, nothing is overwritten. A notice offers **Load the newer version** and asks before it replaces what you typed, so you can copy what you need first. Until then the page saves nothing. If the newer version cannot be loaded, the page says so and keeps your text.
- **Somebody deleted it.** The notice says that the asset was deleted. Your text stays so that you can copy it, and the notice leads back to the list.
- **A skill you may not read.** An agent can only be given skills you may read yourself. A skill it already has stays when you save other changes.
- **A file of a skill that is not allowed.** The refusal names the file and stands under the files of the skill.
- **Anything else** is shown in the words of the instance, above the save bar.
## History and restore

**History** opens a panel beside the editor with the saved revisions, the newest first, 50 at a time. **Restore** makes the content of an older revision the newest one. The asset gets a new revision, so a restore can itself be restored. After a restore the page says which revision it restored. While somebody else's newer version waits to be loaded, History restores nothing.
## Delete

**Delete** is in the menu beside History, for people who hold the delete right on the asset. An asset that another one still refers to is not deleted, and the page says which reference stands in the way.
## Limits
| What                                                 | Value  |
| Rows read per list request                           | 50     |
| Wait after typing before a search                    | 250 ms |
| Skills offered per search in an agent's skill picker | 50     |
The list never holds more than the pages you asked for. History reads 50 revisions of the one asset when it opens, and **Show more** reads the next 50.

pages.title: The Catalyst CLI
pages.description: Install the public catalyst command from one file and use it against an instance.
body: `catalyst` is the command line tool for an instance. It is the public package `@work-shape/catalyst-cli` under the MIT licence and needs Node 22 or later.
## Install
Install the release tarball you were handed:
```sh
npm install --global ./work-shape-catalyst-cli-<version>.tgz
catalyst --help
A team that keeps its tooling with its working copy installs the same file as a development dependency and runs `npx catalyst`.

The package installs from that one file. It depends on two third-party packages, `js-yaml` and `zod`, and on no private package: the asset schemas, the API contract and the API client it uses are built into it. No registry account and no token are needed to install it.
## Commands
- [Assets](/configure/cli/assets/)
- [Log in and API keys](/configure/cli/auth/)
- [Config working copies](/configure/cli/config/)
- [Initialize a working copy](/configure/cli/init/)
- [Workflows, checks and lists](/configure/cli/named/)
- [Catalog operations and Connections](/configure/cli/operations/)
- [CLI maintainers](/configure/cli/maintainers/)
## Log in
[Log in with a personal API key](/configure/cli/auth/#log-in).
## The key
[How the CLI stores and uses its key](/configure/cli/auth/#the-key).

pages.title: Assets
pages.description: Read, write, publish and follow assets with the CLI.
body: ## Follow a held call
A publish that waits for approval exits 3 and prints its Operation Run id. Follow it with:
```sh
catalyst operation show <run-id>
catalyst requests
catalyst requests --withdraw <request-id>

`operation show` prints the status, decision and any failure; add `--json` for the full record. It exits 3 while awaiting a decision, 1 for a failed, denied or expired run, and 0 otherwise. `requests` lists your requests in every state, including the decision; `--json` prints the list as JSON. Withdrawal needs a personal key with an asset write or delete scope (`config_assets:write`). Reading your own runs, listing and counting your own requests uses the `me:read` scope every personal key carries. Another person's run is not found, and their requests cannot be listed or withdrawn through your key.
## One command per asset operation

Every operation on assets has a command, for every kind the instance registers: agents, skills, Apps, Workflows, Connections, Data Stores, guardrails. The kind is the first word, by its id, its plural or with dashes (`data-store`). The instance names its kinds; a kind a later release adds works without a new CLI.
```sh
catalyst context                  # the instance, your rights in it and its workspaces, its kinds
catalyst kinds                    # each kind: lifecycle, folder or definition, rights
catalyst references               # models, efforts and tools a definition may name
catalyst agent list --prefix tax-
catalyst agent show tax-vat
catalyst agent history tax-vat
catalyst skill validate --from skills/tax-guide
catalyst skill put tax-guide --from skills/tax-guide --if-revision new
catalyst agent put tax-vat --from agents/tax-vat.agent.yaml --if-revision 3
catalyst app put offers --from offers --if-revision 4 --workspace <workspace-id>
catalyst app publish offers --revision 5 --workspace <workspace-id>
catalyst agent revert tax-vat --to 2 --if-revision 4
catalyst agent delete tax-vat --if-revision 5
catalyst agent publish tax-vat --revision 6
catalyst agent discard tax-vat --revision 6

A `put` or `revert` of an agent that exists writes its draft and prints the draft revision. `--if-revision` names the live revision. Where the agent has a draft, `--if-draft-revision <n>` names the draft revision you read, the one `show` prints; without it the write expects no draft, and one that finds a draft is refused with its revision and author and changes nothing. `catalyst agent publish <name> --revision <n>` makes that draft revision live, and `catalyst agent discard <name> --revision <n>` drops it and leaves the live agent as it is. `list` shows each agent's pending draft in a column of its own, and `show` names it with its author. An instance's own agent is published without a question, a workspace's agent (`--workspace <id>`) asks as an App does. A key that may not publish, such as a service principal's, is refused with the reason and what to do instead.

`catalyst app publish` and `catalyst workflow publish` ask before they publish. With `--yes` they ask nothing and publish nothing yet: the publish waits in your own Inbox as a confirmation, the command ends with exit code `3` and the request id, and your **Allow** there counts as your click on Publish. A run without a terminal and without `--yes` publishes nothing and exits with 1. When approval is required, the command ends with exit code `3` and the request id, including for an admin's key. An instance approver can approve it in the Inbox ([Guardrails](/manage/guardrails/#publishing-needs-an-instance-admins-approval)). A CLI answer never supplies that approval.

`--from` takes the forms of the working copy: an `.agent.yaml` or any YAML or JSON definition, a skill's folder with its `SKILL.md`, or the folder of a kind whose revisions hold files, such as an App. A write names the revision it was made against with `--if-revision`, or `new` to create; read it with `show` or `history`. `discard-draft`, `set-availability` and `set-default` complete the list; `catalyst --help` shows each with its options. `--json` prints the instance's answer as it came.
Guardrails have four commands of their own beside `put`:
```sh
catalyst guardrail test no-iban --text "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00"   # or --from <file>, --asset skill:<name>
catalyst guardrail dry-run no-iban                 # what the draft would have done in the last 14 days
catalyst guardrail publish no-iban --revision 2    # shows the dry run first
catalyst guardrail unpublish no-iban               # stops it; the draft stays

`test` checks the draft, or `--revision <n>`, and keeps no hit. A first `publish` of a guardrail that would have blocked or held actions asks for `--confirm <n>` with the number the dry run counted. [Guardrails as assets](/configure/config-assets/#guardrails-as-assets) says who may do what.

The instance decides every right, revision and check. A `revert` needs the read right on the asset beside the write right, as it restores content. A refusal is printed as the instance gave it, with each asset, issue or item it names:
```text
Refused by the instance (HTTP 403 FORBIDDEN): Missing the right 'agent.write'

The exit code is 0 when the call was applied, 1 when it was refused or failed, 2 when the command line was wrong and nothing was sent, and 3 when the call waits for another person's approval and has changed nothing yet.
## Apps as a folder

An App is a folder of files with `app.yaml` at its root. Four commands work on that folder. Each one uses the same asset operations as the commands above, so the instance decides every right and every build.
```sh
catalyst app pull offers --workspace <workspace-id>   # the draft into ./offers
catalyst app push offers                              # the folder becomes the next draft
catalyst app status offers offers                     # draft, published, local changes
catalyst app publish offers                           # shows what goes live, then asks
An App belongs to one workspace. The commands take it from `--workspace`, from the folder's last pull, or from the selected instance's `workspace: <id>` in `catalyst.yaml`.

- `pull <app> [dir]` writes the draft into `dir`, which defaults to a folder named after the App. `--published` writes the published revision instead, and `--revision <n>` writes any one revision. Every file is written byte for byte and checked against the hash the instance gave. The folder also gets `.catalyst-app.json`, which records the instance, the workspace, the revision and each file's hash. That file is never sent. A pull refuses to overwrite a file you changed, and it refuses a folder that holds files but no pulled App.
