- `signInPerAddressPerMinute`: the same tries from one client address, whatever the account.
Size it for the largest office that reaches the instance through one address.
There are no settings per operation. A refused API key or server credential is counted per
client address at 60 a minute, which is not a setting. A caller over a limit receives 429 with
the code `RATE_LIMITED`, the seconds to wait in `details.retryAfterSeconds` and in the
`Retry-After` header. Behind a second proxy the client address needs
[`trusted_proxies`](/operate/deployment/).
## Operation policy
Every call of a registered operation is checked against a policy value before it runs. The
`policy` section sets the value for operations that nothing else names one for: no declaration
of the release and no setting of an admin. An instance without the section gets the defaults.
```yaml
policy:
defaults:
reading: allow
changing: confirm
- `reading`: `allow` runs a reading operation, `deny` refuses it with 403 and the code
`POLICY_DENIED`.
- `changing`: `allow` runs a changing operation. `confirm` asks the caller to confirm, and a
person's or a service's own call through the API or the CLI is that confirmation. `deny`
refuses it. `approval` holds a person's call until a person with the right to approve
decided it in the Inbox: the caller receives `202` with the run. An approval queues the call, and
the instance checks it again before it runs. A declined call answers `DECLINED`, and one nobody decided within 7 days answers
`OPERATION_EXPIRED`. A call of a Service Principal cannot be held and is refused with
`POLICY_DENIED`, a release push included. An agent's run cannot wait either, so startup refuses an
enabled changing tool that would wait under this default. Such a tool declares
`permission.mode` `allow` or `deny`. See [How rights work](/operate/how-rights-work/#approvals).
Calls that carry a secret do not follow an inherited `approval`: issuing an API key
(`api_credentials.create`), whose answer is the key, shown once to the person who asks; setting
a user's password (`users.password.reset`); and creating a user with a first password
(`users.create` with `passwordSignIn`). A held call keeps its input and shows it to whoever
decides, and a key shown later reaches nobody, so such a call cannot wait for somebody else.
Under `changing: approval` it is not refused: it runs on its caller's own word, as under
`confirm`, and its run records the decision with the reason `inherited_approval_not_applied`.
To require an approval for one of them on purpose, name the operation or its prefix in a policy
setting (`api_credentials.create` or `api_credentials.*` with the value `approval`). Such a
setting refuses the call with 403 and the code `POLICY_DENIED`, since a secret cannot wait:
nobody issues a key or sets a password while the setting stands. A `users.create` without a
password carries no secret and waits like any other change. A run never keeps the answer of
such a call, and the hash it keeps of the input is taken with the password left out.
See also [Retention, audit and deletion](/operate/governance/#inbox).
## Infrastructure
The `infrastructure` section states what an instance runs on: one provider per port. It is
startup config, so a change needs a deploy.
```yaml
infrastructure:
secrets:
provider: environment # the default
models:
azure-eu:
provider: openai-compatible
region: eu
api: responses
model: gpt-5.5
baseUrl: https://example.openai.azure.com/openai/v1
credentialSecret: AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY
authMode: api-key
mail:
provider: mailjet
region: eu
appUrl: https://chat.example.com
sender:
fromAddress: noreply@mail.example.com
objectStorage:
files:
provider: s3
region: eu
bucket: example-documents
bucketRegion: fsn1
endpoint: https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com
workspaces:
provider: filesystem
root: /var/lib/vivd-catalyst/example/execution-workspaces/objects
sandbox:
provider: docker
image: ghcr.io/example/catalyst-runner-base:v1
- `models` is a map from a provider's name to its entry. The name is what `modelBindings[].providerId`
and an agent's `modelProviderId` refer to. At least one entry is required; there is no default.
Config files merge maps key by key, so an entry of a base file stays unless the overlay
replaces it under the same name.
- `database.poolSize` is how many PostgreSQL connections each process of the instance (the API
and every worker) keeps at most, 10 unless set; raise it when requests wait for a connection
and the database's `max_connections` leaves room for all processes together.
- `mail`, `objectStorage.files`, `objectStorage.workspaces` and `sandbox` are left out when the
instance does not use them. Enabled execution workspaces need `objectStorage.workspaces` and
`sandbox`.
- `provider` picks the adapter. An unknown provider, an unknown setting or a missing setting
stops startup, and the message names the field.
- `region` is `eu` or `global` and says where the provider processes the data it is sent. A
provider that sends data outside the instance (`openai-compatible`, `google-vertex`, `aws-bedrock`,
`mailjet`, `s3`) must state it. A provider that keeps data inside the instance (`deterministic`, `capture`,
`filesystem`, `docker`, `local`) must not. A `docker` sandbox with an `endpoint` runs on
another host and must state it too. A vendor's own region name is a separate setting,
such as `bucketRegion`.
- A setting whose name ends in `Secret` holds the name of a secret, never its value. The
`environment` secret provider reads the variable of that name and, when it is not set, the
file named by the variable `<NAME>_FILE`, which is how a mounted Docker or Kubernetes secret
is read. A name that does not resolve stops startup; the message names the field and the
secret name. So does a `<NAME>_FILE` whose file cannot be read or is empty, also for a secret
the instance may leave unset.
- A secret name reads as an environment variable name: upper-case words joined by underscores,
at most 64 characters. Anything else is refused and never repeated in a message, so a
credential pasted where a name belongs does not reach a log.
- The first entry of `models` serves an agent that names no provider. An id made only of digits
is refused, because such a key is read before the others whatever its place in the file.
Providers and their settings:

| Port            | Provider            | Settings                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

| `models`        | `openai-compatible` | `model`, `api`, `reasoningEffort`, `contextManagement`, `baseUrl`, `credentialSecret` (default `OPENAI_API_KEY`), `authMode`, `organizationSecret`                                                                                                                                            |

| `models`        | `google-vertex`     | `model`, `projectId`, `credentialSecret` (default `GOOGLE_VERTEX_CREDENTIALS`): the JSON key of a service account. Gemini on Vertex AI; `region` decides the endpoint and location.                                                                                                           |

| `models`        | `aws-bedrock`       | `accountId`: the AWS account of the profiles; `model`: the ARN of an application inference profile of that account in `eu-central-1`; `credentialSecret` (default `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`): a Bedrock API key. Claude on Amazon Bedrock; `region` must be `eu`; every model needs a price. |

| `models`        | `deterministic`     | `model`. Answers without a model; for tests and local runs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

| `mail`          | `mailjet`           | `appUrl`, `sender`, `apiKeySecret` (default `MAILJET_API_KEY`), `apiSecretSecret` (default `MAILJET_API_SECRET`)                                                                                                                                                                              |

| `mail`          | `capture`           | `appUrl`, `sender`. Development only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

| `objectStorage` | `s3`                | `bucket`, `bucketRegion`, `endpoint`, `forcePathStyle`, `accessKeySecret` (default `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`), `secretKeySecret` (default `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`). Any S3-compatible store.                                                                                                        |

| `objectStorage` | `filesystem`        | `root`: a directory that the API and its workers share.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

| `sandbox`       | `docker`            | `image`, `cpuCount`, `memoryBytes`, `pidsLimit`, `endpoint` (a `tcp://` or `ssh://` Docker engine on another host; needs `region`). The container has no network and a read-only root file system.                                                                                            |

| `sandbox`       | `local`             | None. Development only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
Every stored byte goes through one object storage port. `objectStorage.files` holds uploaded
documents and what is prepared from them, and is used by the document processing capability, a
paid capability; `objectStorage.workspaces` holds workspace files,
their source files and preview images. Each store names its own provider and its own bucket or
directory, and either provider serves either store. Object keys are the same in both providers
and did not change with the port, so a store written by an earlier release is read as it is.
The platform takes its own secrets from the same provider by fixed names: `DATABASE_URL`,
`BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET`, `CHAT_SESSION_TOKEN_SECRET` and
`CHAT_SERVER_CREDENTIAL`. A data source's `connectionRef: env:NAME` and a seed user's
`passwordEnvName` name secrets too.
### Reading what an instance runs on
The page **Instance > Infrastructure** in the settings and `GET /api/v1/instance/infrastructure`
list every configured entry of this section and the database: the provider, its region, the host
it calls or its bucket, its secrets with whether each is set, and the result of its last check.
Both need `users.manage` and change nothing. A secret value, a connection string, a key and a
path on the host are never part of the answer.
A secret that is set is shown by its name. One that is missing is shown by the key of the config
that names it, such as `credentialSecret`: what stands there resolves to nothing, so the page
does not repeat it. A host is shown when it is a bare host with an optional port and a bucket
when it reads as an S3 bucket name. Anything else is shown as "not shown", and the server log
names the provider and the field in a warning, without the value.
A check is the cheapest authenticated read a provider has: the list of models of a model
endpoint, the account of a Mailjet key pair, one `HEAD` of the bucket of an S3 store, the `head`
of a key that is never written in a filesystem store, one query against the database, the
version of the Docker engine for the sandbox. It generates nothing, sends no mail, writes nothing
and creates no bucket. Creating the provider and asking it end together after five seconds as
`timeout`. The API runs its checks every five minutes, all at once. The workspace command worker
checks the sandbox on the same schedule, because it alone reaches it; an instance without that
worker shows the sandbox with no check reported. **Check now** and
`POST /api/v1/instance/infrastructure/check` run the API's checks once more, at most once a
minute for the whole instance; a call inside that minute answers `429 RATE_LIMITED`. Opening the
page asks no provider.
A failed check shows a class and a sentence of the product: `unreachable`, `timeout`,
`access_denied`, `not_found`, `bucket_missing`, `rejected` or `failed`. What the provider itself
answered is not shown, logged or returned. The outcomes and the time of the last manual check are
kept in the database, in one row of `infrastructure_check_state` per instance, so every API
process shows the same and the results survive a restart. A failing provider does not change
`/ready`.
The keys `modelProviders`, `mail`, `executionWorkspaces.runner` and
`capabilities.documentProcessing.objectStorage` moved into this section. Config that still
carries one of them does not load: startup stops and names the key and its new place. The
variables `EXECUTION_WORKSPACE_OBJECT_ROOT` and `ARTIFACT_PREVIEW_OBJECT_ROOT` are no longer
read; the directory is `infrastructure.objectStorage.workspaces.root`.
When moving an existing instance:
- A model provider whose old `compliance.residency` was `unknown` needs a decision: `region`
is `eu` or `global`. State `global` when no EU processing is agreed.
- A deployment that reached S3 through an instance role or another source of the AWS credential
chain must provide an access key pair as two named secrets. A local S3Mock that ran without
credentials needs both variables set to any value.
- A deployment that set the workspace object directory through the environment moves the path
into `infrastructure.objectStorage.workspaces.root` and removes the variable. Keep the same
directory and the same mount so existing files stay reachable.
- `EXECUTION_WORKSPACE_RUNNER_IMAGE` replaces the image of a `docker` sandbox only.
## Connections
`connections` names the Connections of the instance. It needs the module [`connections`](/configure/modules/#connections); with the module off the section is read and nothing is seeded.
```yaml
modules:
connections:
enabled: true
connections:
crm:
connectorType: mcp
displayName: CRM
description: Customer records, read-only.
settings:
url: https://mcp.crm.example.com/mcp
authScheme: bearer
secret: CRM_MCP_TOKEN
operations:
- name: search_customers
effect: reading
exposure: [agent]
secretStore:
keys:
- id: k1
ref: CATALYST_SECRET_STORE_KEY
egress:
allow:
- protocol: https
host: mcp.crm.example.com
port: 443

Each key under `connections` is the name of a Connection. The instance owns it, and `connection.read` or `connection.use` is [granted](/operate/rights-for-one-person/#grants) on this one Connection. An entry takes `connectorType`, `displayName`, `description`, `settings`, `authScheme`, `secret` and `operations`, and nothing else. `settings` is checked against the strict schema of the connector type before anything is stored, and a `connectorType` this build does not ship stops startup with the place of the fault. An entry of `operations` takes `name`, `effect` (`reading` or `changing`), `exposure` (any of `agent`, `bridge`, `workflow`, `outside`) and optionally `policy` and `schemaFingerprint`; an operation of `http_api` also declares its request ([below](#a-rest-interface-http_api)). What stands in the list is accepted; nothing else of the outside system can be called. Each exposure admits one kind of caller: `agent` an agent, `bridge` an App, `workflow` a Workflow, and `outside` the CLI and the platform MCP server, a caller with an API key or a Service Principal's credential, whose results leave the instance. A person in the browser outside an App and a schedule are admitted by none. `outside` is off unless the list names it.

`secret` is the name of a secret, resolved like every other secret of the instance: from the environment variable of that name or from the file `<NAME>_FILE` points at. It is the only place of a Connection where a secret may stand, and it never holds the value. An `authScheme` other than `none` needs it, and `none` refuses it.
### A REST interface: `http_api`
The connector type `http_api` reads a REST interface by GET. It has no discovery: each operation declares its request, and the declaration is what an agent, an App or a Workflow sees of it.
```yaml
connections:
accounting_source:
connectorType: http_api
displayName: Accounting source
settings:
baseUrl: https://accounting.example.com/api
headers:
x-client-instance-id: 6f1d2c3b-4a5e-4f60-8a7b-9c0d1e2f3a4b
testPath: /health
authScheme: bearer
secret: ACCOUNTING_SOURCE_KEY
operations:
- name: open_items
effect: reading
exposure: [workflow]
method: GET
path: /clients/{clientId}/open-items
description: Reads the open items of one Mandant.
pathParams:
clientId:
schema: { type: string }
query:
fiscalYear:
schema: { type: integer }
required: true
`settings` takes `baseUrl`, `headers`, `testPath` and `headerName`, and nothing else:

- `baseUrl` is the address every path is relative to: `https`, or `http` for a host the egress list names as private. It holds no user name, password, query or fragment. Changing its protocol, host or port clears the stored key, which must then be set again, so the key never goes to a host it was not given for.

- `headers` are sent with every request and are never a credential. A header whose name can carry one is refused with `credential_in_settings`: `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Cookie` and any name that contains `auth`, `key`, `token`, `secret`, `password` or `session`, in any case. The key goes in `secret`.
- `authScheme` `bearer` sends the key as `Authorization: Bearer`; `header` sends it in the header `headerName` names.

- `testPath`, optional, is a GET path that **Test connection** asks, and its answer must be 2xx. Without it the test asks `baseUrl`: 401 or 403 means the key was refused, any other answer that the system is reachable. A test keeps nothing of the answer.
An operation of `http_api` takes, beside `name`, `effect` and `exposure`:
- `method` `GET` and `effect: reading`. Nothing else is accepted; a GET is no proof that nothing changes, so the effect is declared as for any operation.
- `path`, relative to `baseUrl`, with a `{name}` placeholder for each entry of `pathParams`. It holds no query, no address and no segment `.` or `..`, also not written as `%2e`.

- `pathParams` and `query`: each parameter with its JSON `schema` (a path parameter a `string`, `integer` or `number`, a query parameter also a `boolean` or an `array` with scalar `items`), an optional `description`, and for a query parameter `required`. A path parameter is always required and remains scalar. For repeated query keys, declare an array:
```yaml
name: list_postings
description: Reads postings matching every filter, in pages.
method: GET
path: /api/accounting/postings
effect: reading
exposure: [workflow]
query:
filter:
schema:
type: array
items: { type: string }
page:
schema: { type: integer }
page_size:
schema: { type: integer }

Input `{"filter":["client_id eq 1234","fiscal_year gte 20260101"],"page":1,"page_size":100}` sends two `filter` keys, `filter=client_id+eq+1234&filter=fiscal_year+gte+20260101`, alongside `page=1` and `page_size=100`. The order of different keys is not guaranteed: Postgres reorders the saved query declaration. Within an array, order, duplicates and empty strings are preserved. Values are encoded individually, so `&`, `=` and `#` remain part of their value. An empty array or an omitted optional parameter sends no key. The connector also omits null query parameters, but normal calls must satisfy the declared schema.

There is no fixed value-count cap; a declared `maxItems` is preserved in the input schema. The final encoded request URL, including the base address, path and all query values, may be at most **8,000 bytes** (`HTTP_API_REQUEST_URL_MAX_BYTES`). A longer URL fails as `input_invalid` before any request, naming the 8,000-byte limit; a single long scalar counts too. Normal calls with values outside the declared schema fail at schema validation, before reaching the connector. The connector's defensive checks refuse objects, nested arrays and null array items as `input_invalid` when called directly. Array item schemas must name one scalar type; objects, nested arrays and missing item types are refused at save and by the agent's draft tool.
- `description`, what the operation reads and when to call it, which an agent reads, and optionally `title`, its name in words.

A caller fills the declared parameters and nothing else: never the host, the method, a header or the key. A path parameter is percent-encoded and may not be empty, hold a `/`, or be `.` or `..`. Normal calls reject undeclared keys at schema validation; the connector also refuses them as `input_invalid` before anything is sent. No redirect is followed. The answer must be JSON of at most 2 MiB; a list is answered as `{ items: [...] }`, so every result is an object. An answer that is not JSON or too large fails as `output_invalid`, and one that holds the key as `output_rejected`.
An operation that reads the data of one Mandant takes the Mandant as a named parameter and returns it on every item. The key `scope` on an operation is reserved and refused.
### What a start does
The API process reconciles the stored Connections with this section each time it starts, in one transaction under one lock, so several API processes starting together write once. Workers do not seed.
- A new entry becomes a Connection with `origin: release` at revision 1. A changed entry becomes a new revision. An unchanged entry writes nothing.
- An entry that is gone removes its Connection, its stored secret, its state and the grants that allow something on that one Connection. A deny on it stays with the name, as for every asset.
- A renamed entry is a removed entry and a new one: the new Connection starts at revision 1 with no grants of its own, and grants have to be written again.

- The value of `secret` is read once and stored encrypted. A changed value becomes the next version of the secret and no new revision of the Connection. A variable that is not set leaves the Connection in the state `needs_configuration`, and a call of it is refused with `connection_not_configured`.
- A Connection created on the instance is never touched. An entry with the name of such a Connection stops startup.
A seeded Connection is read-only on the instance: `read_only_origin`. Rotate a credential by changing the value of the variable and restarting.
### Secret Store keys

`secretStore.keys` lists the keys that encrypt Connection secrets, each with an `id` and a `ref`, the name of the secret that holds the key. A key is 32 random bytes in base64, for example from `openssl rand -base64 32`. The first key encrypts; every listed key decrypts.
- With at least one entry under `connections`, the first key must resolve. Otherwise startup stops and names the variable, for example `The Secret Store key 'CATALYST_SECRET_STORE_KEY' is not set`.
- A later key that is not set is skipped with a warning that names it. A secret only that key opens reads as `secret_unreadable`, and no call of its Connection is attempted.

- To change the key, put the new key first and keep the old one in the list. A secret that comes from `secret` is sealed again under the first key at the next start. Remove the old key once no row names its `id`.

Secrets are stored with AES-256-GCM, a random 12-byte nonce for every encryption, and associated data made of the instance, the Connection, the credential subject and the version of the secret. A row copied to another Connection does not open. The database holds ciphertext only, so a database backup restores no credential without the key: back the key up apart from the database. A lost key is not recovered; set the secrets again.
Nothing returns a stored secret: no operation, route, CLI command, export, log line, audit event or error. A person sees whether a secret is set and its version.
### Egress

`egress.allow` is the list of outside targets a Connection may reach. It is empty unless set, and an empty list refuses every target. `egress.allowPublicHttps` opens every public HTTPS host beside the list; it is off unless set.
| Key        | Meaning                                                                   |
| `protocol` | `https`, `http` or `postgres`.                                            |
| `host`     | One exact host name or one literal address. No wildcard, no suffix match. |
| `port`     | The one port. A default port is written out.                              |
| `network`  | `public`, the default, or `private`.                                      |
| `cidrs`    | With `private`: the address ranges the host may resolve into.             |
Every connection a Connection opens is checked against this list before a credential is resolved, whatever its connector type:
- Protocol, host and port must equal one entry.

- The host is resolved at the check, and every address it answers is judged. For a `public` entry, one answer that is loopback, link-local, a cloud metadata address or a private range refuses the target, also written as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address. For a `private` entry, every answer must lie in the entry's `cidrs`.
- The connection goes to the address that was checked, with the host name unchanged for TLS, so a second DNS answer changes nothing.
- A redirect and a returned download address are checked as new targets, and the credential is sent to the origin it was configured for and to no other.
- An address with a user name or a password is refused.

- The instance's own database host and port are refused whatever the list says, by name and by address. While the database host does not resolve, every target on its port is refused. When the database address cannot be read as one host and one port, startup logs a warning and every `postgres` target is refused. That is so for a Unix socket, for an address that names several hosts, and for an address without a port while `PGPORT` is set. Give the address as `postgres://host:port/database`.
- Plain `http` is accepted for a `private` entry only.

- Link-local addresses (`169.254.0.0/16`, `fe80::/10`) are reached by no entry. A `private` entry whose `cidrs` cover them stops startup with the range named. Loopback and the private ranges are reachable where a `private` entry names them.
- An IPv4 address carried inside an IPv6 one (IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, NAT64, 6to4, Teredo) is judged as that IPv4 address.
```yaml
egress:
allow:
- protocol: http
host: mcp-internal
port: 8080
network: private
#### Every public HTTPS host

`egress.allowPublicHttps: true` lets a Connection reach a host that no entry names, over `https` on port 443, for an instance whose administrators connect outside services themselves. The operator accepts that any administrator of the instance may then send a Connection, and its credential, to any public HTTPS service.
```yaml
egress:
allowPublicHttps: true
allow:
- protocol: http
host: mcp-internal
port: 8080
network: private

- Such a target is judged as a `public` entry: every address the host answers must be public. Loopback, link-local, cloud metadata addresses, private ranges and their IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms are refused as above.
- The instance's database host is refused on every port, by name and by address.
- Redirects and returned download addresses are checked as new targets, and the credential still goes only to the origin it was configured for.
- Another port, plain `http` and `postgres` still need an entry under `egress.allow`. The entries keep working beside the setting, and a private host is reached only through a `private` entry.
- A start with the setting on logs a warning once.
#### Refusals

A refusal answers `egress_denied` with the host and the port, and nothing else of the address. Its message ends with the setting that would let the target through: an entry under `egress.allow`, `egress.allowPublicHttps` for `https` on port 443, a `private` entry for a host that resolves to a private address, or that no setting does, as for a link-local address or the database host. A target outside the list is refused before its name is looked up. A host that is on the list and whose name gives no address, as with a stopped service or a resolver that is down, is refused as well and nothing is contacted, but it is not `egress_denied`: a call answers `connection_unavailable` and says that the host did not resolve, and a test of the Connection answers `unavailable`. A checked answer is used for 30 seconds, so a call within that time makes no DNS lookup, and a page load makes none at all. A refusal that came from the resolver (a timeout, a failed lookup, no answer) is held for 5 seconds. The list and `allowPublicHttps` are read at start: a change needs a restart.
## Data Stores

With the module `dataStores` on, each Data Store gets a Postgres database of its own on the server of the platform database. The module needs a key under `secretStore.keys`, where the passwords of the store roles are kept, and a platform database role that has `CREATEDB` and `CREATEROLE` and owns the platform database.
```yaml
dataStores:
sizeLimit: 5GB
poolMaxConnections: 5
queryTimeoutMs: 600000
load:
timeoutMs: 600000

- `sizeLimit` is the most one store may hold, as a whole number of `MB` or `GB`. A store's own `sizeLimit` in `store.yaml` names less and never more. At the limit no rows are added and reading keeps working. Every insert reads the size of the database before it writes and after, and is rolled back where it passed the limit: no row that is kept lies beyond it, and the files exceed it only by what the inserts of one moment wrote, under 256 MiB for rows alone. Default `5GB`.
- `poolMaxConnections` is the most connections one process holds to one store at once, between 1 and 10. Default 5.

`queryTimeoutMs` is the deadline for the full cursor of a Workflow query with a dataset destination; ordinary queries keep their inline row, byte and statement bounds. `load.rows`, `load.bytes` and `load.timeoutMs` bound one atomic dataset load. These are operator ceilings: raise them when the instance can handle larger work. A load beyond its row or byte ceiling answers `load_too_large`; produce smaller datasets upstream for separate calls or raise the ceiling. The store's own size limit still applies. Defaults are shown above.
### Records keys in store.yaml
A `records` rule in `store.yaml` names a table and a key column. That column needs
a valid, non-partial, non-deferrable unique key by itself. Publish the rule with
the migrations that create its table and key. Every migration preserves records
keys that already hold; the last migration also checks all newly declared keys.
Rules published while earlier migrations are queued or running receive the same
protection once their keys hold.
A key swap must happen inside **one migration**: drop the old unique index or
constraint and create its replacement for the same column in that SQL file.
Dropping the key in `0002` and adding a new one in `0003` is refused at `0002`
with `record_key_invalid`, naming the migration and `records.<table>.key.<column>`.
That migration rolls back and later files do not run. Correct the pending SQL
and republish. A publish with no pending migrations checks the keys immediately.
### Build rules for data scope
Keep the client (Mandant) on every per-client row and in every reader:

- Give every per-client table a `NOT NULL` column for the client key, named consistently across the store (for example `mandant_nr`), including findings, snapshots, open items and run history. Aggregate views group by that column.
- A Workflow that copies data from an outside system writes the client key on every row and keeps the key in aggregates.

- Every `http_api` operation whose path or result is per client takes the client as a named parameter and returns the client key on every item. Keep a mapping table when source ids and client keys differ.
- App `sql` reads use those per-client tables. Do not put a structured Knowledge Base with free SQL on these stores.

- Say who an App or Workflow is for when it serves only part of the firm. Everyone in that audience must be allowed to see every client the Connection's outside account sees. Limit that account in the outside system to the agreed clients.

Declare one text data scope with `scopes: { mandant: { label: Mandant, valueType: text } }`. On **Instance > Access > Data access**, give people, identity groups and service accounts their values, or all values. Administrators need an explicit assignment too. Nobody saves or lifts their own assignment, including one on a group they belong to; another holder of `users.manage` does. A service account's assignment also needs the right to administer service accounts. Group membership is the list of groups the person's last sign-in carried, and a sign-in without a groups claim leaves them in none, so group assignments work only with an identity provider that sends groups. It is read from the stored identity for personal API keys as well as browser sessions; a person's revocation wins. Assignments carry no row contents and their audit events record counts only. Account deletion removes direct assignments. This feature introduces no outside provider or document retention change.

A store marks each scoped table as `tables: { findings: { scope: { mandant: mandant_nr } } }`. The column must be `text NOT NULL`. A partition, an `INHERITS` parent or child, or a view of a scoped table must be declared scoped too, or the migration is refused; a declared view needs a text column only. Inserts and loads must supply an assigned value; previews, paged rows and single-value reads filter by the caller.

Every SQL read of a scoped store is filtered where it runs: a direct `query`, an App SQL action, draft or published, a named Knowledge Base query and a Workflow step. Each scoped table the statement names reads only the caller's rows, wherever the name stands, so `OR true`, a `UNION` branch or a missing filter cannot widen the result, and a holder of all values reads every row. Joins, aggregates and `WHERE` clauses work as usual. Refused on a scoped store: a schema-qualified name of a scoped table (`public.findings`), a `U&"..."` identifier, functions that read a table by name or run SQL from text (`query_to_xml`, `table_to_xml` and the other `*_to_xml` functions, `ts_stat`, `ts_rewrite`, `crosstab`, `connectby`) and the column statistics views (`pg_stats`). Functions a store's migrations define run unfiltered; do not define one that reads a scoped table.

An App SQL action or a named query may still bind `$viewer.scope('mandant')` and `$viewer.scope_all('mandant')`; the platform binds both from the current caller, never from browser parameters. A Knowledge Base declares `queries: [{ name: findings, file: queries/findings.sql }]`; `catalyst knowledge-base put <name> --from kb.yaml` reads those SQL files, including their `-- @param` headers, into the versioned definition. Call it with `{ query: 'findings', parameters: { ... } }`. Free SQL on a scoped Knowledge Base is refused even for an all-values holder.

Known limits: an insert with `onConflict: "skip"` or `"fail"` tells whether a row with the same unique key exists, also in another client's rows; give scoped tables unique keys that include the scope column. `describe` shows estimated row counts per table. A table with the client column that is not declared scoped is readable in full.

Connection-operation `scope` is still reserved for SCOPE-2. `$viewer.groups` and a caller parameter named `scope` remain refused. Connection output, conversation audiences and document passage filtering follow in SCOPE-2 to SCOPE-4; scoped tables do not replace those gates.
## Config Is Not A Secret Store
Release config may reference secrets, but it must not contain secret values.
Use runtime env files or a secret manager for:
- model provider API keys
- mail provider API keys
- database passwords
- customer API credentials
- object storage credentials
- server-to-server token exchange credentials
## Change Flow
Treat config changes like code changes:
```text
edit static release config and/or agent working copy
-> validate static assembly and agent references
-> run tests
-> push versioned agent assets when changed
-> build and deploy the image when static config changed
-> record active static and asset versions

Interactive administration changes apply to new conversations immediately. Pull and commit those changes when the repository should retain them. Static tool availability, model providers and bindings, capabilities, retention, and security policy still require the normal release/deploy flow.
## Workflow step concurrency
`workflows.stepSlots` caps the Workflow step jobs that each serving process runs at
once across all Workflows. It defaults to **4** and accepts whole numbers from **1
to 64**; startup refuses values outside that range. Waiting steps release their slot.
Set this in release config and restart the workers to apply it:
```yaml
workflows:
stepSlots: 8
Code sandbox jobs also respect `workflows.codeSteps.slots` (defaults to `stepSlots`). Their effective
concurrency is the smaller of the two settings. The startup sandbox memory check
multiplies that effective count by `workflows.codeSteps.memoryBytes`, alongside
workspace commands and Page builds. Raise `stepSlots` (and any explicitly lower code slot setting) to run more code
sandboxes concurrently; the host must have enough memory for them.
A code step that reads or writes datasets gets two directories on the command worker's disk:
its input datasets as read-only files of JSON Lines under `/work/in`, and `/work/out`, where the
script writes the datasets it returns. `workflows.codeSteps.diskBytes` bounds both together, the
input files and what the script writes: **2 GiB** unless set. A dataset the input names twice is
written once. Input that would pass the bound is not written, and a script that writes past it
is stopped; either way the step fails with `code_disk_limit`. The setting is disk, not memory,
so the startup memory check has no term for it; the worker's temporary directory
(`WORKSPACE_COMMAND_TEMP_ROOT`) must hold `diskBytes` for each code step that runs at once. The command worker reads and writes the datasets in the
`files` object store, so its process needs `infrastructure.objectStorage.files` as the API's.
```yaml
workflows:
codeSteps:
diskBytes: 4294967296 # 4 GiB

A Workflow may use every step slot at once, across its runs and their child runs together. A Workflow that should leave room for others sets a lower share with `limits.concurrency` in `workflow.yaml`, up to `stepSlots`. A loop's own `concurrency` still bounds that loop.
## Workflow limits

A Workflow's `limits` in `workflow.yaml` set the bounds of each of its runs: `duration`, `stepRuns`, `loopItems` and `concurrency`. Where a Workflow sets none, its runs get the defaults: 12 hours of run time, 20,000 step runs and 10,000 items per loop. Time a run spends waiting, for work that ends later or for a child run, counts toward no limit: the run's deadline moves later by the time it waited.

`workflows.limits` holds the ceilings a Workflow may raise its limits to. A publish that raises a limit names the raise in its question; a publish above a ceiling is refused with the ceiling named. Lowering a ceiling bounds the runs that start after the restart; it does not unpublish a Workflow.
```yaml
workflows:
limits:
duration: 7d # the default ceiling; `<n>m`, `<n>h` or `<n>d`
stepRuns: 1000000
loopItems: 1000000
pagedStepMinutes: 60
datasets:
pages: 10000
pageBytes: 8388608

A paged reading operation defaults to 60 minutes. Its Workflow may set `limits.pagedStepMinutes` above that default, up to `workflows.limits.pagedStepMinutes`; the publish question names the raise. `workflows.datasets.pages` and `pageBytes` bound the page count and each page's bytes. Connector response bounds still apply: `http_api` accepts at most 2 MiB per response. A reached ceiling fails the step with `dataset_limit` and its name; no consumer receives a partial dataset. Complete pages checkpoint their continuation, and source rate-limit deferrals preserve the page's spent retry attempts.
`datasetBytes` is still not raised above its default of 2 GiB. The ceiling of `limits.concurrency` is `workflows.stepSlots`.

pages.title: Connect a system
pages.description: Connect an outside system through its MCP server, enter its key, test it, and let an agent use it.
body: A Connection lets agents work in another system, such as your CRM or ticket tool. You set it up once in Studio. After that, every agent you give its tools can read or change things there, with the rights of the person it works for.
The German interface shows the labels in quotes.
## Before you start

- The system needs an **MCP server** reachable over HTTPS, which this page sets up. A system with a REST interface that is read by GET is connected with its operations declared, as [Connecting an outside system](/configure/build/#connecting-an-outside-system) shows; one that must be written to needs a [custom tool](/extend/custom-tools/).
- You need the address of its MCP endpoint, such as `https://crm.example.com/mcp`, and its key or token if it asks for one.
- You need to be an administrator. Creating a Connection, entering its key and testing it are rights of the administrator role.
- The operator must allow the instance to reach the server's host. If it does not, the test says **Network denied** ("Netzwerk gesperrt"); ask the operator.

- The operator must have set up a key store for credentials (a Secret Store key). Without it the key you enter is not kept, and **Credential** shows **Not set** ("Nicht gesetzt"). If that happens, ask the operator.
## Create the Connection
1. Open **Studio** and choose **Connections** ("Verbindungen").

2. Click **New connection** ("Neue Verbindung"). Give it a name people will recognise, such as "CRM". Its id, under **Technical details** ("Technische Details"), follows the name and is checked while you type; keep it or change it now, as it cannot change later. Click **Continue** ("Weiter").
3. Under **Server** enter the **Server address** ("Serveradresse"): the https address of the MCP endpoint.
4. Under **Authentication** ("Authentifizierung") choose what the server expects:
- **None** ("Keine"),
- **Bearer token** ("Bearer-Token"), or
- **Key in a header** ("Schlüssel in einem Header"), with the **Header name** the server documents.
5. Paste the key into **Key** ("Schlüssel").
6. Click **Create connection** ("Verbindung anlegen").

The key is stored encrypted and is never shown again, to anyone. Later you replace it on the Connection's page under **Credential** ("Zugangsdaten") with **Enter a new key** ("Neuen Schlüssel eingeben").
Never type a key into a chat. An agent cannot take it from there, and an agent that asks you for one is wrong.
## Choose what agents may do
The instance asks the server which tools it offers. On the Connection's page, **Discovered tools** ("Gefundene Tools") lists them. Each says whether it only reads or also changes something.
1. For each tool you want, check **What it does** ("Was es tut"): **Reading** ("Lesend") or **Changing** ("Ändernd").
2. **Agents can use it** ("Agenten dürfen es nutzen") is already ticked. Untick it if agents should not call this tool.
3. Click **Accept** ("Akzeptieren"). The tool moves to **Operations** ("Operationen").
Accept only what you need. You can **Remove** ("Entfernen") an operation later.
If the server adds tools later, click **Read tools again** ("Tools neu lesen").
## Test it

Click **Test connection** ("Verbindung testen"). The **Status** shows **Ready** ("Bereit") when the server answered with the key you gave. Any other status says on the page what to do. The most common:
| Status                                    | What to do                                                                         |
| **Unauthorized** ("Nicht autorisiert")    | The server refused the key. Enter a new key under **Credential**, then test again. |
| **Not configured** ("Nicht konfiguriert") | No key yet. Enter it under **Credential**, then test again.                        |
| **Unavailable** ("Nicht erreichbar")      | The server did not answer. Check the address under **Settings** ("Einstellungen"). |
| **Network denied** ("Netzwerk gesperrt")  | The instance may not reach this host. Ask the operator to allow it.                |
[The page of a Connection](/configure/build/#the-page-of-a-connection) lists every status.
## Give an agent the tools
1. In **Studio**, open **Agents** ("Agenten") and the agent.
2. Go to the **Tools** section ("Werkzeuge"). Under **Connections** ("Verbindungen") there is a group for your Connection.
3. Tick the operations this agent may use, and save.
Only operations that are ready and allowed for agents appear here.
## Let people use it
An agent acts with the rights of the person it works for. So the person who chats needs the right to use the Connection too. Administrators have it. For anyone else:
1. Open **Settings > Instance > Access** ("Einstellungen › Instanz › Zugriff").

2. Click **New right** ("Neues Recht"), choose **Connections** and the level **Use** ("Verwenden"): "Let agents this person builds or runs call the outside system through it." Pick the person and the Connection.
**Read connections** lets someone see the Connection and its status in Studio, never its key.
## Good to know
- One key serves everyone who may use the Connection. The outside system sees every call as that one account, and the instance records who asked for it.
- A Connection set up by the operator in the release config opens read-only. Changes to it go through the operator.
- A Connection cannot be deleted while an agent still has one of its tools or an App uses it. Take the tools off the agents and the Connection out of the Apps first.
## Person context on a shared REST key

An HTTP API Connection can set `settings.personContextHeader` to the header its outside system uses to select a person's data. This is off by default. The name must not carry credentials or collide with a fixed, authentication or transport header.

On the Connection page, an administrator maps each person and each service principal to its outside value. A call sends the acting identity's mapping, including when a chat agent works for a person. A live Workflow sends its own service principal's value; a live child Workflow sends its own principal's value. The publisher and the person starting a live run contribute no mapping. A test run sends the tester's own mapped value on both the root and child runs. A Workflow with an unmapped principal cannot be published. Every call checks again, so removing a mapping stops subsequent calls. A missing mapping is refused as `person_context_unmapped` before any request reaches the outside system; the header is never omitted.

Mappings are bound to the Connection's origin and header. Changing either requires mapping again. Only `connection.write` holders may read or change them; `connection.use` remains required for calls. Mapping values are runtime data in `connection_bindings`, with no token or secret handle, and are not exported as config. They remain until the Connection is deleted; removing one revokes it and clears its value while preserving its version. The audit event `connection.person_context_set` names the identity and Connection and whether it was mapped, never the value. Operation Runs keep no mapping value. Mapping values leave only for the configured outside origin, whose retention and region follow the customer's provider agreement. Returned data follows the existing retention and model-region rules for Connection results.

Person context is not available in Apps yet. App exposure (`bridge`) is refused while a Connection has person context enabled: remove App exposure before setting the header, or remove the header before enabling App exposure. Release config that sets both stops the instance at startup. Any call an App action makes of such a Connection is refused as `person_context_app_unavailable` before any request reaches the outside system, also when an agent calls the action as its tool. An agent's own call of the Connection still sends the mapped value.

This selects data at the source. It does not retract copied data or replace App data-isolation guards. Enable it for a real provider only after confirming that the shared key may send that header and that the source enforces the intended rights.

pages.title: Write a code tool
pages.description: Write source-controlled tools that run inside a client instance.
body: Custom code tools are the primary extension point for a Workshape Catalyst client instance.
A tool lets the agent do a bounded action: look up a record, create a ticket, fetch a document, send a draft to review, or call an internal service.

For larger reusable behavior, author a capability package with `@work-shape/catalyst-capability-sdk`. Capabilities can contribute tools, attachment handlers, managed object readers, and lifecycle cleanup while consuming platform-owned services such as the datasource registry and Managed Object Access.
## Configured Tool Shape
Use the public tool SDK and product-owned types. Prefer configured tool factories when customer-specific values should live in release config.
```ts
import { defineConfiguredTool, defineTool } from "@work-shape/catalyst-tool-sdk";
import { z } from "zod";
export const lookupTicketToolFactory = defineConfiguredTool({
name: "support.lookup_ticket",
configSchema: z.object({
permissionRef: z.string().min(1).default("support-ticket-reader"),
create(config) {
return defineTool({
name: "support.lookup_ticket",
description: "Look up a support ticket by its public ticket id.",
inputSchema: z.object({
ticketId: z.string().min(1),
outputSchema: z.object({
status: z.string(),
summary: z.string(),
permission: {
mode: "allow",
requiredPermissionRefs: [config.permissionRef],
async execute(input, context) {
const ticket = await context.secrets
.get("support-api")
.then((secret) => fetchTicket(secret, input.ticketId));
return {
status: "success",
output: {
status: ticket.status,
summary: ticket.summary,
auditSummary: {
message: "Ticket metadata returned to agent.",
Plain `defineTool(...)` exports are still useful for tests or fixed tools that do not need release-config parameters.
## What A Tool Tells People
The `description` is for the model. The agent page in Studio shows people something else: the
tool's `title` and a one-sentence `summary` of what it does for them, both in English and German.
A tool without them is shown by its name.
```ts
defineTool({
name: "support.lookup_ticket",
title: { en: "Look up ticket", de: "Ticket nachschlagen" },
summary: {
en: "Finds a support ticket and its status by its number.",
de: "Findet ein Support-Ticket und seinen Stand über seine Nummer.",
A deployment's tool stands in the group of this instance's own tools. Its wording lives with
the tool in the deployment repository, not in a platform package.
## Client Assembly Registration
Register tool factories explicitly in `src/client.ts`.
```ts
import { defineClientInstance } from "@work-shape/catalyst-client-assembly";
import { createEscalationToolFactory } from "../tools/create-escalation";
import { lookupTicketToolFactory } from "../tools/lookup-ticket";
export default defineClientInstance({
rootDir: new URL("..", import.meta.url),
tools: [lookupTicketToolFactory, createEscalationToolFactory],
Agents reference stable tool names in release config. They do not reference file paths.
```yaml
tools:
- name: support.lookup_ticket
enabled: true
config:
permissionRef: support-ticket-reader
- name: support.create_escalation
enabled: true
agents:
support_agent:
tools:
- support.lookup_ticket
- support.create_escalation
## Tool Design Rules
Make tool descriptions concise and model-facing.
Validate inputs with schemas.
Return structured output.
Use `output` for data the model should see in later agent-visible history.
Use `privateOutput` for data the platform may store, hydrate, or render but must never send to the model.
Use `display` for transient typed UI outputs. For a keyed domain result that should also appear
as a current, revisioned conversation resource, return `structuredResult` instead:
```ts
return toolSuccess(
{ key: "review", message: "Review replaced." },
structuredResult: {
key: "review",
kind: "support.review",
schemaVersion: 1,
title: "Support review",
data: review,
The platform derives the typed side-panel display from this single payload and exposes its current
revision through `structured_result.read`. The resource is projected from immutable tool history;
domain tools remain responsible for validating and replacing their complete result. The first valid
publication fixes the `kind` for a key. A later same-key publication with another `kind` remains in
the immutable message history but is ignored by the current-resource projection, rather than
silently reinterpreting the resource. Publications are resolved by message creation time and then
their persisted insertion ordinal, so equal timestamps still produce a deterministic revision and
snapshot.
Built-in HTML displays provide Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, and runtime theme variables inside
the rendered iframe. For ordinary model-authored HTML, use Tailwind utility classes and Lucide
markers such as `` instead of bundling those libraries into
every result. For canvas rendering, read colors from `window.vivdCatalystTheme.chartColors()`
or CSS variables such as `var(--foreground)`, `var(--border)`, and `var(--primary)`.
Do not hard-code white cards, gray/slate text, fixed dark backgrounds, or `!important`
color overrides unless a color is genuinely data-semantic.
A view loads Tailwind CSS and Lucide from the instance itself, in pinned versions served
under `/app-runtime/view/<version>/`, and no script file from anywhere else. A reverse proxy in
front of the instance must route `/app-runtime/*` to the API. To let views load scripts from
other hosts, for example a charting library, name each host in the instance config:
```yaml
views:
allowedScriptSrc:
- https://cdn.jsdelivr.net
Entries are HTTPS origins or paths; `"*"` allows every HTTPS host. The default is an empty
list. The list is release config and applies when a view is shown, so it also governs views
saved earlier: a view may load from a host once it is named and no longer after it is removed.
A view that asks for a script from another host is shown without that script. The tool stores
only the model's HTML with any CSP tag stripped; the interface composes the content policy
when it shows the view, and `connect-src` and external image loading remain blocked.
Every view is framed in a shell document the instance serves under
`/app-runtime/view-shell/<version>/`. Its policy keeps a view from moving its own frame to
another address, and the view's bootstrap takes the address from every link. Do not put
links into a view. [What A View Can Reach](/configure/release-config/#what-a-view-can-reach)
states the guarantee and its limits.
Private hydrated views get no library and no script host, whatever `views.allowedScriptSrc`
says, and they are static: no script runs in them, because a script can send packets to
another host over WebRTC and no browser lets a document forbid that. The tool places the rows
in the template as HTML-escaped text where `{{ROWS_JSON}}` or `{{DATA_JSON}}` stands, or at
the end. When the view is shown, the interface writes its body anew from an allowlist of
elements and attributes: text, headings, lists, tables, inline formatting, inline styles
without `url(`, embedded images and plain inline SVG. Links lose their address, and scripts,
forms, frames, `link` and `meta` elements are left out. The frame of such a view has a fixed
height and scrolls inside.
When `display` needs a polished visual treatment, register a client-owned widget for the
returned `display.kind`. Concrete widgets belong in `clients/*/widgets` for reference
clients or in deployment-owned code for customer assemblies. Platform packages only provide
the generic widget registry, tool frame, and fallback rendering.
Use `auditSummary` for minimized governance metadata, not raw sensitive payloads.
Do not pass broad database handles or global service containers into tools. Give tools explicit capabilities and scoped secrets.

For configured customer/domain databases, prefer platform `dataSources` and the datasource registry of the open platform. If a datasource enables `tools.query`, the platform exposes guarded `data.<source>.query` and `data.<source>.describe` tools. The description tool lists readable relations or returns columns and key relationships for one relation, so an agent can discover unfamiliar schemas without hand-writing catalog queries. The private data view capability (part of the paid capabilities and not in the open repository) uses the same registry without owning SQL execution, secret resolution, or read-only guardrails.

For byte-backed files or artifacts, use the Capability SDK's Managed Object Access rather than passing storage object keys through capability workflows. The platform owns managed file/artifact metadata; a capability may provide a byte-store adapter and object-key adapter when its storage layout is capability-specific.
## Permission Policy
Every tool should have an explicit permission expectation:
- safe read-only metadata lookup
- sensitive read
- write action
- external communication
- destructive action

A tool declares its `effect` as `reading` or `changing`; an instance with a tool that declares none does not start, and the message names the tool. A tool declares `permission.mode` as `allow`, `deny` or `approval_required`. A tool that declares no mode takes the instance default of its effect from `policy.defaults`: reading calls are allowed, and changing calls default to `confirm`, which an agent's call cannot wait for, so an instance with an enabled changing tool without a mode does not start either. Declare `allow` on a changing tool an agent may call on its own. This release runs `allow` and `deny`. It cannot pause an agent run for a person's decision and continue it afterwards, so an instance with an enabled `approval_required` tool does not start: startup validation names the tool. The API reference lists the operation `conversations.runs.command` for continuing a waiting run; in this release it answers `CONFLICT`.

What a person can approve today is a skill change. An agent with the tool `propose_skill_change` files an approval request and its run goes on without waiting; the change applies when a reviewer approves it, see [Agent skill changes](/configure/config-assets/#agent-skill-changes). `skill_change` is the only kind of approval request in this release.

pages.title: Run code execution locally
pages.description: Test execution workspaces from the repository and see what an instance needs to run them.
body: Execution workspaces give an agent a file area per conversation and a bounded command tool. The code is in the open repository: the tools `workspace.exec`, `workspace.write_file`, `workspace.edit_file`, `workspace.apply_patch`, `workspace.import_files`, `workspace.list_files`, `workspace.read_file`, `workspace.preview_images` and `workspace.promote_artifact`, the command queue, the worker and the runner image.

The reference client enables execution workspaces with the Docker sandbox: its Compose files build the runner image and start a workspace command worker, and its agent names the workspace tools. Another client assembly has to do the same, as described under [What An Instance Needs](#what-an-instance-needs).
## Requirements
- Node.js and pnpm in the version the repository's `packageManager` field names
- a disposable Postgres database for the tests, in the variable `POSTGRES_STORE_TEST_DATABASE_URL`; its role needs `CREATEDB`
- Python 3 on the path, which the command tests call
- Docker, for the runner image and the Docker sandbox
## Run The Tests
From the repository root, after `pnpm install` and `pnpm build`:
```bash
export POSTGRES_STORE_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/catalyst_test
pnpm exec vitest run tests/workspace-command-runner.test.ts
pnpm exec vitest run tests/workspace-command-worker.test.ts
pnpm exec vitest run tests/workspace-tools.test.ts
One more test builds the runner image and runs a script in it. It needs Docker and only does so when asked:
```bash
CATALYST_WORKSPACE_RUNNER_IMAGE_SMOKE=1 pnpm exec vitest run tests/artifact-preview-runtime-wiring.test.ts
## What An Instance Needs
A client assembly runs execution workspaces when all of these are in place:
- `executionWorkspaces.enabled: true` in release config
- `infrastructure.objectStorage.workspaces`: a `filesystem` root that the API and the workers share
- `infrastructure.sandbox`: `docker` with a runner image, or `local`
- a worker process beside the API, started with `runWorkspaceCommandWorker()` of the instance's `defineClientInstance` object
- the workspace tools enabled under `tools` and named in the `toolNames` of the agents that use them

Startup stops when execution workspaces are enabled without the object storage or the sandbox. [Release configuration](/configure/release-config/#infrastructure) describes both settings, and [Operate code execution](/operate/execution-workspaces/) the roles in a deployment.
## Sandbox Providers
The `local` sandbox executes commands in a temporary directory on the host. It is accepted only for a client instance whose environment is `development`, and it is for development and tests.

The `docker` sandbox is the production-shaped path. It starts a short-lived runner container per command, mounts `/workspace`, applies no-network defaults, and removes timed-out or cancelled containers. The runner image is the target `workspace-command-runner` of `docker/vivd-client.Dockerfile`.
## Debugging
When a command fails, inspect:
- the command status and error category
- bounded stdout/stderr previews in the tool result
- `workspace_command.*` audit events
- worker telemetry logs for queue counts and stale recovery
- object root and temp root paths
Do not paste workspace object keys, raw command text, stdout/stderr, or file contents into shared logs.

pages.title: Connect a local agent
pages.description: Connect Claude Code, Codex or another AI tool on your computer in one step, from Settings, Connect a local agent at /settings/you/connect.
body: A local agent is an AI tool on your own computer, such as Claude Code or Codex. Connected to the instance, it works through the `catalyst` command line tool as you: it reads and changes what you may read and change, and no more than the key you give it allows. It is not one of the instance's agents.
## Connect it
1. Open **Settings > Connect a local agent** (German: **Einstellungen > Lokalen Agenten verbinden**), at `/settings/you/connect`. The page is there when your instance offers personal API keys.
2. Pick your tool: **Claude Code**, **Codex** or **Other** (German: **Anderes**).
3. Copy the command and run it in a terminal on your computer. It needs Node 22 or later. It looks like this:
```sh
npm install --global @work-shape/catalyst-cli@<version> && catalyst setup claude-code --instance https://chat.example.com
The page fills in the instance's address and the version of the CLI published for it. Until one is published, the page says the command is not available yet and shows none.

4. Your browser opens **Settings > API keys** (German: **API-Schlüssel**) with a code. Check that it is the code your terminal shows, tick what the key may do and until when, and click **Confirm** (German: **Bestätigen**). The reading, writing and publishing rights you hold start ticked, so the key can pull, push and publish as offered, and so does the **Use** level (German: **Verwenden**); see below. Deleting is never ticked for you.
5. The terminal says which key it saved and where it wrote the skill. Start your tool.

The command installs the CLI, logs it in with a key of your own, and writes a skill that teaches your tool to use it: for Claude Code to `~/.claude/skills/catalyst/SKILL.md` (below `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` where that is set), for Codex and other tools to `~/.agents/skills/catalyst/SKILL.md`. For another tool, point it at that file. Nothing else of your tool's settings changes.

If a different file is already at that path, the command keeps it and says so. Run it again with `--force` to replace it; the old file is then kept as `SKILL.md.bak`, or as `SKILL.md.bak.1` and so on where that name is taken. The command never writes through a link at that path.
## Later
- Run the same command again to update the skill to a new release. A key that still works is kept.
- The key is listed under **Settings > API keys** with the name of the tool and your computer, such as "Claude Code on laptop". Revoke it there and the tool can no longer reach the instance.
- `catalyst logout --instance <address>` removes the key from your computer.
## What the tool may do

The key acts as you and never does more than you may do at the moment of each call. The scopes you tick narrow it further, for example reading agents only. A right an administrator takes from you is gone from the key at once.

The **Use** level lets the key use the Connections, Data Stores, Knowledge Bases and Workflows you may use: `connection.use`, `data_store.insert`, `data_store.execute`, `knowledge_base.use` and `workflow.use`. Settings offers the ones you hold. Your tool needs them to publish a Workflow whose Service Principal uses a resource, since publishing lends the Service Principal's rights and you may lend only what you hold. With them the tool can also start a Workflow you may start. For a key that only reads or writes, untick the level.
The skill tells the tool to pull before it pushes, to show you a change before it is sent, to never delete assets on the instance without asking you, and to treat a refusal as final.
## Keys stay with you

Nobody sends you a key, and no agent can make one. The page itself issues nothing: a key exists only after you confirm the code your own terminal shows. An agent in the chat that is asked for a key answers with the link to Connect a local agent. Never confirm a code somebody else sent you.
Run `catalyst docs` for this release's product docs index, or `catalyst docs <page>` for a page from it.
When `catalyst context` finds an older CLI than the published version the instance names, it prints an npm update command on stderr; it leaves stdout unchanged and never updates itself.

pages.title: Run the reference client locally
pages.description: Start the repository's reference client as a local test instance.
body: The repository includes a reference client at `clients/demo`. It runs as a local test instance and shows how a client assembly is put together.
## Requirements
- Node.js compatible with the workspace toolchain
- pnpm 10
- Docker for the local Postgres service, the workers and the command sandbox
- an OpenAI API key for the default model
## Start It
From the repository root:
```bash
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env
pnpm build
pnpm dev
Add your OpenAI API key to `.env` before you chat with an agent. The reference client keeps
its tools, prompts, and tool result widgets under `clients/demo`.
This starts:
- the chat UI on `http://127.0.0.1:5173`
- Postgres through `clients/demo/docker-compose.yml`
- the artifact preview worker and the workspace command worker, which runs the agent's commands and Page builds in containers of the runner image it builds
## Default Standalone Users
The reference client seeds standalone users from release config.
Use the credentials configured by:
- `DEMO_SUPERADMIN_EMAIL` / `DEMO_SUPERADMIN_PASSWORD`
- `DEMO_USER_EMAIL` / `DEMO_USER_PASSWORD`
The example values in the repository are:
- `superadmin@example.test` / `demo-superadmin-password`
- `user@example.test` / `demo-user-password`
Replace seeded credentials before using any production-shaped standalone deployment.
## Useful Checks
```bash
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test
pnpm build
pnpm check
pnpm test:e2e
`pnpm test:e2e` uses deterministic fixture config and does not require an OpenAI key.

pages.title: Ways to run an instance
pages.description: Choose whether the dedicated instance is operated for you or by you.
body: Every Workshape Catalyst deployment is a dedicated client instance. The main decision is who operates it.
## Operated Dedicated Instance
Use this when a team wants the chat outcome but does not want to run infrastructure.
The customer provides:
- the instance brief
- user and role expectations
- agent instructions and workflow examples
- custom tool requirements or tool code
- model provider and region constraints
- retention, deletion, and audit requirements
- branding and chat copy
- customer application integration details
The instance operator owns:
- Docker images and runtime services
- database, object storage, and backups
- reverse proxy and TLS
- migrations and deploy scripts
- health checks and incident response
- production env files and secret handling
This is often the right starting point. The customer still controls the workflow and sensitive-data assumptions, but does not need to become the platform operator.
## Self-Operated Instance
Use this when the customer needs direct operational control or wants to run the instance inside its own infrastructure boundary.
The customer owns both layers:
- client assembly code and release config
- tool implementations and integrations
- runtime infrastructure
- backups, monitoring, TLS, secrets, and restore drills
- provider contracts and region controls
The same platform package boundaries apply. Self-operation should not mean forking the platform.
## Customer-Hosted Integrations
Some systems remain outside Workshape Catalyst even when the instance is operated for the customer.
Examples:
- a customer API called by a custom code tool
- an internal document system called by a custom code tool
- a customer endpoint that exchanges an existing app session for a short-lived chat session token

These are customer-hosted integrations. They are not part of the Workshape Catalyst runtime, but the instance must document how it authenticates to them, what data it sends, and what failures look like.
## Choosing A Path
Choose operated dedicated instance when speed and low operational burden matter most.
Choose self-operated instance when infrastructure location, network boundaries, internal policy, or direct operational ownership matter most.
In both cases, write the [instance brief](/operate/instance-brief/) before implementation.

pages.title: What the platform provides
pages.description: How Workshape Catalyst is meant to be used by teams configuring their own agent chat.
body: Workshape Catalyst gives an organization a dedicated agent chat instance without asking that organization to fork the platform.
The platform provides the reusable pieces:
- chat API and streaming path
- standalone and embedded chat surfaces
- auth adapter boundary
- agent runtime boundary
- tool execution boundary
- release config validation
- conversation storage
- usage governance
- minimized audit events
The customer-specific layer provides the narrow pieces:
- enabled tools and modules
- custom code tools
- branding and chat copy
- retention and usage policy
- auth integration settings
- deployment wiring

What people build on a running instance is not part of that layer. Agents, skills, Apps, Workflows, Connections and guardrails live in the instance's database and change at runtime, in Studio, through an agent or with the [CLI](/configure/cli/), without a deployment.
## Who This Is For
These docs are for instance operators and technical teams who want a chat agent for their company, internal process, product, community, or other endeavor.

Some teams will run the infrastructure themselves. Others will only provide the instance brief, config, tools, and integration details while someone else operates the dedicated instance. Both paths use the same product model.
## What You Should Not Do
Do not copy platform internals into your client instance.
Do not add runtime-only tools by mutating a live server.
Do not put customer-specific prompts, labels, examples, or tool behavior into platform packages.
Do not treat audit logs as full transcripts. Audit events should be minimized governance metadata.
## First Decisions
Before writing tools or deploying anything, decide:
- who operates the instance
- what the agent is allowed to help with
- which users may access it
- which customer systems and documents it may touch
- what should be retained, audited, deleted, and backed up
- which model provider and region are acceptable
Start with [Ways to run an instance](/getting-started/operating-models/) and then write the [instance brief](/operate/instance-brief/).
## How Work Flows
```text
instance brief
-> release config
-> custom tools and integrations
-> client assembly validation
-> build and deploy
-> governed chat use

This keeps the instance explainable: what it runs can be traced back to source-controlled config, tool code and platform package versions, and every change to an agent, skill, App, Workflow, Connection or guardrail is a revision with its author.

pages.title: Rights at a glance
pages.description: Three pictures that explain who may do what in Catalyst, where an App's data comes from, and what a workspace gives its members.
body: This page is for the administrators of a Catalyst instance. It all comes down to two questions: who are you, and what may you do? [How rights work](/operate/how-rights-work/) explains the same system in full detail.
## Two questions

**Who are you?** A person who signs in. A person who is a member of a workspace also gets what is shared there. A Workflow runs as a technical account. By default it gets its own when it is first published, with only the rights its steps need, and only rights the person publishing holds themselves. A Workflow can instead name an existing shared account. An agent has none: it acts with the rights of the person it works for, and a tool on an agent adds no right.

**What may you do?** A right is an action in a place, for example "use the accounting Connection". The place is one workspace, one item, or the whole instance. A role bundles rights; the three roles User, Admin and Superadmin are fixed. A right is given to a person, to a Workflow's technical account, or comes with a role.
Three rules always hold:
- Nothing is allowed until it is given.
- A deny beats every allow, even an administrator's. Exporting an agent and setting the default agent are not affected.
- Using is not editing. Whoever may open an App may not change it for that reason.

## Where an App gets its data, and who sees it

An App shows data in two ways: live from an outside system, or from its Data Store. A Data Store is filled by Workflows, by the App's own actions that add rows, and by people with the right to add rows. The two ways follow different rules. The numbers in the picture are the four decisions on the way.
People can be granted `data_store.read`, `data_store.insert` and `data_store.execute` on one
store, on the stores a workspace owns, or on the instance. `insert` adds rows; `execute`

default; Builder and Publisher do not. An agent acts with its person's rights, and merely

1. **Catalyst decides who may reach the outside system.** The App calls the Connection as Anna. Anna needs the right to use the Connection herself; the App lends her none. The operation must also list Apps under **Callable by** ("Aufrufbar durch").
2. **The outside system decides what it shows.** It answers with what the account the Connection signed in with may see there.

3. **The Workflow runs as its technical account,** whether a person or a schedule starts it. It can do only what that account may. Whoever publishes it decides what gets copied. A test run of a draft is different: it acts as the person testing, and can do only what both that person and the Workflow's account may. For a Workflow with its own account, that means the rights the draft's steps need, even before the first publish.
4. **Whoever may open the App sees what its queries show.** For an App in a workspace, these are the workspace's members, and the instance's administrators.
So two rules apply:
- **Read live:** the rights of the person looking count.

- **Stored:** like an exported report, the App is the gate. Whoever may open it sees what its queries show, without a right on the Connection. The person who publishes the App needs the right to read the Data Store where the App reads from it, and the right to add rows where the App adds rows.
## Workspaces
A workspace is where a team works together. Members see its shared conversations, open its Apps and use the agents offered there. Private conversations stay private.

Being a member is not building. Editing a workspace's agents and skills is a right of its own, given on the Access page. Someone who only builds need not be a member and sees no conversations. A workspace's Apps are edited by administrators.
