An agent of the whole instance can be offered in several workspaces under **Available in** ("Verfügbar in"). Only someone with the right to edit agents on the whole instance can change where it is offered.
## Connections

A Connection is signed in with one shared account ("Ein gemeinsames Konto"). Everyone who may use it sees the same in the outside system: what that account sees. If a team should be able to do less, create a second Connection with fewer operations and give the right to use it to each person of that team.
A right on a Connection is given on that one Connection. Writing, deleting and approving Connections stay with the Admin role.

pages.title: Guardrails
pages.description: Rules that check an action just before it happens and warn, ask for an approval or block; how to read them in Studio, and how to write, test and publish one.
body: A guardrail is a rule that checks an action just before it happens, for example "no bank account numbers in skills". When the rule matches, the guardrail warns, sends the action for approval, or blocks it.
The German interface shows the labels in quotes.
## When a guardrail runs
A guardrail is bound to one moment:
- before an asset is saved, such as an agent, a skill or an App draft, whether in Studio, by an agent or with the CLI;
- before any operation is called, by a person, an agent, an App or a Workflow;
- before an App, a Workflow or a Data Store is published;
- before a request for approval is filed, such as a skill change an agent proposes.
It can be narrowed further, for example to skills only, to one agent, or to one workspace.
Studio says this in one sentence for each guardrail, under **When it runs** ("Wann sie greift"). For example:
> Runs before an agent saves a skill, in workspace Finance. Checks the content for a text pattern. Blocks if the check fails.
> Läuft, bevor ein Agent einen Skill speichert, im Workspace Finance. Prüft den Inhalt auf ein Textmuster. Blockiert, wenn die Prüfung anschlägt.
## What happens when one matches
| On a hit ("Bei einem Treffer") | What the person sees |
| **Warns** ("Warnt") | The action goes ahead. The reason is shown and kept beside it. |

| **Needs approval** ("Braucht Freigabe") | A change waits in the **Inbox** ("Eingang") until someone who may decide approves it. A read can't wait, so it is refused; so is a change that can't wait, such as an agent saving into an App draft. |
| **Blocks** ("Blockiert") | Nothing happens. The person or the agent is told the guardrail's reason. |

When a guardrail blocks something an agent tried in a chat, the agent's step shows as failed, such as "Could not change …", "Could not read …" or "The save failed", followed by the guardrail's reason, or "A guardrail blocked the call" when it gives none.
Every guardrail that applies runs, and the strictest answer wins. A guardrail can only make things stricter: it never allows what a right or the policy refuses.

A guardrail checks either for a **text pattern** ("Muster"), such as the shape of an IBAN, or with a **model** that reads the content against a written rule. A model check is a model call of the instance and counts toward its usage.
## Read them in Studio
Open **Studio** and choose **Guardrails** ("Leitplanken"). Each row has the sentence that says when it runs, and what it does on a hit. Open one to see:
- **Check** ("Prüfung"): when it runs, what it applies to ("Gilt für"), how it checks ("Wie sie prüft") and what it does on a hit;
- **Recent hits** ("Letzte Treffer"): how often it warned, held or blocked in the last 7 and 30 days, and the newest hits.
Hits never name a person. They say which rule, when, and what kind of thing was checked, not who did it. A list of who tripped which rule would make the instance a tool for watching employees.
The page in Studio only reads. You write a guardrail with the CLI, as below.
## Publishing needs an instance admin's approval

Every instance carries one guardrail of the platform, **Publishing needs an instance admin's approval** ("Veröffentlichen braucht die Freigabe eines Instanz-Admins"). It stands above the list in Studio, under **Shipped with the platform** ("Mit der Plattform geliefert"), and is on.

- A holder of `app.approve` or `workflow.approve` at instance scope clicks **Publish** in the app: the new version is live at once, and the record names them as publisher and approver. A workspace-scoped approve right does not count. A CLI publish always waits when approval is required, even for an admin: the server cannot tell a person at a terminal from an agent driving it, and keys never carry approve rights. The CLI names the request; an instance approver can approve it in the **Inbox**.

- Anyone else who may publish waits: their publish lands in the **Inbox** ("Eingang") of the instance admins as **App to publish** ("App zur Veröffentlichung") or **Workflow to publish** ("Workflow zur Veröffentlichung"). The item shows the version and the one it replaces, the files that differ, the changing actions or steps that are new or changed, the outside hosts it adds, the Connections, the Data Stores and the account a Workflow runs as. **Approve and publish** makes exactly that version live; if the draft or the live version changed meanwhile, the item says so and can no longer be approved. Publishing again replaces the waiting request.

- An instance admin can switch it off on that card, after a question. Then whoever may publish makes a new version live with their own click. Switching it off and on is recorded in the audit log, and an update of the platform never switches it back on.

Whatever the switch says, a new version goes live only on a person's click. `--yes` on the CLI publishes nothing by itself: the publish waits in your own Inbox, which nobody else sees, and your **Allow** there is your click on Publish. An instance approver's Allow makes it live at once; anyone else's files the item above for the instance admins. A publish from an agent or another program publishes nothing.
## Where guardrails come from
- **The operator's floor.** The operator sets guardrails in the release config. They always run, nobody can change or stop them in the product, and Studio marks them "set by the operator".

- **Guardrails written as assets.** An administrator writes further guardrails for the whole instance or for one shared workspace. They add checks to the floor and never remove one. A workspace's guardrail checks only what happens in that workspace.
Only the operator's guardrails check changes to guardrails, so a guardrail can never stop you from fixing one.
## Write, try and publish a guardrail

You write a guardrail as a file and save it with [the CLI](/configure/cli/): `catalyst guardrail put <name> --from <folder> --if-revision new`, or `catalyst config push` from a working copy. [Guardrails as assets](/configure/config-assets/#guardrails-as-assets) shows the file. A new guardrail is a **draft**: it checks nothing until it is published.
1. **Try it on an example.** `catalyst guardrail test <name> --text "<sample>"` says what the draft would answer. `--asset skill:<name>` tries it on an existing skill. A test keeps no hit.
2. **See what it would have done.** `catalyst guardrail dry-run <name>` counts what the draft would have warned on, held or blocked in the last 14 days, without names.

3. **Publish it.** `catalyst guardrail publish <name> --revision <n>` shows the dry run first. If the guardrail would have stopped actions, it asks you to confirm with the number it counted (`--confirm <n>`). Tip: publish it with the outcome "warn" first and watch its hits for a while.
4. **Stop it** with `catalyst guardrail unpublish <name>`. The draft stays.

Publishing is a right of its own. Administrators hold it for the instance. To let someone set the rules of one shared workspace, an administrator opens **Settings > Instance > Access** ("Einstellungen › Instanz › Zugriff"), clicks **New right** ("Neues Recht") and chooses **Guardrails** with the level **Publish** for that workspace: "Make a guardrail of this workspace enforce, or stop it. A guardrail stops other people's work in the workspace."
## More detail
- [Guardrails as assets](/configure/config-assets/#guardrails-as-assets): the file format and the rules for workspace guardrails.
- [Release config, Guardrails](/configure/release-config/#guardrails): the floor, every field, and how content and files are read.
- [How rights work](/operate/how-rights-work/#guardrails): where guardrails sit among rights and policy.

pages.title: Sign-in and embedding
pages.description: Connect Workshape Catalyst to users in an existing customer application.
body: The embedded chat path should rely on the customer application as the login authority.
Workshape Catalyst receives a short-lived chat session token and maps it into a product-owned authenticated user.
## Recommended Embedded Flow
```text
authenticated customer app session
-> widget asks customer backend for a chat session token
-> customer backend verifies its own user
-> customer backend calls chat backend token endpoint
-> chat backend returns short-lived chat session token
-> widget calls chat API with that token
The browser never receives the customer app's server-to-server credential.
## Browser Origins
Configure each embedding site's exact origin through the client assembly's `allowedOrigins`,
`CHAT_UI_ORIGIN`, or `auth.standalone.trustedOrigins`. The assembly merges these into one list
for Better Auth, CORS, and session-cookie origin checks. Development expands configured
loopback origins to `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, and `[::1]` at the same port. Without configured
origins, same-origin requests still work; cross-origin requests receive no CORS grant.
Both the assembly and direct `createChatServer` callers accept `allowedOrigins` as a string
or an array of strings. Startup validates HTTP and HTTPS URLs, serializes their origins,
and removes duplicates. Wildcards, opaque origins, and other value types are rejected.
Cookie-authenticated writes require an allowed or same-server `Origin`. When `Origin` is
absent, only `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` is accepted. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are exempt.
Bearer tokens, API-key exchange, and server credentials do not require this cookie check,
but browser callers still need their origin configured for CORS. Custom cookie auth adapters
must return `authenticationMethod: "session-cookie"` on the authenticated user.
An `Authorization` or `X-Server-Credential` header excludes standalone cookie and development
authentication, regardless of adapter order. Invalid explicit credentials never fall back to
a standalone session. Token-authenticated requests do not use the cookie origin check.
The cookie-only `/api/auth/*` endpoints, including session lookup and sign-out, reject
requests carrying either explicit credential header without accessing the session.
The API client omits cookies whenever `getToken` is configured, even if it currently returns
no token. Passing a widget `token` also selects this mode. Token-mode downloads and event
streams use the same transport; browser-managed downloads are disabled even if requested.
Without a token source, standalone requests, downloads, and event streams keep using cookies.
Every auth adapter must declare `credentialMode: "ambient"` or `"explicit"`. Only explicitly
marked credential adapters are consulted when an explicit credential header is present;
unmarked adapters are excluded too. Wrappers must preserve the wrapped adapter's mode.
## Token Claims
Keep token claims minimal:
- stable external user id
- display label
- optional verified email
- roles or permission refs
- client instance id
- expiry
- correlation id where useful
Do not put sensitive documents, tool outputs, long-lived credentials, or workflow payloads in the token.
## Identity Mapping
Conversation ownership should use a product-owned user identity.
External auth-source ids map to product users through user identity mappings. This allows standalone and embedded identities to share one conversation owner when linking is allowed and unambiguous.
Verified email can be a linking hint. It should not be the durable account key.
## Standalone And Control Plane Login
Standalone chat and control-plane routes may need their own login path.

The platform default is to keep that behind the same product-owned auth contract and use a self-hosted auth implementation internally. Do not expose auth-library user or session types across platform public boundaries.
## API Keys
An instance has two kinds of API keys. Both are exchanged at `POST /api/v1/auth/access-token` for a short-lived access token, and both need `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` (below).

- **A personal key** acts as the person who issued it, narrowed to the scopes ticked when it was made, and never does more than that person may at the moment of a call. A person issues one under **Settings > You > API keys** (German: **Einstellungen › Du › API-Schlüssel**) or with `catalyst login`, which saves it for the CLI. A key lives at most a year, and no key issues another key. This needs the module `personalApiKeys`. See [Log in](/configure/cli/#log-in).
- **A service principal's key** is for automation such as CI or another system. It acts as the service principal and never as a person.
### Service Principals

Non-human clients are service principals, not product users. A service principal owns permissions and may have multiple independently revocable API keys. An API key is exchanged at `POST /api/v1/auth/access-token` for a short-lived service access token; normal API calls use that access token and do not create a product-user record.

Set a stable, high-entropy `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` of at least 32 characters on the API server to enable exchange. It signs short-lived service tokens, must match across replicas, and must remain stable across restarts. API keys themselves live hashed in the database; their plaintext value is shown only once at creation and must be stored in an operator or CI secret store.

Keep machine credentials separate from embedded-chat credentials. `CHAT_SERVER_CREDENTIAL` authorizes a trusted customer backend to issue human chat session tokens at `POST /api/v1/instance/session-tokens` with the `x-server-credential` header; the CLI does not use it.
## Embed Surface
The embed surface should be small:
- load the chat shell
- request or receive a chat session token
- pass safe client config to the UI
- send chat requests to the dedicated chat backend
Customer application code should not need to know agent runtime, tool execution, or database internals.

pages.title: Capacity and limits
pages.description: Size an instance using the limits enforced by the platform code.
body: For an instance serving 5,000 to 10,000 people, size against simultaneous runs, model calls, uploaded files and retained conversations. The code states limits for individual requests and workers. It does not state a supported people count or a hardware size for that population.

The tables below describe the platform packages in this repository. A capability can add its own limits. Check its implementation separately, especially for document ingestion. Defaults are the values used when the setting is omitted. MiB means 1,048,576 bytes and KiB means 1,024 bytes. Source paths are relative to the repository root.

**Fixed** means there is no release config or environment knob. Where a TypeScript constructor option exists, the table names it separately. A page size bounds one response or screen, not the number of stored records. A renewable lease detects a lost worker; it is not a maximum job duration.
See [deployment](/operate/deployment/), [release config](/configure/release-config/) and [governance](/operate/governance/) for deployment and policy details.
## Chat and runs
Runtime defaults come from `packages/config-schema/src/schemas.ts`. The implementation is in `packages/agent-runtime/src/local-agent-runtime.ts`.

| What it bounds                                                                              | Default                                             | Grows with                            | Knob and source                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | What a person sees at the limit                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

| Model steps in one agent run                                                                | 64                                                  | Runs and tool rounds                  | `runtime.maxSteps`; an agent's `maxSteps` overrides it. Runtime fallback: `DEFAULT_MAX_STEPS` in `local-agent-runtime.ts`.                                                                                                                                                     | The run fails with “Agent exceeded the maximum step limit”.                                                                                                                                                                                       |

| Identical calls to the same tool with the same input in one run                             | 3                                                   | Runs and repeated tool calls          | `runtime.repeatedToolCallLimit`; fallback `DEFAULT_REPEATED_TOOL_CALL_LIMIT` in `local-agent-runtime.ts`.                                                                                                                                                                      | The fourth call returns a `repeated_tool_call` failure to the agent, which can continue with a different call.                                                                                                                                    |

| Wait for the source of an agent's data tools, at the start of a run and at each call of one | 10 seconds                                          | Runs of agents that list data tools   | `runtime.dataToolDescribeTimeoutMs`; fallback `DATA_TOOL_DESCRIBE_TIMEOUT_MS` in `packages/agent-runtime/src/model-tool-materialization.ts` and `packages/tool-execution/src/tool-operation.ts`. When it is reached the run goes on without data tools, or the one call fails. |

| Recent history projected to a model without provider compaction                             | Target of 20 messages                               | Conversations and messages            | `DEFAULT_CONVERSATION_HISTORY_LIMIT` in `local-agent-runtime.ts`; TypeScript option `historyMessageLimit`, no release config knob.                                                                                                                                             | Older context is omitted from the model request. Complete history groups are kept, so the result can exceed 20 messages. The stored conversation is unchanged.                                                                                    |

| Provider compaction threshold                                                               | Unset                                               | Conversation context                  | `infrastructure.models.<id>.contextManagement.compaction.compactThresholdTokens` in `packages/config-schema/src/infrastructure.ts`; requires `api: responses`.                                                                                                                 | When configured, the provider compacts context at its threshold and the runtime keeps a continuation. This threshold does not cap stored messages.                                                                                                |

| Text from each tool result projected to the model                                           | 60,000 estimated tokens; no byte setting by default | Runs and tool output                  | `modelContext.toolOutput.maxTokens` and optional `maxBytes` in `schemas.ts`; projection in `packages/agent-runtime/src/model-context-projection.ts`.                                                                                                                           | The model receives the head and tail plus a bounding notice. Full output stays in history. These are projection targets, not strict byte ceilings.                                                                                                |

| Simultaneous active runs in one conversation                                                | 1                                                   | Conversations and runs                | Fixed in `packages/server/src/conversations/run-start-service.ts` and `packages/postgres-store/src/postgres-agent-run-operations.ts`.                                                                                                                                          | Another message is refused while the conversation has an active run.                                                                                                                                                                              |

| Durable run observations read per poll                                                      | 100 every 500 ms                                    | Runs and observation events           | TypeScript options `observationBatchSize` and `pollIntervalMs` in `packages/agent-runtime/src/store-backed-agent-runtime.ts`; no release config knob.                                                                                                                          | Events beyond a batch arrive on later polls.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

| Recent conversations in the conversation palette                                            | 8                                                   | Conversations per person              | Fixed `PALETTE_RECENT_LIMIT` in `packages/chat-ui/src/chat/workspace/conversation-palette.tsx`.                                                                                                                                                                                | Only eight recent choices appear before searching. This does not cap the sidebar or storage.                                                                                                                                                      |

| Conversation search results                                                                 | 20                                                  | Conversations per person or workspace | Fixed `CONVERSATION_SEARCH_RESULTS` in `packages/chat-ui/src/shared/api/conversation-search-query.ts`.                                                                                                                                                                         | Search shows the most recently changed matches. A narrower search finds other matches.                                                                                                                                                            |

| Source text and model time for a generated title                                            | 800 characters; 60 seconds                          | New conversations                     | `MAX_TITLE_SOURCE_CHARS` (`conversations/conversation-title.ts`), `CONVERSATION_TITLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (`conversations/conversation-service.ts`) in `packages/server/src`.                                                                                                          | Source text is shortened. A title call that times out leaves the existing title and follows the title job's retry policy.                                                                                                                         |

| Result retained for replay of a changing operation                                          | 256 KiB                                             | Operation runs and result size        | Fixed `OPERATION_RUN_OUTPUT_MAX_BYTES` in `packages/tool-execution/src/operation-execution.ts`.                                                                                                                                                                                | The original call can succeed. Repeating it with the same key returns `409 OUTPUT_NOT_RETAINED` if its result was too large to keep. A call whose result holds a secret, such as a new API key, keeps no result at any size and answers the same. |

A data tool is an agent tool that exists as data, such as an operation of a Connection (`connection.<name>.<operation>`). It is called as an operation like every other tool, so the same policy applies: a changing data tool is refused for an agent under the default `confirm`, and it runs without a confirmation where an administrator's central setting says `allow`.

The conversation list uses the shared API paging defaults of 50 items, at most 200 per request (`listQuerySchema` in `packages/api-contract/src/shared.ts`). The sidebar asks for 30 conversations at a time (`RAIL_PAGE_SIZE` in `packages/chat-ui/src/shared/api/rail-conversations.ts`): one request when a workspace opens, and one more each time a person scrolls to the end of the list or picks "Load more". The browser holds the pages a person has loaded until they switch workspace, so the rows held are 30 times the pages loaded, and every loaded row is on the page. While a run is active outside the open conversation, or a new conversation waits for its title, the sidebar reads its first page again every 2 seconds (`RAIL_REFRESH_INTERVAL_MS` in `packages/chat-ui/src/chat/workspace/use-conversation-list-refresh.ts`); no request reads more than one page.

## Workflow datasets

Dataset ceilings are operator settings under `workflows.datasets`, rather than fixed customer limits. `rows` defaults to 5,000,000; `bytes` to 2 GiB per dataset; `rowBytes` to 256 KiB; `runBytes` to 10 GiB owned by a run at once; and `instanceBytes` to 50 GiB. EW-LIM's `limits.datasetBytes` may lower the per-dataset ceiling. A producer that reaches one fails with `dataset_limit` and the setting's name; other runs continue.

The writer accumulates one 4 MiB uncompressed part, makes a contiguous copy for compression, and holds the compressed part during upload, plus one row. `DATASET_PART_BYTES` in `packages/workflows/src/datasets.ts` controls this checkpoint size, not the customer's dataset capacity. Byte admission uses transactionally locked instance/run counters, so its query cost does not grow with the number of datasets. Row processing grows with the rows read or written. Loop reads seek by part metadata and stream the part containing the requested item.

The real-Postgres regression writes and resumes 9,000 rows with 1,024-character values across three parts, then verifies every index exactly once. A separate concurrent test admits one of two writers under a 100-byte instance ceiling. These are correctness checks, not a production throughput benchmark (`tests/workflow-dataset-storage.test.ts`).

Parts use the `files` object store's region and encryption. Exclude `workflow-runs/` from backups: restored metadata without its parts answers `dataset_expired`. Run/Workflow deletion marks records before asynchronous prefix cleanup. Successful runs release intermediates; failed runs retain them for the seven-day resume window. Root outputs default to seven days, may set `retention.datasets`, and never exceed step-data retention. Test roots retain no output datasets. Rows require `workflow.read_run_data`; ordinary run views receive only schema, counts and size.

## Model usage and admission

Usage safeguards stop a loop that runs away; the spend budget is what limits cost. They hold per person, across API processes and workers, so one person who reaches one stops only themselves. Each person has two buckets of the same size: one for their own calls (chat, agent runs, the query of a Knowledge Base search) and one for the calls the product makes for them (titles, guardrail checks, document extraction). The calls of no person, such as workflow runs of a service principal, share one bucket of seven times a person's (`UNATTENDED_SAFEGUARD_FACTOR` in `packages/usage-governance/src/index.ts`). Knowledge Base ingestion is outside chat safeguards and spend budgets (KB-ISO); query embeddings remain chat. The spend budget counts chat calls of the instance together. Admission reserves capacity before calling the provider. These safeguards can be exceeded when a completed call uses more than its reservation; they are not provider output caps.

At the default 200 million tokens per person per day, the unattended bucket holds 1.4 billion tokens. At 2 million counted tokens per minute it takes 700 minutes per daily window, or at most 1,400 minutes (23 h 20 min) if a loop crosses the UTC reset. Ten workflows each using twice the measured busy day need about 686 million tokens/day and 15.1 billion/month, below the shared 1.4 billion/day and 28 billion/month. A person has 100 minutes per daily window at that rate. Custom limits change these bounds.

The defaults fit a long working day of a busy person about five times. In the acceptance walk of 2026-10-18 one person's normal agent use made 91 model calls holding 2.5 million tokens in 35 minutes: about 1,250 calls and 34 million tokens in 8 hours, and 754 million tokens in 22 working days.

Admission updates database counters atomically: for every call the counters of the instance and of the call's bucket, each for the day and the month. A person's counters exist only for the current day and month; reconciliation removes older ones, and the deletion of the person's account removes theirs. The calls of a deleted account stay on the instance's counters only. Admission, settlement and reconciliation lock counters in one order, the instance's first. API request rate counters are held in process memory, so the current deployment contract calls for one API process. Adding workers does not multiply the usage allowance, but a second API process would have separate request rate counters.

A config push is one `assets.sync` call: at most 2,000 items for a holder of the release right and 200 for every other caller (`ASSET_RELEASE_SYNC_MAX_ITEMS`, `ASSET_SYNC_MAX_ITEMS` in `packages/api-contract/src/assets.ts`), in a request body of at most 20 MiB (`ASSET_SYNC_BODY_MAX_BYTES`, the same file), of which one put item takes at most 2 MiB (`ASSET_SYNC_ITEM_MAX_BYTES`). All four are fixed. The body is parsed in memory before any check, so one push costs up to that much memory and blocks the process while it is parsed; the write rate limit bounds how many arrive. A push takes one lock per instance on the asset set, so pushes and saves of one instance are applied one after another, each for the time of its own items. Under the lock the statements grow with the items in steps of 500 (`ASSET_WRITE_CHUNK` in `packages/postgres-store/src/postgres-config-asset-operations.ts`), not per item: the rows of all named assets in one read, their highest revisions in one, then inserts and one update per 500 items. Measured on a local Postgres 17 with small skills: 200 updates in 7 statements and about 40 ms, 2,000 creates in 12 statements and about 200 ms, 2,000 updates in 13 statements and about 170 ms. Larger definitions add transfer time, bounded by the 20 MiB body. Before the write the lock also covers one read of the active revision ids of the instance (one row per active asset), and a full read of the asset set only when another write changed it since this one was checked. The CLI says to push in parts with `--only` at either limit. A first `catalyst config pull` reads each asset with one `assets.get`, eight at a time, so it grows with the asset count and is bounded by `rateLimits.readPerMinute` (default 6,000); later pulls read only assets whose revision changed. No total asset-count ceiling exists; that gap is listed below.

The row setting therefore bounds the returned result, not all rows already fetched into memory.

The separate `@work-shape/catalyst-postgres-connector` executor enforces the following ceilings. Its source is `packages/postgres-connector/src/executor/limits.ts`. `PostgresLimits` is a TypeScript target option, not a release config key, and can only lower the four stated limits.

| What it bounds                                           | Default                                                                        | Grows with                 | Knob and source                                                                                                                                                                       | What a person sees at the limit                                                                                         |

| Connections to one target under one credential           | 4                                                                              | Concurrent query runs      | `POSTGRES_POOL_MAX_CONNECTIONS`; lower with `PostgresLimits.maxConnections`.                                                                                                          | A query waits for a connection.                                                                                         |

| Wait for a connector connection                          | 5 seconds                                                                      | Concurrent query runs      | Fixed `POSTGRES_POOL_ACQUIRE_WAIT_MS`.                                                                                                                                                | The executor returns a `busy` failure when no connection becomes free. This is a wait deadline, not a queue length cap. |

| Query execution time                                     | 15 seconds, plus 1 second for the executor's cancellation deadline             | Query work                 | `POSTGRES_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS`; lower with `PostgresLimits.statementTimeoutMs`. Fixed `POSTGRES_DEADLINE_GRACE_MS`; cancellation repeats every `POSTGRES_CANCEL_REPEAT_MS` (100 ms). | A timed-out query fails and is cancelled.                                                                               |

| Returned rows and bytes                                  | 1,000 rows; 2 MiB                                                              | Query result size          | `POSTGRES_RESULT_MAX_ROWS`, `POSTGRES_RESULT_MAX_BYTES`; lower with `PostgresLimits.maxRows`, `maxBytes`.                                                                             | The result reports `truncatedBy: rows` or `bytes`.                                                                      |

| Cursor fetch batch and socket read margin                | 100 rows per batch; 16 MiB beyond the result byte cap                          | Rows and large values      | Fixed `POSTGRES_CURSOR_BATCH_ROWS`, `POSTGRES_READ_MARGIN_BYTES`.                                                                                                                     | Caps are checked after batches. A read far beyond the byte cap can end the connection before the value is fully read.   |

| Query input                                              | 20,000 characters; 100 parameters                                              | Query text and parameters  | Fixed `POSTGRES_QUERY_TEXT_MAX_CHARS`, `POSTGRES_PARAMETERS_MAX_COUNT`.                                                                                                               | Oversized input is rejected before execution.                                                                           |

| Privilege objects listed in a probe                      | 200                                                                            | Connected database objects | Fixed `POSTGRES_PRIVILEGE_OBJECTS_MAX_LISTED`.                                                                                                                                        | The probe lists a bounded sample of objects.                                                                            |

| Connector connection startup, idle close and replacement | 30-second connect timeout; 60-second idle close; 2,700-second maximum lifetime | Connections                | Fixed `POSTGRES_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `POSTGRES_POOL_IDLE_CLOSE_SECONDS`, `POSTGRES_CONNECTION_MAX_LIFETIME_SECONDS`.                                                             | Connection startup can fail; idle or aged connections are replaced.                                                     |

For 5,000 to 10,000 people, record the expected peak active runs, model calls per run, documents and bytes per day, asset count, and retained conversation volume before assigning hardware. Validate those workloads against the instance's actual configuration and capability packages. This page supplies code limits; it supplies no measured throughput claim.
## Workflow batch measurements
EW-BATCH was measured on 2026-10-18 at core commit `6c9136836`, on a Blacksmith 4-vCPU
Ubuntu runner with real Postgres 17 and an in-memory object store. The source streams
synthetic `{ index, valid }` rows. Elapsed time covers start, dataset capture, batch calls,
audit and step persistence, and completion; fixture setup and upstream network latency are
outside the measurement. Other test files share the runner. These figures describe the
engine workload exercised, with 100,000 rows as the largest measured input.
| Input rows      | Rows per batch | Iterations | Step runs | Elapsed  |
The acceptance test verifies every row exactly once and one parent dataset for all views.
It also writes one failures dataset per batch call, including empty failure results; those
are operation outputs, so the three cases have 4, 601 and 201 dataset records respectively.
No parent rows are copied into slice objects or iteration records. The 600-row and
100,000-row measurements are separate workloads; upstream per-client processing adds its
own work.
Scheduling and persistence grow with batch iterations, and reads grow with decoded bytes.
A range can reread its boundary compressed part. `DATASET_PART_BYTES` in
`workflows/src/datasets.ts` bounds a part at 4 MiB; `batch` changes the number of iterations
and boundary rereads, and loop concurrency and instance step slots bound concurrent work.
The normal dataset byte/row limits and run budgets apply. The tests lower `limits.loopItems`
to 600 and 200 respectively to prove that it counts iterations, while using the normal four
step slots. Raising a customer limit is unnecessary for either workload.
Evidence: `tests/workflow-batch.test.ts` (WF 114) and the
[hosted measurement run](https://github.com/work-shape/catalyst-core/actions/runs/39090640234).
The same test emits timings on subsequent hosted runs; timings vary with runner contention.
## Knowledge Base processing review measurement

Measured on 2026-10-18 on a Blacksmith 8-vCPU Ubuntu runner, using the pinned Postgres 17 image. Each synthetic content has one live document and one chunk; one content changes processing. Values are the median of three complete processing-review calls after fixture loading and `ANALYZE`, including classification, token estimation and confirmation construction. They are latency observations, not a production capacity promise.
| Contents / chunks     | Before   | After    |

The review still classifies live content metadata. Token estimation now visits only affected contents' active chunking revisions through `chunks_content_sha256_chunking_revision_position_key`, rather than aggregating every chunk. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` at both sizes showed one chunk index scan, one loop and one returned chunk. More chunks on unaffected contents no longer increase token-aggregation work; metadata classification still grows with the live content count. No content-count cap or timeout increase was added; the owned-store statement deadline remains 30 seconds (`KNOWLEDGE_DOCUMENTS_TIMEOUT_MS`).

The [hosted timing and mutation probe](https://github.com/work-shape/catalyst-core/actions/runs/39095494167) contains all samples and query plans. Its temporary workflow and benchmark fixture are outside the product PR.

pages.title: Deployment
pages.description: Package and run a dedicated client instance.
body: Workshape Catalyst runtime services are packaged as Docker images. Docker Compose is the default local and first production-friendly deployment target.
## First Production Shape
```text
reverse proxy / TLS
-> chat API service
-> standalone or embedded chat frontend assets
-> optional tool worker service
-> Postgres
-> object storage or backup target
-> logs, metrics, backups, and deploy scripts
Caddy is the default reverse proxy/TLS choice for the first VPS or VM deployment because it keeps automatic HTTPS and routing simple.
The API limits how often one caller may call an operation, and counts a caller who is not
signed in by client address. It reads that address from `X-Forwarded-For` only when the request
comes from a loopback or private address, which is the reverse proxy on the Compose network.
Caddy as the outermost proxy passes the real client address without configuration.
Where another proxy or load balancer stands in front of Caddy (Traefik, a cloud load
balancer), Caddy must be told to trust it. Without this Caddy reports the outer proxy as the
client, and everyone who signs in shares one count:
```caddyfile
servers {
trusted_proxies static private_ranges
Name the outer proxy's addresses instead of `private_ranges` where they are known. After the
change, sign in from two networks and check that the API's request log shows two different
`remoteAddress` values.
The counters live in the API process, so an instance runs exactly one API process. The numbers
are set in the release config, see [Rate limits](/configure/release-config/#rate-limits).
## Agent Runs
An Agent Run is a row and a job of the kind `agent_run.execute`. The API writes both in the
transaction that accepts the message and never executes a run itself. A job worker claims the
job, the job claims the run, and every event and message of the run is stored under the lease
of that job.
Where the worker runs is set in the client assembly with `agentRunWorker`:
- `"in_process"` (default): the API process serves the runs with a second job worker. Closing
the API process ends its runs as interrupted at once.
- `"separate"`: only the processes started with `runAgentRunWorker` serve the runs. On SIGTERM
such a process takes no new run and gives its runs `AGENT_RUN_WORKER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` to
end, 15 minutes unless set. A second signal ends the drain. In Compose, set the worker's
`stop_grace_period` to at least the drain timeout plus 30 seconds; with less, Docker kills
the worker mid-drain and its runs fail as lost after the lease time.
One process executes `AGENT_RUN_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` runs at once, 8 unless set. The runs of an
instance that execute at once are that number times its worker processes; further runs wait
queued in the order they were accepted. Keep the default of 8 unless measured otherwise: a
worker process with 8 runs in progress was measured at 201 MB. A run is never executed twice:
- The worker of a run was killed: after the lease time of 90 seconds the next pass of any job
worker of the instance, the API's included, fails the run with `AGENT_RUN_WORKER_LOST`, the
reply is shown as interrupted and the conversation takes the next message. Until then the
reply stands still. No worker has to come back for this.
- The worker was stopped and the run did not end within the drain time: the run fails with
`AGENT_RUN_RUNTIME_INTERRUPTED`.
- A run stored no event for 30 minutes: it fails as interrupted.
- No Agent Run worker takes a run within 10 minutes of its acceptance: the run fails with
`AGENT_RUN_NOT_STARTED`, the person is told that the reply could not be started, and the
conversation takes the next message. The same happens when the backlog is longer than the
workers take in that time, so add slots or processes before the wait of a healthy instance
comes near it. Instance > Jobs marks `agent_run.execute` with "No worker takes these" when
its jobs have been due for a minute and none is running.
A stop request reaches the worker within about a second. The answer of a run and the end of the
run are stored together, so a worker killed at the end of a run leaves no answer beside a
failed run.
Rolling back to the previous release in the single-process topology leaves the runs that were
in flight `running` for up to 30 minutes, with their conversations answering 409, until that
release's own recovery fails them.
## Page Builds

With the module `apps` on, the tool `workspace.open` stores a folder of a conversation's Execution Workspace as a revision of the conversation's preview. The build is the job kind `page.bundle`, and the workspace command worker serves it:

- The worker reads the files by the index the save recorded, checks size and checksum of each, and writes a copy into a temporary directory of its own under `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_TEMP_ROOT`. The directory is removed when the build ends.

- The build is the fixed command `catalyst-page-build` of the runner image, run in the sandbox like a workspace command: no network, read-only root file system, no capabilities, and the CPU, memory and process limits of `infrastructure.sandbox`. Only that directory is mounted. The command gets no environment variable of the worker.

- The worker treats what the command left behind as untrusted data. It reads regular files only, follows no link, refuses a path that leaves the directory or has a `__catalyst` segment, and stops at the file and byte limits instead of reading past them.
- No file of a Page is parsed or run in the API process or in a worker process.
An instance with `modules.apps.enabled: true` needs:
- `executionWorkspaces.enabled: true` and, outside development, `infrastructure.sandbox.provider: docker`. The instance does not start otherwise and names the setting.
- A running workspace command worker. It needs `infrastructure.objectStorage.files` and its credentials in addition to the workspace store. A worker that does not serve `page.bundle` does not start.

- A runner image of the same release. Both runner images carry the command: the platform's `workspace-command-runner` target and the runner image of the capabilities repository. Each runs `catalyst-page-build --check` when it is built, which builds a small Page, so an image without a working command does not come out of its build. An older image has no `catalyst-page-build`; every save then fails with a message that says the runner image must be rolled out. The Infrastructure page does not show this.
The same worker keeps the repositories of assets whose files are one, with two more job kinds:

- `asset_repo.commit` makes the commit of a save. The worker reads the bundles the ledger names from the `files` store, each to no more than the size the ledger recorded, and hands the command only a bundle whose SHA-256 is the recorded one; any other ends the save with `bundle_hash_mismatch`. The commit is the fixed command `catalyst-asset-repo` of the runner image, which runs git in the sandbox under the same limits as a build. The worker believes the result only when the bundle the command left has the size and the hash the result names. It names the bundle on the save's row before it puts the object.
- `asset_repo.sweep` runs every hour. It gives up the saves that did not finish within a day and removes their objects. The object store is never listed: an object is found by its row.

A commit keeps everything it works on below one directory on the disk of the worker, which is the only directory its container mounts: the files, the bundles of the repository, the command's repository and the new bundle. Nothing of it is in the `/tmp` of the sandbox, so a commit takes none of the container's memory for its files; the memory limit of the sandbox (4 GiB unless the instance sets another) holds git and the command, which read one file of at most 2 MiB at a time. One commit takes at most 550 MiB of disk (`ASSET_REPO_COMMIT_DISK_BYTES`: five times the 50 MiB a tree may have and three times the 100 MiB a history may have), two run at a time, and the directory is removed when the commit ended. The worker starts no commit on a disk with less room and refuses the save with `no_space`, as it does when the disk fills on the way; an operator frees space on the worker. A save reads every bundle of the repository. Together they may have 100 MiB (`ASSET_REPO_MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES`); a save that would leave more is refused with `history_too_large`.

Git is in the runner image alone. An older runner image has no `catalyst-asset-repo`; a save then fails with a message that says the runner image must be rolled out. On a `local` sandbox the command runs the git of the machine, which has to be 2.47 or later.

Neither a save nor a command waits for a worker that is not there. Every job worker reports every 10 seconds which kinds of job it claims. A `workspace.exec` call whose command has been due for 30 seconds while the workers of its kind reported nothing for 30 seconds fails: the agent reads that code execution is unavailable and tells the person, and the run goes on. A command behind a worker that reports waits. Instance > Infrastructure shows the sandbox as failed with the time of the last report once the workers were silent for 30 seconds, and `codeExecution` of `GET /instance/infrastructure` says whether code runs and since when. Both recover when a worker is back.

The same rule holds for a save. When a build has been due for 30 seconds and the workers reported nothing for 30 seconds, the save fails and says that no workspace command worker takes Page builds. A worker that reports is waited for; a save whose wait runs out behind it says that the workers are busy.

A build that is published is published once. The revision and the result of the build are written in one transaction while the worker holds the job; a job that is delivered again after a worker stopped finds the result and stores nothing, and a save that gave up gets no revision.

A worker that is killed can leave a build's directory under `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_TEMP_ROOT` and, with the Docker sandbox, its container. Every worker removes directories named `catalyst-page-build-*` and containers named `catalyst-workspace-command-page-build-*` that are older than 15 minutes when it starts and every 10 minutes while it builds.
| Setting                  | Default | Meaning                                                                         |
| `PAGE_BUILD_CONCURRENCY` | 2       | Builds one worker process runs at once. One conversation never has two at once. |
| `PAGE_BUILD_TIMEOUT_MS`  | 60000   | A build that runs longer is stopped, its container removed, and the save fails. |

A build takes at most 500 files, 2 MiB per file and 25 MiB in all, and may leave 500 files of 50 MiB in all, in at most 2,000 files and folders nested 32 deep. Memory, CPU and process count are those of the sandbox (4 GiB, 1 CPU and 128 processes by default); there is no disk quota on the build's directory beyond the timeout. A save waits five minutes for its build; when no worker takes it in that time the save fails and a worker that comes later stores nothing.
## Deployment Flow
Separate publishing from deployment:
```text
run checks
-> build Docker images
-> tag release
-> push images
-> explicitly deploy target client instance
-> run migrations
-> restart services
-> health check
Production deploys should be explicit. A GitHub Actions workflow can call the same deploy script that an operator can run manually with the right credentials.
For an instance that Workshape operates, the deployment kit runs this flow. [Operated Instances](/operate/operated-instances/) covers its accounts, Terraform, releases, backups and bucket retention.
## Environment Contract
Do not commit production env files.
Document these values per instance:
- database URL
- model provider credentials
- auth token signing or exchange secrets
- object storage endpoint and credentials
- backup bucket
- public origin
- CORS or embed allowlist
- retention and audit env overrides, if any

For machine API access, configure a `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` of at least 32 characters before starting the API. Treat it as a server signing secret: keep it stable across restarts and identical across replicas. API keys are separate database-backed credentials created in the API Access control plane and supplied only to callers as `CATALYST_API_KEY`; they do not belong in the server deployment environment.
## Database
Postgres is the baseline application store.
Managed Postgres is preferred for production when available. Running Postgres on the same VPS is acceptable for early instances only when backup and restore are treated as product features.
Minimum requirements:
- persistent volume outside the app container lifecycle
- automated external backups
- documented restore procedure
- migration procedure
- monitoring for failed backups
- least-privilege backup credentials
Database schema changes must be shipped as committed Drizzle migration files. Do not use `drizzle-kit push` or any direct schema-push workflow.

Migrations run as an explicit step before the API and the workers start. Each client builds `dist/migrate.js`, and the Compose `migrate` service runs `node <client folder>/dist/migrate.js`. In the operated production Compose files the deploy script runs that service after the pre-deploy backup and before `up`; the services themselves only wait for a healthy Postgres there. In local Compose the API waits for the `migrate` service to complete, and the workers wait for the API. The step holds a Postgres advisory lock on one session, applies each committed migration once, prints the names it applied and names the migration that failed, also when the server ended its connection. While another step holds the lock it waits, and says so on standard error when it starts to wait and every 30 seconds after; it has no deadline.

The API and the workers never migrate. When one starts, it reads the migration state: a database that lacks committed migrations stops it with their names, so a production stack started without the migrate step fails instead of serving an old schema. A database ahead of the release starts, so the previous release keeps serving while a newer one is rolled out. There is no `RUN_MIGRATIONS` switch.

Schema changes expand before they contract. A new migration may hold the additive forms: a new table, type, schema or sequence; a nullable or defaulted column; a column default; a relaxed `NOT NULL`; a constraint added `NOT VALID` and its later validation; inserts and updates; and, in a migration of its own, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS`. Every other statement is a contract step, among them a drop, a rename, a new `NOT NULL`, a column type change, `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE` and a `DO` block: it ships in a later migration under `-- contract-after: <tag>`, once the oldest supported release in `packages/postgres-store/migration-policy.json` has reached that tag. A required column without a default and a blocking index build never pass. `pnpm check:migrations` enforces this for every migration the base branch lacks and rejects any change to a committed migration; `pnpm test:compatibility` runs the database tests of the previous and the oldest supported release against the new schema, and `pnpm test:upgrade` migrates a database of the oldest supported release.

A concurrent index build runs outside a transaction. When it fails, the migration is not recorded and the index stays behind as invalid; repair what stopped it and run the step again, which drops the invalid index and builds it anew.
### Data Stores on the database server

With the module `dataStores` on, each Data Store has a database of its own on this server and two roles, named `catalyst_ds_...`. The platform takes from those roles every way to the platform database and to each other's databases. Three things it leaves to you. Every job of a store looks for them and names them on the store's record, and a name goes once its cause is closed. `GET /api/v1/data-stores/<store>` answers them for one store, each with these steps in a sentence, beside the store's migration level, its size against its limit and how its last migration ended:

- `server_databases_open`: a store role can connect to another database of the server, such as `postgres` or `template1`, where it reads the catalog and nothing else. The platform changes no grant of a database it does not own, because the server may hold more than this instance. On a server that is this instance's alone, run `REVOKE CONNECT ON DATABASE <name> FROM PUBLIC` for each such database as its owner. On a shared server add the line below to `pg_hba.conf`, above the lines that admit the platform, and reload Postgres. Postgres shows that file to no ordinary role, so the condition stays.

- `sessions_open`: the platform's database role is no superuser, so it cannot take the functions that list and end sessions from the roles of a store. A query of a store can then see the sessions of the server and end another query of that store.

- `temp_files_unbounded`: the platform's database role is no superuser, so it cannot set `temp_file_limit` on the roles of a store. A statement of a store that sorts or joins without end fills the disk with temporary files until its timeout.
```text
host postgres,template1 /^catalyst_ds_ all reject

A role of a store may change its own password. The platform sets it again before it connects as that role, so keep the Postgres port closed to everyone but the platform: whoever reaches it in between logs in with what the role last set.

A store at its size limit takes no further rows. What a refused insert wrote is given back by a `VACUUM` the platform runs as the owner of the store's database; the autovacuum of the server does the rest.
## Health And Readiness
Two unversioned addresses answer without a credential.
- `GET /health` says the process is up. It reads nothing.

- `GET /ready` says whether this process can serve, and is the check for rotation: use it for the proxy's upstream check and for the deploy script's wait after `up`. The container healthcheck stays on `/health`: other services wait for a healthy API container, and a healthcheck on `/ready` would keep the proxy from starting during a database outage. `/ready` answers `200 { "status": "ready", "migration": "<newest migration of the release>" }` when the database answers within two seconds and holds every migration the release was built with. Otherwise it answers `503 { "status": "not_ready", "reason": "database_unreachable" }` or `503 { "status": "not_ready", "reason": "database_behind", "missing": ["<migration>", ...] }`. A database ahead of the release is ready, so the previous release stays in rotation while a newer one is rolled out.

`/ready` checks the database and nothing else. A model or mail provider outage does not take the API out of rotation. The answer names migrations only: no host, no account, no connection string and no driver error. The document worker answers `/ready` on its own port with the same body and status.
The proxy has to forward `/ready` to the API like `/health`; it is outside `/api/*`.
## What The Proxy Routes To The API
Everything else goes to the interface. A deployment with its own proxy routes these to the API:
| Address             | What it is                                         |
| `/api/*`            | The product API.                                   |
| `/auth/*`           | Sign-in of an instance with standalone auth.       |
| `/health`, `/ready` | The two checks above.                              |
| `/app-runtime/*`    | The runtime and the shell of a generated view.     |
| `/app-content/*`    | The files of a Page, when the module `apps` is on. |
`docker/Caddyfile` routes all of them.

An address below `/app-content/` holds a token in its path: `/app-content/<file set>/<token>/<file>`. The token is a bearer capability. The API mints it after it has checked that the person may read the Page, and for one hour (`APP_CONTENT_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS`) it serves the built files of that one revision to whoever holds the address, as long as that person may still read the Page. The API asks again every 30 seconds per address (`APP_CONTENT_VIEWER_CHECK_SECONDS`): once the account is deactivated or the person no longer reads the conversation, the address answers `404` at most 30 seconds later. It is not bound to the person's session: signing out does not end it before the hour is over.
So no layer may write these addresses down:
- The API writes no request line for them, whichever way the address is spelled.
- `docker/Caddyfile` writes no access log. If you add a `log` directive, leave these addresses out with `log_skip /app-content/*`.
- `docker/nginx-spa.conf` answers `/app-content` with `404` and `access_log off`, for the case that such an address reaches the interface's server.
- Any other proxy, load balancer or CDN in front must be set the same way, and must not cache these answers: they carry `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store`.

A proxy's error log is not its access log: when the API does not answer, Caddy writes the address of the failed request to its error log, so proxy error logs can hold the address of a Page that stays valid for up to the lifetime of its token.
A Page's own script can read the address it was loaded from. The token is therefore a secret from other people and not from the Page.
## Production Readiness Checklist
Before a real deployment:
- release config validates
- migrations run cleanly
- `/health` answers and `/ready` answers `200` on the API and the document worker
- TLS is configured
- production secrets are not in Git or images
- backups run and restore has been tested
- model provider billing alerts or budgets exist
- retention and deletion behavior is documented
- audit views are permissioned
- user access path is tested
- customer-hosted integrations have timeout and failure behavior
## Release Gate For The `/api/v1` Cutover

The release that moves the product API under `/api/v1` answers 404 at every old path, with no alias. Interface, CLI and server ship together, so the only callers it can break are outside ones: a backend that issues chat session tokens for an embedded chat.
Before deploying that release to an operated instance:
1. Search the instance's access log for `POST /auth/session-token` and `POST /api/superadmin/session-tokens` over the log's whole retention.

2. Record the result with the release: the two paths, the period searched, and per path the request count and the calling hosts. Record metadata only, never request bodies, tokens or the server credential.
3. Move every caller found to `POST /api/v1/instance/session-tokens` in the same release. The `x-server-credential` header and the payload are unchanged.
4. Give every CLI runner a `CATALYST_API_KEY`; the CLI no longer signs in with the server credential. The server needs `SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` for the key exchange.
5. Tell users to reload open tabs after the upgrade. A tab loaded before it calls the old paths and shows "Operation is not available"; later releases show a notice with a reload action instead.
A reverse proxy that forwards `/api/*` and `/health` needs no change.

pages.title: Operate code execution
pages.description: Operate workspace command workers, runner images, cleanup, and artifact promotion.
body: Execution workspaces give agents a persistent conversation-scoped file area and a bounded command primitive. Operators should treat the feature as a worker-backed artifact pipeline, not as shell access inside the chat API.
## Runtime Roles
The production-shaped deployment has these roles:
- chat API: validates tool calls, enqueues workspace commands, exposes promoted artifacts, and never runs shell commands
- workspace command worker: runs the job of each command on the job executor, hydrates workspace files, starts a short-lived runner, syncs changed files, and records terminal status
- runner container: executes the agent-authored command with no platform secrets and no network by default
- object storage: stores workspace file bytes and promoted artifact bytes
- Postgres: stores workspace, file manifest, command queue, leases, audit events, and managed artifact records

Commands wait in the durable Postgres queue until worker capacity is available. Each command is a job of the kind `workspace.command`; one workspace runs one command at a time, in the order they were queued. A command runs once: when its worker dies, the command fails with the category `worker_lost` after its lease of two minutes and is not started again; until then the later commands of that workspace wait. `executionWorkspaces.worker.concurrency` is the deployment control for simultaneous runner containers; queued commands are not rejected through separate per-user or global admission caps. Size worker concurrency for the host, and use queue wait time as the signal to add execution capacity.
## Runner Image

The platform Dockerfile exposes a `workspace-command-runner` target for the `infrastructure.sandbox.image` container. It includes `/bin/bash`, Node, Python artifact libraries, LibreOffice, Poppler, fonts, ImageMagick, and common shell utilities so `workspace.exec` can run ordinary script-first DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, PDF, and image workflows without package installs at command time.

The image target intentionally does not copy the chat API build or deployment secrets. The `workspace-command-worker` target remains the trusted control process image with Docker CLI access; it starts short-lived runner containers from the configured runner image.

Capability-owned Catalyst helper CLIs such as `docx_render`, `xlsx_scan_errors`, `pptx_render`, `pdf_inspect`, and `promote_artifact` are part of the paid capabilities and not in the open repository. Deployments that license those helpers layer the capabilities helper package onto the platform runner image and publish that layered image tag through `EXECUTION_WORKSPACE_RUNNER_IMAGE`.
## Operational Signals
Workspace command lifecycle audit events use these event types:
- `workspace_command.queued`
- `workspace_command.running`
- `workspace_command.completed`
- `workspace_command.failed`
- `workspace_command.timed_out`
- `workspace_command.cancelled`
- `workspace_command.recovered_stale`

Audit metadata includes command id, workspace id, conversation id, timeout, attempts, counts, error code/category, and duration where available. It must not include command text, stdout, stderr, file contents, or object-store credentials.

The worker also emits operator telemetry logs with `workspace_command.*` event types. These logs include active queued/running/cancelling counts, terminal status, timeout categories, and temp cleanup counts. Use these logs for queue pressure and failure-rate alerting.
## Cleanup

Conversation deletion and retention expiration call execution workspace cleanup before the conversation is marked unavailable. Cleanup deletes internal workspace object bytes, removes workspace file manifests, removes workspace command rows, and marks the workspace deleted.
A periodic cleanup job also scans for active workspace metadata attached to already deleted or retention-expired conversations. This catches interrupted delete/retention paths.

The worker keeps a hydrated local workspace directory after each command and reuses it until `executionWorkspaces.cleanup.hydratedWorkspaceIdleTtlMs` expires. Set the value to `0` to disable reuse. Before every command, the worker reconciles the directory with the durable workspace manifest, and after every command it syncs changed files back to durable storage. Runner containers remain short-lived.

Empty directories remain available while that warm local copy is reused. The durable manifest stores files, so empty directories do not survive cache eviction, worker restart, or execution on a different worker.

The same periodic cleanup removes expired or orphaned directories with the `catalyst-workspace-` prefix. The durable source of truth is object storage plus the workspace manifest, not hydrated directories or runner containers.
## Promoted Artifacts

Users should only receive promoted artifacts. Internal workspace files and logs are visible to agent tools for debugging and follow-up commands, but they are not projected as user-downloadable artifacts until `workspace.promote_artifact` or an expected promoted output creates a managed artifact.
## Incident Checks
For command failures:
- check `workspace_command.failed` and `workspace_command.timed_out` audit events
- check worker logs for queue counts and for commands that failed as `worker_lost`
- verify the workspace command worker is running
- verify the runner image tag matches the release
- verify object storage root or credentials are writable by the worker
- verify Docker can start a no-network runner container
Do not inspect or paste raw workspace files, command strings, stdout, or stderr into support tickets unless the customer has approved that specific data access path.

pages.title: Retention, audit and deletion
pages.description: Run sensitive chat workflows with retention, audit, usage, and deletion controls.
body: Governance is the minimum set of controls needed to run a sensitive client instance responsibly.
It is not a broad compliance suite. It is explicit behavior for access, audit, retention, deletion, and usage visibility.
## Retention
Define retention for:
- conversations
- messages
- tool call records
- document outputs
- managed file references
- model usage events
- audit events
- backups

A Conversation is deleted `retention.conversationDays` after the last message a user sent in it. Set `retention.extendOnActivity: false` to count from its creation instead, as a fixed maximum age. In its last seven days, or the last half of a shorter period, the conversation list marks it with a clock, and the open Conversation says when it will be deleted. See [release config](/configure/release-config/#retention).
Conversation retention and audit retention may be different. Audit events should avoid raw sensitive payloads so they can safely outlive conversation content where policy requires it.

Audit retention is enforced. Once a day the API process deletes the audit events of its instance that are older than `retention.auditDays` (default 365) and records one `audit.pruned` event with the number of rows it removed. There is no switch: an instance that has to keep audit events longer sets a higher `auditDays`, up to 3650, before it upgrades.
## Audit
Audit events should record governance metadata:
- actor id
- event type
- conversation id
- message id
- tool call id
- file id
- status
- reason code where required
- correlation id
- timestamps
Audit events should not store:
- full prompts or completions
- full document text
- raw file bytes
- secrets or tokens
- unnecessary personal data
## Usage Governance
Model usage is governance metadata, not provider billing truth.

Admin-facing usage views expose consumption volume and customer billable totals: model calls, total and cached input tokens, configured non-financial safeguards, recent model usage metadata, and the persisted rate-card amount the customer should expect to be invoiced. Per-day and per-calendar-month summaries use “Billable” until an invoice is issued. They do not expose applied rates or internal pricing provenance. Web-search costs are displayed only when web search is enabled for the instance.
Record:
- provider id, and the region of the provider entry: `eu`, `global`, or none for a provider that runs inside the instance
- model id, and the model binding the call named
- token counts when reported by the provider
- conversation id, where a conversation caused the call

- agent run id and agent name, or for a call the product made for itself what it was for: `conversation_title`, `guardrail_judge`, `document_extraction`, `knowledge_embedding` (the chunks of a Knowledge Base at ingestion and re-index), `knowledge_field_extraction` (its model-extracted fields) or `knowledge_query` (the query of a Knowledge Base search)
- the user who caused the call and the workspace it happened in, where there is one
- correlation id
- persisted customer billable cost and completeness state

Every model call leaves one record, including conversation titles and guardrail checks, and including a call that failed, timed out or was stopped. Titles and guardrail checks count toward the limits of the instance like every other call.
A record has a status:
- `pending`: the call was admitted and has not ended. The Usage page shows it as "Running".
- `settled`: the call ended with usage. The Usage page says where the amounts come from: "Reported by provider", "No usage reported" when the provider answered and reported none, or "Estimated".
- `failed`: the call failed, was stopped or timed out before any of its answer arrived. It counts as one call toward the daily call limit and uses no tokens. The Usage page shows it as "Failed".

- `abandoned`: the process that made the call went away before the call ended. The job `usage.recover_abandoned_calls` runs every 10 minutes and takes a call that is still `pending` six hours after its admission as abandoned. The Usage page shows it as "Abandoned".

A streamed call that is stopped or breaks off after its answer began has cost something, and its provider reports no usage for it. Where the provider had reported the usage before the stream broke off, the call is settled with it. Otherwise it is settled with an estimate: every three characters that were sent and every three that arrived count as one token, a character outside the Latin alphabet counts as a token of its own, the input of a tool call counts as output, the input counts as not cached, and a web search that had started counts as one search. An estimate is at most 10,000,000 tokens of input and as many of output. Its record is marked `estimated`.
### How a call is admitted

A call is admitted against the limits in the database, in one statement on two counter rows: the day's and the month's. Several API and worker processes together admit no more than the limits allow, for calls, tokens and spend. Admission reads no usage record and no process waits for a lock per instance.

At admission a call reserves the most it can use: its input by the size of the request, 16,000 output tokens, and both at the highest price the rate card has for the model. When the call ends, the reservation is replaced by what the call used. A failed or abandoned call releases its reservation.
This has three consequences for how you set limits:
- A call is refused when its reservation no longer fits, so a token or spend limit is reached slightly before it is used up.
- A token limit at or below the 16,000 reserved output tokens would admit no call. The config is refused with a message that names the limit and the reservation.

- With a spend budget, a model without a price on the customer rate card is refused. A `deterministic` provider needs no price: it bills nothing, and its calls reserve no cost. A run that is refused this way fails with the code `MODEL_NOT_PRICED`. The chat tells someone with `usage.view` that the price is missing and to choose another model until the operator has added it under `usage.costs` in release config, and anyone else to choose another model or ask an administrator. Startup validation asks a price of the models agents start on, of conversation titles and of guardrails; it does not ask one of a model an agent only offers for selection, so give every binding of a billed provider a price.

Knowledge Base ingestion records its usage and attribution but counts against no chat safeguard or spend budget (KB-ISO). Query embeddings remain chat. The spend budgets (`usage.budget`) hold for chat across the whole instance. The safeguards (`usage.safeguards`) stop a loop that runs away and hold per person: their own calls in one bucket, the calls the product makes for them, such as titles and guardrail checks, in a second of the same size, so a check the company adds never uses up a person's own safeguard. The calls of no person share one bucket of seven times a person's. When the deletion of an account takes the person off their usage records, the person's safeguard counters are removed and what those records hold stays on the instance's totals and budgets only, so deleting accounts never fills the shared bucket. A run refused by a budget or a safeguard fails with the code `MODEL_USAGE_LIMIT_REACHED`; an API call refused the same way answers `403 FORBIDDEN` with `details` `{ reason: "MODEL_USAGE_LIMIT_REACHED", period, metric, scope }`, where `period` is `day` or `month`, `metric` is `modelCallCount`, `tokens` or `costMicros`, and `scope` is `user`, `system` or `instance`. Run errors carry these three fields in `error.usageLimit`, including after reload. The chat notice names the limit and its UTC reset; older run errors without those fields keep a generic notice.

The limits are protective safeguards, not exact caps. A call reserves a fixed amount at admission and settles its real usage when it ends, and the request sets no maximum for the answer, so a call can use more than it reserved. The most a limit can be passed by is the sum, over the calls in flight when it is reached, of what each used minus what it reserved. The reserved output is the constant `MODEL_CALL_RESERVED_OUTPUT_TOKENS` (16,000) in `@work-shape/catalyst-core`. Set a limit with that margin in mind, and keep a provider-side budget as the hard stop.
A cost that cannot be settled, such as one whose provider reported no cached tokens, counts toward a spend budget at the highest price of the model. It does not stop later calls.

The Usage page lists the caller and the provider with its region for the recent calls. Its sums are read from daily sums that are kept as each call ends. The summary of the API also answers `attributedUsage`: the last 30 days by day, model, provider, region and purpose or agent.
### What stays after a deletion

Usage records are the accounting of the instance and are kept. When an account is deleted, the user is removed from its usage records together with the conversation id, the agent run id, the operation id and the correlation id. A call that ends or is recorded after the account is gone is written without them. The amounts, the model, the provider and the agent or purpose stay. When a workspace is deleted, the workspace is removed from its usage records and the amounts stay.
### After an upgrade

Records written before provider region, purpose, user and workspace were recorded are filled by a background job, `usage.backfill_attribution`. It needs no action. Until it ends, older records show no region. A record whose provider and model are no longer in `infrastructure.models` keeps no region, because nothing says where it was processed.
Use provider-side billing alerts or budgets as an external backstop.
## Background Jobs
