Now she tries the same on `hr-onboarding`, which a colleague sent her as a link.
1. Sign-in: yes. Module: on.
2. Right `agent.read` on `hr-onboarding`: her grant covers what Tax team owns. The instance owns this one. Nothing else covers it.
3. The instance answers `403 FORBIDDEN`. Studio says "You may not read this asset."
4. The refused call is on the Operations page with the status "Denied".
## Give a colleague the right to edit an agent
You need "Manage users" yourself. Open **Settings > Instance > Access**, the tab **Rights**, and choose **New right**. In the German interface the button is "Neues Recht". The dialog has five fields.

| Field           | What you choose                                         | What it means                                                                                                                                                                       |

| Person          | One person from the list                                | The right is for this person alone. To give it to three colleagues, send the dialog three times.                                                                                    |

| Kind            | Agents                                                  | One kind per dialog. A colleague who edits skills too needs another right for Skills. Other kinds appear where their modules are on; see the table under Grants.                    |

| Actions         | Read, Write, Delete                                     | Tick Read and Write for somebody who should edit. Tick Delete only if they should remove the agent too. The dialog writes one row per tick.                                         |

| Where and asset | **On one asset** ("An einem Asset"), then the one agent | The right covers this agent, which exists now. **In a shared workspace** ("In einem geteilten Arbeitsbereich") would cover every agent the workspace owns instead, also later ones. |

| Effect          | Allow or Deny                                           | Allow gives the ticked actions there. Deny refuses them there and beats every allow and every role. For this task choose Allow.                                                     |

Press **Create right**. Under the default policy the right works at once. On an instance that sends changes to an approval, it works once the approval is given. Your colleague sees **Studio** in the main rail the next time the interface loads, with the agent. If these rights are all they hold, they see nothing else. For a team with several agents, choose the Shared Workspace instead of repeating this for each agent.
Three things to know afterwards.
- You can send the same dialog again. Rows the person already has are left alone, and the dialog says how many it added.
- **Check** on the same page confirms the result. Choose the person, enter the agent's name and read the answer for each action. You need "View agent configuration" for that.
- A save can still be refused for a reason that is not a right. An example is a model setting that needs "Manage agent model settings". The Check tab lists such reasons under its result.
To take the right away, open the menu of the line in the list and choose **Revoke** for the action. Once the revocation has run, the next call of your colleague is refused.
## API keys and Service Principals

The Catalyst CLI does not sign in as a person. It works as a Service Principal, and so should a script. Whoever manages Service Principals, an Admin for example, creates a **Service Principal** on **Settings > Instance > API access** and gives it one or both of two rights:
- "Read configuration assets", to pull and compare agents and skills.
- "Release configuration assets", to push them with `catalyst config push`. Only a Superadmin gives this one.
Then a person with "Manage API access" creates an **API key** for it and picks the key's scopes from the rights the Service Principal holds. The key is shown once.

Nobody gives a Service Principal more than they hold themselves. Giving it a right, switching it back on and issuing it a key each ask whether the person holds every right the Service Principal would act with. Where a personal API key makes the call, its scopes count too. A refusal names the first right that is missing, and the asset only where the person may read it. Taking a right away and switching a Service Principal off ask nothing of it.

A Service Principal has no role. Whoever manages Service Principals can allow one to use a single named resource they may use themselves, such as one Connection: a grant with the holder kind `service_principal`, a use right, and that one asset as scope. The use rights are `connection.use`, `workflow.use`, and `data_store.read`, `data_store.insert` and `data_store.execute` for the rows of a Data Store, each where its module is on. No other grant can be written for one: no right that writes, publishes, deletes or manages, no workspace or instance scope, and no deny. A Service Principal never writes a grant, also not for itself. Disabling a Service Principal leaves its grants recorded and without effect. The interface does not offer these grants; they are written through `POST /api/v1/instance/access/grants`.

A release push reaches every agent and skill of the instance and is not held back by the editing limits of the interface. It is still bound by a deny on an asset. See [config assets](/configure/config-assets/#permissions).
## Which screen for what
| You want to                                        | Screen                                         | You need                                                    |
| Make somebody an Admin or a Superadmin             | Settings > Instance > Users, Role              | Manage users. Superadmin for the Superadmin role.           |
| Give or take one right for the whole instance      | Settings > Instance > Users, Rights            | Manage users                                                |
| Let somebody edit an agent                         | Settings > Instance > Access, Rights           | Manage users                                                |
| Find out why somebody can or cannot do something   | Settings > Instance > Access, Check            | Manage users and View agent configuration                   |
| Create a key of your own for the CLI               | Settings > You > API keys, or `catalyst login` | The module `personalApiKeys` on                             |
| Create a Service Principal or give it a right      | Settings > Instance > API access               | Manage Service Principals, and the right you give           |
| Create a key for a script or CI                    | Settings > Instance > API access               | Manage API access, and every right of the Service Principal |
| Decide a call or a skill change that waits         | Inbox                                          | Approve skill changes                                       |
| See what was called, by whom, and what was refused | Settings > Instance > Operations               | View audit log                                              |
| See who changed which right                        | Settings > Instance > Audit                    | View audit log                                              |
| Switch a feature on or off, set the policy         | Release config, then a deploy                  | The operator                                                |

pages.title: Instance brief
pages.description: The thin documentation every client instance should have before implementation.
body: Write a short instance brief before configuring a client instance.
This is not a long specification. It is the minimum shared context that keeps tools, prompts, auth, retention, and deployment choices aligned.
## Template
```md
# Instance Brief
## Purpose
What should this chat help users accomplish?
## Users
Who can use it? Which roles or permission refs matter?
## Operating Model
Who operates the dedicated instance?
- operated dedicated instance
- self-operated instance
- mixed, with customer-hosted integrations
## Data
Which sensitive data can enter the chat?
Which data must never enter the chat?
## Agent
What should the agent do?
What should it refuse or escalate?
Which language or tone constraints matter?
## Tools
List each proposed tool:
- stable tool name
- purpose
- source system
- read or write action
- required permission
- expected audit summary
- output shown to the model
- output shown to the user
## Chat Experience
Branding, welcome text, suggested prompts, locales, and domain UI outputs.
## Auth And Access
How does an authenticated user reach the chat?
How are roles or permission refs mapped?
## Retention And Deletion
Conversation retention, audit retention, backup retention, and deletion expectations.
## Model Provider
Provider, model, region, budget, and external billing controls.
## Deployment
Runtime owner, target environment, database, object storage, proxy/TLS, monitoring, and backup owner.
## Open Questions
Anything that must be answered before production use.
## Keep It Current
Update the brief when the workflow scope changes, not for every code detail.
Implementation choices belong in release config, tool code, planning docs, or ADRs. The brief exists so everyone can understand the instance boundary quickly.

pages.title: Operated Instances
pages.description: Set up, release and back up an instance operated with the deployment kit on one Hetzner VM per environment.
body: An operated instance runs on one Hetzner Cloud VM per environment, usually `staging` and
`production`. Each VM runs Docker Compose: Caddy with TLS, the API, the interface, the workers,
the command containers and Postgres. Two Hetzner Object Storage buckets per environment hold the
files and the database backups, and Cloudflare holds the DNS records. The images are on GHCR. A
release is a manifest of image digests that staging runs first and production runs unchanged.
This page holds what every such instance needs. The commands of the release and deploy tooling
are in `packages/deployment-kit/README.md`. What belongs to one instance, such as its hostnames,
buckets, model providers and approvals, stays in the README and `docs/` of its deployment repo.
## Repositories
Local source development uses three repositories, checked out next to each other.
Release CI checks out only the deployment and installs its published dependencies:
| Checkout                 | Repository                         | Visibility |
| `platform/`              | `work-shape/catalyst-core`         | private    |
| `capabilities/`          | `work-shape/catalyst-capabilities` | private    |
| `deployment.<instance>/` | `work-shape/deployment.<instance>` | private    |
The deployment repo builds the images, because it owns the combination of platform,
capabilities, client assembly, registry names and deploy rights. Its layout is the same in every
instance:
| Path                                                        | What it is                                                                                              |
| `src/client.ts`                                             | The client assembly: capabilities, tools and hooks of this instance.                                    |
| the rest of `src/`, `index.html`, `vite.config.ts`          | One entry point per process (`server.ts`, the workers, `migrate.ts`, `seed-auth.ts`) and the interface. |
| `config/`                                                   | Release config, one base file and an overlay per environment.                                           |
| `config-assets/`                                            | CLI working copies of agents and skills, one folder per environment.                                    |
| `docker-compose.yml`                                        | The local development stack.                                                                            |
| `docker-compose.prod.yml`, `deploy/Caddyfile`               | What runs on a VM.                                                                                      |
| `deploy/docker-bake.hcl`, `.github/workflows/`              | The image builds, the deploy workflow and a manual build workflow.                                      |
| `deploy/deployment.env`                                     | The kit's one input.                                                                                    |
| `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`                            | One exact published Catalyst version for every Catalyst package, and the standalone frozen lockfile.    |
| `deploy/scripts/check-release-policy.sh`                    | The instance's own release assertions.                                                                  |
| `infra/terraform/`                                          | The module `compose-host` and one root per environment.                                                 |
| `.env.example`, `.env.staging.example`, `.env.prod.example` | The local env file, and the templates of the env files on the VMs.                                      |
| `docs/`                                                     | Runbooks and decisions of this instance.                                                                |
The Compose files, the Caddyfile, the bake file, the workflows and the Terraform module are
copied from one deployment repo to the next. The kit does not ship them.
## Accounts and tokens
Provider tokens stay out of Git. On the workstation they live in an untracked `.env.deploy` at the
workspace root, the directory that holds `platform/` and the deployment checkouts:
```sh
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=replace-with-token
CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID=replace-with-zone-id
HETZNER_API_TOKEN=replace-with-hetzner-project-token
HETZNER_OBJECT_STORAGE_ACCESS_KEY=replace-with-object-storage-access-key
HETZNER_OBJECT_STORAGE_SECRET_KEY=replace-with-object-storage-secret-key
GITHUB_TOKEN=replace-with-bootstrap-token
GHCR_USERNAME=replace-with-github-username-or-bot
GHCR_PULL_TOKEN=replace-with-read-packages-token
Load it in the shell that runs Terraform, from the deployment repo:
```sh
source node_modules/@work-shape/catalyst-deployment-kit/lib/load-deploy-env.sh
The script exports `HCLOUD_TOKEN`, which the Hetzner provider reads, from `HETZNER_API_TOKEN`, and
the zone id and the Object Storage key pair as `TF_VAR_` variables. It stops when one of them is
empty. Without an argument it reads `.env.deploy` at the workspace root, from any directory; an
argument names another file.
- **Cloudflare.** Use an account token when one token should manage several zones. It needs
`Zone` → `Zone` → `Read` and `Zone` → `DNS` → `Edit`. Give it all zones only when it is meant
to be reused, otherwise the one zone of the instance. The zone id is on the zone's Overview
page, in the API section of the right sidebar.
- **Hetzner Cloud.** A project API token. `HETZNER_API_TOKEN` is only the local name for it.
- **Hetzner Object Storage.** Files and backups go through its S3-compatible API. Hetzner
documents bucket creation with Terraform through the `aminueza/minio` provider, with S3
credentials generated in the Hetzner Console. Create one key pair for the Terraform bootstrap;
Terraform creates the buckets of both environments with it. The env files on the VMs may use the same pair
during bootstrap; split it into narrower keys per bucket once the console's restrictions are
set up. The backup script reads a pair of its own, `BACKUP_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`BACKUP_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`.
- **GitHub.** `GITHUB_TOKEN` is for bootstrapping on the workstation only. The deployment's
workflow token reads its own repository and publishes its images and release manifest.
- **GHCR.** A token with `read:packages` lets a VM pull the images. It goes into the VM's env
file as `GHCR_USERNAME` and `GHCR_PULL_TOKEN`, and a deploy logs in with them.
## GitHub
The deployment repo has `NPM_READ_TOKEN`, a granular read-only token for the private
`@work-shape` packages. CI writes it into a temporary npmrc for the standalone install and
mounts that file as a BuildKit secret. Keep the earlier source-checkout token until two
package-built production releases exist, so pre-switch release tags can still recover;
removing that token is a separate owner action.
It has two GitHub Environments, `staging` and `production`. `production` requires a reviewer
before its deploy job runs; `staging` needs none once the first deploy works. Each Environment
holds two secrets:
- `DEPLOY_HOST`: the SSH host of that environment's VM.
- `DEPLOY_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY`: the private half of the deploy key whose public half Terraform
installs for the user `deploy`.
The workflow token pushes the images and the build cache to GHCR
and creates the GitHub release with the manifest. Model provider keys and object store keys stay
in the env file on the VM, because the deploy workflow ships only images and Compose wiring.
Make a deploy key for the instance instead of using a personal key. One key for both
environments works, and so does one per environment:
```sh
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C "github-actions-<instance>-deploy" -f ~/.ssh/<instance>-deploy
Terraform reads the public half from the path in `ssh_public_key_path`.
## Terraform
The module `infra/terraform/modules/compose-host` creates, per environment:
- one Hetzner Cloud server for Docker Compose;
- a Hetzner firewall that opens SSH, HTTP and HTTPS;
- the Cloudflare DNS records of the environment's hostnames;
- the files bucket and the backup bucket, with the rules under [Bucket retention](#bucket-retention).
Apply staging first, then production:
```sh
cd infra/terraform/environments/staging
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
terraform init
terraform plan
terraform apply
Git ignores `terraform.tfvars`, the state and the provider lock. The state is local during
bootstrap. Before production changes depend on it, move it to a remote backend, such as a bucket
in Hetzner Object Storage or Terraform Cloud, and write the backend down in the deployment repo.
The server type is a variable of each root. Check the prices in the Hetzner API or console before
changing the server family; a newer generation is not always cheaper. On 2026-06-20 the API
listed lower monthly gross prices for the `cx` line than for `cpx22`.
## The host
Compose on a VM reads `/etc/vivd-catalyst/<instance>/app.env`. Start the file from
`.env.staging.example` or `.env.prod.example`, replace every placeholder, and keep it readable by
root and the group `deploy` only:
```sh
sudo install -d -o root -g deploy -m 0750 /etc/vivd-catalyst/<instance>
sudo install -o root -g deploy -m 0640 app.env /etc/vivd-catalyst/<instance>/app.env
- `CLIENT_CONFIG_PATH` selects the release config, for example
`/app/deployment.<instance>/config/app.production.yaml`.
- `PUBLIC_HOSTNAMES` lists every hostname Caddy serves, separated by commas.
- A deploy writes `IMAGE_REPOSITORY`, `IMAGE_TAG` and the image digests into the file. Leave them
to it.
A host can keep a small zram swap device for short memory peaks, without writing process memory
to disk. It is a safety buffer, not capacity: sustained use means the host or the runner limits
need changing. Before raising the number of commands a worker runs at once, watch sustained swap
use, host memory pressure and the working sets of concurrent runners. The kit's script sets up a
2 GB device with swappiness 20:
```sh
rsync -az ../platform/packages/deployment-kit/host/configure-zram.sh deploy@<host>:/tmp/configure-zram.sh
ssh deploy@<host> 'chmod +x /tmp/configure-zram.sh && sudo /tmp/configure-zram.sh'
The script can run again without harm. It installs the optional Ubuntu kernel module that zram
needs and keeps that module installed across generic kernel updates. Change `ZRAM_SIZE` or
`ZRAM_SWAPPINESS` only after looking at the host's workload and memory pressure.
## Releases
A release is a list of image digests. CI builds it once, for staging, and production runs the
same images. Nothing is rebuilt on the way to production.
```text
pnpm publish:staging      tags staging-<date>-<n> on main
-> CI: release checks and image builds in parallel
-> CI: release-manifest.json on the GitHub release of the tag
-> CI: deploys the manifest to staging
pnpm publish:prod         tags v<date>-<n> on the commit of the staging release
-> copies the manifest to the GitHub release of the v* tag
-> CI: fetches the manifest, requires a successful staging deployment,
deploys the same digests to production
`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` is the only deploy path.
- `pnpm publish:staging` runs the release gate locally, then creates and pushes the next annotated
`staging-*` tag. The tag starts the build and the deploy.
- `pnpm publish:prod` promotes the staging release of `origin/main`, and
`pnpm publish:prod --release staging-<...>` promotes another one. It refuses a release without a
manifest or without a successful staging deployment, and the workflow checks both again.
- The `:watch` variants, such as `pnpm publish:staging:watch`, follow the deploy run until it ends.
- A manual run of the workflow never builds. It deploys the manifest of the tag it was started
from, so every production release was a staging release first.
To roll back, run the workflow from an earlier release tag. It deploys the digests, the Compose
file and the Caddyfile of that tag:
```sh
gh workflow run deploy.yml --ref v2026.10.01-1 -f environment=production
Staging works the same with `-f environment=staging` and a `staging-*` tag. A rollback changes
the application only. Migrations only move forward, so a release keeps working on the schema of
the release after it; read the rollback notes of the platform changelog for the releases in
between before rolling back. To go back to an earlier database, restore a backup.
### The release gate
`pnpm release:check` runs the installed `catalyst-deploy check`. It checks exact, equal package
pins and tarball integrity, then the deploy policy of the Compose file, bake file and workflow.
The full gate requires a frozen standalone install of those published packages, checks the env
examples, builds the deployment assembly and starts every built entry point once per release
config with `--resolve-only`. It renders production Compose against the example env files,
validates Caddy and ends with `deploy/scripts/check-release-policy.sh` when present. Platform
and capabilities passed their own release checks. `pnpm publish:staging` runs `check --static`
locally; CI runs the full gate beside the image builds and publishes the manifest only after it
passes. The kit README has the policy it enforces.
### The manifest
The manifest is the asset `release-manifest.json` on the GitHub release of the tag. GitHub
releases hold it because the repository has them already, and both CI and a workstation read them
with `gh`, without another registry or tool. Staging releases are marked as pre-releases.
```json
"schema": 2,
"release": "staging-2026.10.16-1",
"catalystVersion": "0.8.0",
"commits": {
"deployment": "<deployment commit sha>"
"images": {
"api": "ghcr.io/work-shape/catalyst-acme-api@sha256:...",
"doc-worker": "...-doc-worker@sha256:...",
"workspace-command-worker": "...-workspace-command-worker@sha256:...",
"artifact-preview-worker": "...-artifact-preview-worker@sha256:...",
"runner": "...-catalyst-runner-base@sha256:..."
`catalyst-deploy manifest` writes, fetches and validates manifests (`fetch TAG FILE`,
`check FILE`) and checks the staging deployment (`staging-deployed FILE`). A successful staging
deployment means that the GitHub Environment `staging` has a successful deployment for the
release tag and its commit; the deploy job records it. The deploy job also requires that the kit
it runs has the Catalyst version the manifest names.
### Pinned package version
The deployment's `package.json` pins every `@work-shape/catalyst-*` dependency to one exact
published version, including the deployment kit and CLI. Commit its own `pnpm-lock.yaml`;
CI installs it frozen and builds from the deployment folder alone. Private npm read auth is
mounted as a BuildKit secret and stays outside the images.
From the deployment repo, bump with the installed kit:
```sh
pnpm exec catalyst-deploy bump 0.8.0
The kit refuses a version missing from npm, updates every Catalyst dependency together,
regenerates `pnpm-lock.yaml` with `--ignore-workspace` and prints the intervening release notes.
Read those notes for config or migration changes, then commit `package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`
together. `catalyst-deploy check` refuses ranges, unequal versions and local package specs.
The manifest records `catalystVersion` and the deployment commit.
Local development from the workspace root keeps source links through the root overrides.
Use `catalyst-deploy pack-local` for images built from unpublished local packages.
## Images
A release has six images, built from `deploy/docker-bake.hcl`:
| Manifest key               | Image                                          | Used by                                 |
| `api`                      | `${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-api`                      | `api`, `agent-run-worker`, `migrate`    |
| `ui`                       | `${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-ui`                       | `ui`                                    |
| `doc-worker`               | `${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-doc-worker`               | `doc-worker`                            |
| `workspace-command-worker` | `${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-workspace-command-worker` | `workspace-command-worker`              |
| `artifact-preview-worker`  | `${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-artifact-preview-worker`  | `artifact-preview-worker`               |
| `runner`                   | `${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-catalyst-runner-base`     | started by the workspace command worker |
`IMAGE_REPOSITORY` comes from `deploy/deployment.env`, for example
`ghcr.io/work-shape/catalyst-acme`. Production Compose names each image as
`${IMAGE_REPOSITORY}-<suffix>:${IMAGE_TAG}@${<NAME>_IMAGE_DIGEST}`. Docker resolves the digest;
the tag only names the release in `docker ps`. Every deploy writes `IMAGE_REPOSITORY`, `IMAGE_TAG`
(the staging release tag) and the six digests into the env file.
The release images come from the kit's `docker/deployment.Dockerfile`.
The images `api`, `ui`, `workspace-command-worker` and `artifact-preview-worker` build in one `docker buildx bake` run, so the dependency install and the server
build run once. The document worker and the runner build in jobs of their own. Images with a slow
system layer keep a registry build cache under the tag `buildcache`.
To build locally, run from the deployment repo:
```sh
docker buildx bake -f deploy/docker-bake.hcl client
The manual workflow `.github/workflows/build-images.yml` runs the same builds from any ref,
without a release and without a deploy. Its input `push_images` defaults to `false`.
## Deploy
The kit README lists what `catalyst-deploy deploy` does on the VM: it pulls the images of the
manifest by digest, backs up the database, migrates, starts the services, rolls the agent-run
worker and runs the upload check. It also checks the API's health, and it fails unless every
service runs the image of the release. Agent-run workers of the previous release that still drain
are the one exception.
The workflow calls it. For the first setup or a break-glass deploy, check out the release tag
and install its frozen dependencies in the deployment repo, so the Compose file and kit match
the release. Then run:
```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-workspace
pnpm exec catalyst-deploy manifest fetch staging-2026.10.07-1 /tmp/release-manifest.json
pnpm exec catalyst-deploy deploy --host staging.chat.example.com --manifest /tmp/release-manifest.json
Earlier schema 1 digest manifests remain readable for rollback. For a release from before the
package switch, use the kit and recovery instructions committed with that release tag.
A deploy is done when every container on the host runs and one signed-in action worked, not when
the script ends.
## Backups
Every deploy puts the kit's `backup-postgres.sh` and `restore-postgres.sh` into the app directory,
`/opt/vivd-catalyst/<instance>`. The kit README says what a backup holds and how `list`, `verify`
and `recover` work. The scripts find the backup bucket in the env file:
- `BACKUP_OBJECT_STORE_ENDPOINT`
- `BACKUP_OBJECT_STORE_BUCKET`
- `BACKUP_OBJECT_STORE_REGION`
- `BACKUP_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`
- `BACKUP_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
Every deploy also writes the systemd unit and timer to `deploy/systemd/` in the app directory.
Install them once, after the first deploy:
```sh
cd /opt/vivd-catalyst/<instance>
sudo cp deploy/systemd/vivd-catalyst-<instance>-backup.* /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now vivd-catalyst-<instance>-backup.timer
The timer runs at 02:15 UTC and writes under the key prefix `postgres/`. A deploy writes under
`pre-deploy/`, with the release tag in the name, before it migrates. Test a restore on staging
before production holds real data: take a backup, verify it in a scratch database and recover from
it.
## Bucket retention
The module `compose-host` sets the same lifecycle rules on both environments. Its defaults:
| Bucket  | Keys                                         | Rule                                                                        |
| backups | `postgres/`, the nightly backups             | deleted 35 days after upload                                                |
| backups | `pre-deploy/`, backups taken before a deploy | deleted 90 days after upload                                                |
| files   | the prefixes the application writes          | versioned; a deleted or overwritten object is removed for good 7 days later |
Hetzner runs lifecycle rules on its own schedule, so an object disappears some time after it
passes its window, not at an exact moment.
Backups:
- The backup bucket is not versioned. An expired backup cannot be recovered.
- A rule matches by key prefix only. A backup gets the 90-day window only when it is uploaded under
`pre-deploy/` (`BACKUP_PREFIX=pre-deploy`). One under `postgres/` expires after 35 days, whatever
its file name says.
- Keys outside both prefixes never expire. Upload backups nowhere else.
- A backup holds every conversation and audit row that existed when it was taken. Data the
application has deleted stays in backups for up to 35 days, or 90 days in a pre-deploy backup.
Files:
- The application deletes an object without naming a version. With versioning that hides the
object and keeps its bytes as a noncurrent version. The lifecycle rule removes that version 7
days later, then the delete marker left behind.
- A file the application has deleted, by a user, by the retention job or with an account, is gone
from the application at once and from storage up to 7 days later. When someone asks how long
files are kept, quote `retention.conversationDays` plus these 7 days, counted as
[Governance](/operate/governance/#retention) describes, not the application's window alone.
- The rule never expires current objects. Only the application removes those.
- A prefix without a rule keeps its deleted objects in the versioned bucket for good. The
application writes uploaded documents under `documents/`, and with the module `apps` on also
Pages under `pages/` and asset files under `assets/`, so the rules have to name all three there.
- To erase a file before the window ends, delete its versions by id, as Hetzner's
[versioning guide](https://docs.hetzner.com/storage/object-storage/howto-protect-objects/protect-versioning/)
describes. To recover a deleted file inside the window, remove its delete marker, or copy the
noncurrent version back onto the same key.
Hetzner specifics, checked against its documentation on 2026-10-06:
- Lifecycle rules support `Expiration` by days, `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` with
`NoncurrentDays` only, `ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker` and `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload`.
- Every rule needs a non-empty key prefix. For a rule without a prefix the `aminueza/minio`
provider sends an `ObjectSizeGreaterThan` filter, which Hetzner does not document.
- The provider (3.38) does not send `abort_incomplete_multipart_upload`, so these rules leave the
parts of a failed backup upload behind.
## Model providers
Before a model provider serves staging or production, run a smoke test against it with synthetic
prompts only, and keep to synthetic data until its residency, processing agreement and retention
controls are approved. An EU endpoint alone proves no residency: the provider account or project
has to be confirmed as EU-resident as well. Provider keys live in the env file of each VM, never
in Git or GitHub. Which providers an instance may use, and the record of each approval, belong to
that instance.
## Local development
A deployment repo starts its local stack with:
```sh
cp .env.example .env
pnpm dev
The development Compose stack runs Postgres, S3Mock, the API, the workers and the interface. Each
deployment repo uses ports of its own, so the stacks of several instances can run at once.
`pnpm dev` fingerprints the dependency manifests, the lockfiles, the Dockerfiles and the Compose
build configuration, and builds images only when one of them changed or an image is missing.
Otherwise it starts the existing images and attaches Compose watch with an initial source sync.
Compose watch copies TypeScript and config changes into the containers, where the API and the
workers run from TypeScript in watch mode and Vite reloads the interface. A source edit therefore
rebuilds no image, also in the document worker.
- `pnpm dev:rebuild` discards the saved fingerprint and rebuilds every development image.
- `pnpm dev:runner` rebuilds the runner image. `pnpm dev` builds it only when its local tag is
missing, so run this after changing the runner Dockerfile or the artifact helpers, then restart
the stack.
- `pnpm dev:db` starts only Postgres and S3Mock.

pages.title: Rights for one person or asset
pages.description: Give one person rights on one asset, and check what a person may do.
body: Instance roles and the rights set on the Users page apply to the whole instance. The page **Instance > Access** is for everything narrower: one person, one kind of asset, one place. It is shown to users who hold `users.manage`, and opens on its first tab, **Rights**; **Check** follows. An instance that still has a Namespace from an earlier release shows a third tab, **Namespaces**, until NS-RETIRE removes them.

Every agent and skill belongs to the instance or to the one Collaboration Workspace it was made in, a Personal or a Shared Workspace. A right in a Shared Workspace covers everything that workspace owns. A right on one asset covers that asset alone.
## Grants

A grant gives one person one action in one place. A Service Principal's grants are written on **Settings > Instance > API access**, not here. The **New right** form takes a person, a kind, a level and the place, and writes one row per action of the level. Each level includes the ones below it: **Use**, **View**, **Edit**, **Publish** and **Delete**, as far as the kind has them. For Workflows and Connections, **View** comes before **Use**: starting a Workflow or calling a Connection acts with the asset's own rights, so a person can be given View without Use, and Use brings View with it. A right that is no level, such as adding rows to a Data Store or reading a Workflow's run data, is ticked on its own under **Further rights**. It offers only rights and places the giver holds. Giving a right or lifting a deny also checks that the giver holds what it would give; nobody changes their own grants.

For agents and skills, the actions are read, write and delete. **In a shared workspace** ("In einem geteilten Arbeitsbereich") covers every asset of that kind the workspace owns, including later ones, and gives no access to its conversations. **On one asset** ("An einem Asset") covers one existing asset. Instance-wide rights for agents and skills stay on the Users page.
Other kinds appear where their modules are on:

- **Connections:** read and use, separately. Reading shows configuration; using permits calls without showing configuration. Both support one Connection or the whole instance. The instance owns every Connection, so the server refuses new workspace grants with `invalid_scope`. Old workspace rows remain recorded until revoked, but cover no instance-owned Connection. Writing, deleting and approving stay with the administrator role. Removing or renaming a release-config Connection removes its allow rows at the next start; write the grants again for a renamed Connection.

- **Apps and Data Stores:** read, write, publish and delete, in one Shared Workspace, on one asset or for the whole instance. A workspace right covers what it owns. Using an App comes from workspace membership. These Data Store rights govern its definition, not access to its rows.
- **Knowledge Bases:** read, use, write, publish and delete, on one asset or for the whole instance.

- **Workflows:** read, use, write, publish and delete, on one asset or for the whole instance. Reading shows the Workflow and its runs; using starts it; writing edits its draft; publishing makes a revision live. Workflows are still instance-owned. Publishing also checks every right of the service principal the revision runs as. A Workflow whose principal holds `config_assets.release` cannot be published. **Read run data** supports one Workflow only and lets a person pass a complete dataset of that Workflow's runs to the inputs of a new Workflow run. Reading still shows only a dataset's row schema, row count and size, never its rows, and downloading a dataset is not available yet. Giving it or lifting a deny checks every right of the principals named by both the draft and published versions.
- **Guardrails:** publish, in one Shared Workspace or for the whole instance, separately from other kinds.

The dialog offers only places supported by every selected action; it hides the place step where only one is supported. Selecting run-data access limits a Workflow right to one asset. Without it, the other Workflow rights can also be given for the whole instance. See [How rights work](/operate/how-rights-work/#grants) for the scope table.
A row the person already has is left as it is, so the same form can be sent again after it stopped half way: it adds what is missing and says how many rows it added and how many were there already.

The list shows one line per person and scope, and says it as a sentence: "may view and edit agents in Kai Spezis", in German "darf in Kai Spezis Agenten ansehen und bearbeiten". A deny is a sentence of its own with the mark "Denied": "may not edit, publish, or delete the agent tax-helper". Each action is revoked from the menu of its line.
A deny is the exception, so the form keeps it behind **Refuse instead** ("Stattdessen verweigern"). A deny refuses the chosen level and every level above it.
- A deny wins over every grant and role that would allow the same action there.
- A deny is not a wall. A person with instance-wide rights can still export a denied agent or set it as the default, because those are decided for the instance.
- Whoever is denied reading or writing an asset cannot delete it.

- A deny on one asset belongs to its name. Deleting the asset removes the allow rows on it and keeps the deny rows. The list then shows the row as "Asset no longer exists". It applies again when an asset with that name is created, and stays until you revoke it.

**Revoke** removes one allow row at once, **Remove deny** one deny row. Rows held by a superadmin are shown to superadmins only. When the person who wrote a row is hidden from you, "Granted by" reads "Not available". A grant for a person whose account is being deleted is refused with "User account is being deleted".

A row on one asset names the asset only for a reader who may read that kind of asset (`config_assets.read`, or `agent.read` or `skill.read` for the instance). Any other reader sees the asset's id and whether the asset still exists. In the API, `scopeAsset.name` is absent for such a reader.
## Check
Choose a person, a kind and an asset, each from a list by its name. For each action the tab says whether it is allowed and what decided:
| Reason           | Meaning                                           |
| Role             | A role the person holds, built in such as Admin or custom such as Buchhaltung, allows or denies it; the reason names the role and where it applies. |
| Individual right | A right set or revoked on the Users page decides. |
| Given right      | A row in a workspace or on the asset allows it.   |
| Deny             | A deny row refuses it.                            |
| No right         | Nothing covers it.                                |
An account that is not active has no rights, whatever its rows say.
The server decides the result, by the same rule that guards every request; the tab only shows it. A row in the workspace that owns the asset counts.
The result is the right alone. A save the tab calls allowed can still be refused for a reason outside rights:
- a changed model setting without `agent_models.manage`
- the first agent of an instance and the last one change the default agent, which needs the instance-wide right to write agents
- agent configuration in the interface is switched off for the instance
A read that is allowed through a grant opens that asset. The overview of all agents and skills and the export need the instance-wide right to read.

The tab gives a result only when it has everything it decides from: the person's rights, the grant rows and the agents and skills of the instance. While one of them loads, or when it could not be loaded, the tab says so and shows no result, because a result without them could miss a deny on one asset. A refusal there names an instance admin to ask, never a page the reader cannot open.
## Effective rights on the Users page

A person's detail on **Instance > Users** shows **Effective rights**: every right the person holds, grouped by kind of asset with the administration last. Each line says where it applies, whether it holds, and where it comes from: a role by its name ("Rolle Buchhaltung"), a right given directly, or a workspace membership. A refused line names the deny that refuses it and, when the deny applies elsewhere, where. The view only reads; rights are changed where they are set.
## API

Every person may read their own effective rights through `permissions.effective`, `permissions.rights` (each right decided, with its origin) and `permissions.check` (one asset), without `users.manage`. Reading another person’s effective rights, origins, check or grant rows requires `users.manage`. A holder of `service_principals.manage` may read a technical account’s effective rights and grant rows; without `users.manage`, a grant-list request must explicitly select `holderKind=service_principal`. This gives no access to people’s rights. Credential scopes still apply.
The page uses the operations under `/api/v1/instance/access`. See the [API reference](/reference/api/).

pages.title: Runner security
pages.description: Security boundary and assumptions for execution workspace runners.
body: `workspace.exec` is a high-risk capability. The product boundary is that agent-authored commands run outside the chat API, inside a short-lived runner with no broad secrets and no network by default.
## Required Boundaries
Runner containers must not receive:
- platform database credentials
- model provider keys
- customer API tokens
- object-store credentials
- the Docker socket
- internal network access
- outbound internet access

The workspace command worker is the trusted control process. It can read and write the exact workspace objects required for a command, then starts the sandboxed runner with only the mounted workspace and bounded environment variables.
## Docker Policy
Every command in a runner container, an agent's command and a Page build alike, is started by one `docker run` call with:
- `--user 10001:10001`: the command is not root
- `--cap-drop ALL` and `no-new-privileges`: no capabilities, and none to gain
- `--network none`
- a read-only root filesystem
- writable `/workspace`, which is the home directory, and tmpfs for `/tmp` and `/var/tmp` owned by the same user
- CPU, memory, and pid limits
- Docker's default seccomp profile
- bounded wall-clock and idle timeouts
- bounded stdout and stderr previews
None of these is a setting. The runner image should contain approved runtimes and artifact helpers at build time. Agents should not install packages dynamically in production.
## The Runner's User

The user id and the group id are both `10001`, the constants `RUNNER_USER_ID` and `RUNNER_GROUP_ID` in `packages/tool-execution/src/docker-workspace-command-runner.ts`. Both runner images create this user as `catalyst-runner` with the home directory `/workspace` and start as it, so a container started by hand is not root either. The ids on `docker run` are numbers, so a runner image of an older release, which has no such user, still runs commands as `10001`.

The worker is root in its own container. Before each command it gives the directory it filled to `10001:10001`, and afterwards reads and removes the files as before. A link in the directory is given away itself and is not followed. If the directory cannot be given away, the command does not start and fails with `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_SPAWN_FAILED`, or the Page build with "could not be started". It never starts as root instead.
What an operator must know:

- **Ownership on the host.** Files under `WORKSPACE_COMMAND_TEMP_ROOT` belong to user `10001` on the host while a command or build runs. Nobody has to create that user or prepare the directory. Do not give the id `10001` to a person or a service on the host.

- **The filesystem must keep ownership.** The directory has to lie on a filesystem where root may change the owner of a file: a local disk or a Docker volume. A network share that maps root to another user (NFS with `root_squash`) refuses it, and every command then fails as described above.

- **No user namespace.** The product does not turn on rootless Docker or user-namespace remapping. Without them, `10001` in the container is `10001` on the host, and root in the worker's container is root on the host. With either turned on, the worker and the runner must run under the same engine so both see the same mapping; this combination is not tested by a release.

- **The worker holds the Docker socket.** Whoever takes over the worker process can start any container and is as powerful as root on the host. The non-root user protects against a command in the runner, not against the worker.
- **A worker that is not root**, as on a developer's machine, cannot give files away. It runs commands as its own user and group instead, and no ownership changes. This case is not root either.
## Page Builds

With the module `apps` on, the same sandbox builds saved Pages. The build is the fixed command `catalyst-page-build` of the runner image, with a temporary directory of its own instead of a workspace. The files of a Page are written by an agent or a person and are not trusted, and the build tools that read them are third-party code. The sandbox is therefore the boundary: nothing of a Page is parsed or run outside it, and what the command writes is read back as untrusted data. See [Page Builds](/operate/deployment/#page-builds).
## Data Handling

Workspace file contents live in managed object storage and are referenced by manifest rows. Command audit events and operator telemetry must record minimized metadata only. Bounded stdout/stderr previews are command result data, not audit data, and should not be projected to users as final content.
Promoted artifacts are managed artifacts scoped to the conversation. Internal workspace files remain hidden from user download surfaces.
## Known Limits

Docker isolation is acceptable for the first dedicated VPS deployment. A command shares the host's kernel, filtered only by Docker's default seccomp profile, and runs without a user namespace. Higher-risk environments may require rootless Docker, user namespaces, an own seccomp profile, gVisor, Firecracker, or a managed sandbox service before enabling `workspace.exec` for sensitive workloads.
Network-enabled execution, package installation, and cross-conversation file libraries are not part of the v1 security model.

pages.title: App bridge v1
pages.description: The messages and calls between an App and the interface that shows it, frozen as version 1.
body: An App, and a Page of a conversation, runs in a sandboxed frame without an origin. It holds no credential and reaches nothing but the interface that shows it. The two talk through the bridge: messages posted between the frame and the interface. The App Kit (`@work-shape/catalyst-app-kit`) is the App's half; an App calls the kit and never posts a message itself.
## Version 1 is frozen
The bridge protocol is version 1. Every message of either side carries `catalystBridge: 1`, and the interface drops a message without it. What this page lists is the contract an App can build on:
- Version 1 is the set of messages and calls listed on this page. Further calls of the platform's bridge design, such as `files.open`, arrive additively within version 1.
- Changes to version 1 are additive only: a new message type, a new call of the kit, or a new optional field. An App written against version 1 keeps working.
- A new call needs a named App that cannot be built without it. It is added as a new member, never by renaming one.
- A breaking change, such as removing or renaming a message, a field or a call, or changing what one means, is version 2. Version 2 runs beside version 1, and the interface keeps answering version 1.
- A kit version is frozen too. An App names the exact kit version it was built with (`kit` in `app.yaml`) and keeps loading those files. A new Page or App names kit 1.6.0.
## Calls of the kit

| Call                                              | What it does                                                                                                                                     |

| `getContext()`                                    | Greets the interface and answers the context below. It waits up to 10 seconds, then rejects: a Page runs inside the platform.                    |

| `onThemeChange(callback)`                         | Calls back with `{ theme, mode }` whenever the colours or the mode of the interface change. Answers the function that stops it.                  |

| `navigate(path)`                                  | Tells the interface the route the App shows.                                                                                                     |

| `resize(height)`                                  | Tells the interface the height of the App's content, in pixels.                                                                                  |

| `actions.call(name, input?, { idempotencyKey? })` | Kit 1.1.0 and later. Calls a named action of the manifest with the viewer's rights. Answers the result below, or rejects with an `AppCallError`. |

| `workflowRuns.get(runId)`                         | Reads a Workflow Run that a `workflow` action of the App started, as the viewer who started it. Kit 1.3.0 and later.                             |

| `useWorkflowRun(runId)`                           | A React hook that reads the run every second until it ended. Kit 1.3.0 and later.                                                                |

| `storage.get(key)` / `storage.set(key, value)`    | Kit 1.6.0. Small JSON state private to the current App and person (64 KiB). A save waits for persistence; shared records belong in a Data Store. |

| `mountApp({ routeTree, element? })`               | Renders a React App with its routes and the look of the interface.                                                                               |

An App reaches a Connection, a Data Store or a Workflow only through a named action in its folder: `actions/<name>.action.yaml` for an operation of a Connection or a Workflow, `actions/<name>.sql` for a statement on a Data Store. Each call goes through the policy, the audit and the viewer's rights.
## Messages the App sends
| `type`          | Fields                                                                                          | Answered with         |
| `ready`         | none                                                                                            | `context`             |
| `navigate`      | `session`, `path` (a route of the App: one leading `/`, no host, at most 2048 characters)       | nothing               |
| `resize`        | `session`, `height` (0 to 100000)                                                               | nothing               |
| `action`        | `session`, `requestId`, `name`, `input` (an object), optional `idempotencyKey`                  | `action_result`       |
| `storage_write` | `session`, `requestId`, `mutation` (`set` with string key/value, `remove` with key, or `clear`) | `storage_result`      |
| `workflow_run`  | `session`, `requestId`, `runId`                                                                 | `workflow_run_result` |

The runtime installs personal storage before App scripts run and supplies its session to storage writes. Every other message after `ready` names the session the interface gave in `context`. A message of another shape, with an unknown key, or naming another session is dropped.
### Retired: `connection_call`

Kits 1.1.0 to 1.3.0 have `connections.call(connection, operation, input)`, which sends `connection_call`; kit 1.0.0 had no call of a Connection, and kit 1.4.0 has none. The free call of a Connection from the browser was removed before version 1 was frozen. The interface answers it at once with an `action_result` whose error is `connection_call_removed`, not retryable, and whose message names the fix: an action file `actions/<name>.action.yaml` with `connection`, `operation` and `effect`, called with `actions.call('<name>', input)`. A call of it that waited for an approval when it was removed is ended when it is approved: it never reaches the Connection, and its run fails with the same message.
## Messages the interface sends
| `type`                | Fields                                                |
| `context`             | `session`, `context`                                  |
| `theme`               | `theme`, `mode`                                       |
| `action_result`       | `session`, `requestId`, `ok`, and `result` or `error` |
| `storage_result`      | `session`, `requestId`, `ok`                          |
| `workflow_run_result` | `session`, `requestId`, `ok`, and `run` or `error`    |

The context holds `viewer` (`kind: member`, `id`, `displayName`), `workspace` (`id`, `name`, or `null`), `locale`, `theme` (seven colours: `surfaceColor`, `backgroundColor`, `textColor`, `mutedTextColor`, `borderColor`, `accentColor`, `accentStrongColor`), `mode` (`light` or `dark`), `pageId`, `fileSetNumber`, `initialRoute`, and `can`: for each action, what a call of the viewer would come to now (`allow`, `confirm`, `approval` or `deny`). `can` is a hint for what the App shows; each call is checked again.
The result of an action is one of:
- `{ runId, status: "done", result }`: the operation ran, and `result` is what it answered.
- `{ runId, status: "pending_approval" }`: the call waits for another person's approval. The run says how it ends.

- `{ status: "dry_run", message, result }` (kit 1.3.0 and later): a draft or a Page of a conversation carried nothing out. `message` is the platform's sentence of what the call would have done; show it as it is.

A run (`workflow_run_result`) holds `id`, `workflow`, `status` (`queued`, `running`, `waiting`, `done`, `failed`, `cancelled` or `limit_reached`), and where known `output` or `outputTruncated`, `error`, `startedAt` and `finishedAt`.

An error holds `code` (such as `action_unknown`, `draft_safe_mode`, `forbidden`, `input_invalid`, `rate_limited` or `connection_call_removed`), `message`, and optionally `right` (the right a `forbidden` call lacks), `retryable` (`false` where the same call cannot come out differently) and `runId`. The kit rejects with an `AppCallError` that carries the same fields. A call nothing answers within 180 seconds rejects with `timeout`.

pages.title: What the release contains
pages.description: What the current release contains.
body: Workshape Catalyst is an early product: configuration keys and package APIs can still change between releases.
## In The Current Release
The open platform contains:
- the chat API under `/api/v1` with streamed agent runs, described by an OpenAPI document, see the [API reference](/reference/api/)
- the standalone chat interface and an embeddable chat widget, with session tokens issued by a host backend
- agents and skills as config assets in the database, edited in Studio or synchronized with the `catalyst` CLI; skills may carry files of any type, and a few skills ship with the platform
- Previews an agent opens in a conversation, and Apps saved from them, with a draft whose changing actions are simulated, **Run live once**, and publishing (module `apps`)
- Workflows with a canvas, test runs, schedules, code steps and a list of runs, acting as a service principal (module `workflows`)
- Connections to remote MCP servers and to REST interfaces read by GET (`http_api`), created in Studio or in release config, with a key entered on the Connection's page (module `connections`)
- Data Stores: one Postgres database per store for Apps and Workflows (module `dataStores`)
- custom code tools through the tool SDK, and capabilities through the capability SDK
- data sources with guarded, read-only Postgres query tools
- generated views, web search and web fetch
- standalone sign-in, service principals with API keys, personal API keys and `catalyst login` (module `personalApiKeys`), roles, individual rights, and grants in a workspace or on one asset
- retention for conversations and audit events, minimized audit events, usage records with budgets and a customer rate card, and rate limits
- modules, mail for invitations and password reset, and the background jobs page
- execution workspaces with a sandboxed command runner, off unless an instance enables them
- approval requests for skill changes that an agent proposes, and for calls the operation policy holds, decided in the Inbox

- guardrails that check saves, operation calls, publishes and approval requests: the operator's floor in release config, and further guardrails written as assets, tested, dry-run and published with the CLI; Studio > Guardrails lists them read-only with their hits
- the chat dock, which keeps a conversation open beside any page
- Docker images, Compose files, an explicit migration step, and the `/health` and `/ready` probes
Document processing, the artifact helper commands for execution workspaces and the private data view are paid capabilities. They are not in the open repository.
Each page of these docs describes the current release unless it says otherwise.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.description: The terms these docs and the interface use, with the German screen names.
body: ## Customer
An organization that uses the agent chat platform for its own internal users and domain workflows.
## User
A person authenticated by a customer application or standalone login path who may interact with the chat.
## Client Instance
A separately deployed product instance for one customer, with its own infrastructure and operational boundary.
## Instance Operator
The party responsible for running a client instance. This may be Workshape or the customer.
## Operated Dedicated Instance
A dedicated instance hosted and maintained by an operator for one customer.
## Self-Operated Instance
A dedicated instance run by the customer in its own infrastructure or chosen hosting environment.
## Customer-Hosted Integration
A customer system, API, MCP server, or data source that a client instance calls but does not operate.
## Client Assembly App
The TypeScript application that imports platform packages, registers client tools, loads release config, and builds the deployable client-specific server image.
## Release Config

Version-controlled configuration deployed with the client assembly app. It sets what needs a deployment to change: modules, model providers and bindings, tool enablement, the guardrail floor, Connections from config, egress, retention, usage policy, mail and infrastructure. Agents, skills, Apps, Workflows and guardrails written as assets are not in it; they live in the database and change at runtime.
## Module

One optional feature of the product with one switch in release config, `modules.<name>.enabled`, such as `apps`, `workflows` or `connections`. The interface lists them under **Settings > Instance > Modules** (German: **Module**). See [Modules](/configure/modules/).
## Workspace

Where your conversations and Apps live. Your **Personal workspace** (German: **Persönlicher Arbeitsbereich**) is yours alone. A **Shared workspace** (listed under **Geteilte Arbeitsbereiche** in German) has members; its owners manage them under **Settings > Workspace** (**Einstellungen › Arbeitsbereich**).
## Studio
The area of the interface where builders make and look after agents, skills, Connections, Data Stores and guardrails. It has the same name in German. Only a person who may read one of these sees it.
## Agent
A configured AI behavior with instructions, model settings, available tools, and skills. Agents live in the database and are edited in Studio or with the CLI.
## Skill

Instructions an agent reads when a task calls for them, as a folder with a `SKILL.md` and optional files. Some skills ship with the platform and are read-only; **Copy to edit** makes an editable copy.
## Preview

What an agent opens beside the chat in one conversation (German: **Vorschau**): an HTML file or an App's folder, built as it is, without a name or a history of its own. Saving it makes it an App: the agent's `app.save`, or **Save as app** (German: **Als App speichern**).
## App

Screens plus named actions that work with data outside a chat, saved in a workspace. An App has a draft and a published revision: members of the workspace see the published one, and changing actions in the draft are only simulated, unless a person who may edit the App uses **Run live once** (German: **Einmal live ausführen**) for one call. See [Build an App](/apps/build/).
## Workflow

A fixed sequence of steps the platform runs without a conversation, started by hand or on a schedule. It acts as one service principal, whoever starts it. A Workflow is drafted, tried with a test run and published. It has its own row in the main rail, **Workflows**.
## Connection

The access to one outside system: a remote MCP server, or a REST interface read by GET (`http_api`). It holds the address and, stored encrypted, one key for everyone who may use it. Agents call the operations it offers once a person has accepted them. In the interface: **Studio > Connections** (German: **Studio › Verbindungen**).
## Data Store
A SQL database the platform hosts for Apps and Workflows, one per store, changed only through the migrations of its definition. In the interface: **Studio > Data stores** (German: **Datenspeicher**).
## Guardrail

A rule that checks an action just before it happens, such as saving an asset, calling an operation or publishing an App, and answers allow, warn, ask for an approval, or block. The operator's floor comes from release config; further guardrails are written as assets and published. In the interface: **Studio > Guardrails** (German: **Studio › Leitplanken**). See [How rights work](/operate/how-rights-work/#guardrails).
## Inbox

Where requests for approval wait: skill changes an agent proposes, and calls that the policy or a guardrail holds. German: **Eingang**. A person who may decide sees **To decide** (**Zu entscheiden**) and **Decided** (**Entschieden**); everyone else sees their own requests.
## Custom Code Tool
A tool implemented with customer-specific code that runs inside the client instance or one of its execution runtimes.
## Embed Surface
The customer-facing integration point that renders chat inside a customer application.
## Conversation
A persisted chat history owned by an authenticated user and retained according to the client instance retention policy.
## Audit Event
A minimized governance record of a security, data, tool, config, or lifecycle action. It is not a full transcript.

pages.title: Your first conversation
pages.description: Pick an agent, start a chat, add files, and find your way around Catalyst.
body: In Catalyst you work with **agents**: assistants set up for a task, such as answering client questions or drafting offers. You talk to one in a chat. The German interface shows the labels in quotes.
## Start a chat
1. Click **New chat** ("Neuer Chat") in the main rail. If your workspace offers only one agent, this starts a chat with it.
2. If your workspace offers more than one agent, the rail also shows **Agents** ("Agenten"). It lists them; pick one to start a chat with it.
3. Type what you need and press Enter.
To add files, click **Add attachment** ("Anhang hinzufügen") or drop them onto the chat.
If the agent offers more than one model, the chat shows a picker with **Model** ("Modell") and **Reasoning** ("Denkaufwand"). More reasoning takes longer and uses more of your quota.
## Find it again

**Recent** ("Zuletzt") in the main rail lists your conversations, and **Search** ("Suchen") finds them. A conversation may be deleted after a while, as your organisation set it; the chat then says "Will be deleted automatically on …" ("Wird am … automatisch gelöscht").
## What appears beside the chat
- When the agent builds something for you, such as a small tool with screens, it shows it beside the chat. You can keep it as an App: see [Apps for people](/automate/apps/).

- When you open a chat from another page, for example with **Edit with the agent** on an App, the chat stays open on the left of that page as you move on. **Close chat** ("Chat schließen") hides it, **Chat** brings it back, and **Open as full chat** ("Als ganzen Chat öffnen") gives it the whole window.
## The rest of the main rail
Which of these you see depends on your rights and your workspace.
- **Apps**: the Apps of your workspace.
- **Workflows**: work the platform does by itself. See [Workflows](/automate/workflows/).
- **Inbox** ("Eingang"): requests waiting for an approval.
- **Studio**: where agents, skills and connections to other systems are made. It shows only for people who build them. On an agent's card, **Edit in Studio** ("Im Studio bearbeiten") opens it there.

- Your name at the bottom of the rail opens **Profile** ("Profil") and **Language and appearance** ("Sprache und Darstellung"). Your **API keys** ("API-Schlüssel") are on the same Settings page. Workspace owners and administrators also get a **Settings** ("Einstellungen") button.
Next: [Workspaces](/start/workspaces/).

pages.title: Workspaces
pages.description: Your personal workspace, shared workspaces, and who sees what.
body: A workspace is where your conversations and Apps live. The German interface shows the labels in quotes.
- Your **personal workspace**, shown as "Anna's workspace" ("Annas Arbeitsbereich"), is yours alone.
- A **shared workspace** has members. Its conversations, agents and Apps are there for the team.
## Switch, create or join
Open the workspace menu in the main rail (**Switch workspace**, "Arbeitsbereich wechseln").
- Pick a workspace to switch to it. The rail then shows its agents, Apps and conversations.
- **Create** ("Erstellen") makes a new shared workspace. You are its owner.
- **Browse** ("Durchsuchen") lists the shared workspaces you may find. **Request access** ("Zugriff anfragen") asks their owners to let you in.
## Who sees what

In a shared workspace the owners choose, under **Settings > Workspace > General**, whether **New conversations are** ("Neue Unterhaltungen sind") **Private to their author** or **Visible to the workspace** ("Für den Arbeitsbereich sichtbar"). A change applies to new conversations only.
Published Apps of a workspace are open to all its members. Which agents a workspace offers is set in Studio.
## Manage members
Owners manage a shared workspace under **Settings > Workspace** ("Einstellungen › Arbeitsbereich"):

- **Members** ("Mitglieder"): **Add member** ("Mitglied hinzufügen"), give someone the role **Owner** ("Besitzer"), **Admin** ("Administrator") or **Member** ("Mitglied"), or remove them. Open access requests wait here too.
- **General** ("Allgemein"): the name, whether the workspace is **Discoverable** ("Auffindbar") or **Private** ("Privat"), and who sees new conversations.
